chapters.title: Chapter 1: A History of Research on Nonverbal Communication: Our Divergent Pasts and Their Contemporary Legacies

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: Six Heritages of Nonverbal Research
assets.visual_frame_description: A video-scrubber interface runs along the chapter's history: frames show a 1959 copy of The Silent Language, the 1970 Kinesics and Context, and a 1978 FACS diagram, while a caption bar updates with each scholar's name and heritage color as you drag the playhead.
assets.player_mission: Scan Manusov's timeline of the field and scrub through each heritage - rhetorical, linguistic, sociological, cultural, ethological, and psychological. Match each founding scholar and landmark book (Darwin, Hall, Birdwhistell, Goffman, Ekman, Mehrabian) to the heritage it seeded, then flag the one-line claim that best summarizes each tradition's legacy.
key_concepts: The chapter charts six heritages of nonverbal communication research: rhetorical, linguistic, sociological, cultural, ethological, and psychological.
Manusov argues that each heritage takes researchers along certain paths that provide only a partial view of the large and varied field.
The rhetorical heritage is most well-known among communication scholars, while the psychological heritage is more likely to be followed by psychologists.
Charles Darwin's 1872 book The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals helped set a trajectory for the ethological heritage.
E. T. Hall's 1959 book The Silent Language engaged his ideas around variance in nonverbal displays based in culture.
Goffman's 1959 book The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life brought attention to the interactive functions that nonverbal cues may serve.
Ray Birdwhistell's 1970 book Kinesics and Context treated body motion as a learned form of communication patterned within a culture.
Ekman and Friesen created the Facial Action Coding System in 1978 as an elaborate research tool for the measurement of facial movement.
Nancy M. Henley put forward the subordination hypothesis in 1977, proposing that male-female behavioral differences align with high and low status or power.
The conclusion notes that certain heritages are tied to certain intellectual areas and shape what scholars include or miss in their individual inquiries.
Manusov states that the study of nonverbal communication has a rich history that runs both deep and wide.
Seeing the heritages as a broad set of research programs meant to understand the myriad modes of communicating makes them all worth illuminating.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Dialogue with the Rhetorical and Linguistic Heritages: Bodies, Codes, and Syntax
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen film reels room shows two looped black-and-white clips of everyday scenes; beside them a taxonomy board fills in with kinesic categories, while a speech-toast dialogue bubble quotes Burke's somatic line of inquiry and a glossary chip flips between haptics, tacesics, and chronemics.
assets.player_mission: Step into a film-analysis dialogue with the early field: review frame-by-frame footage the way Birdwhistell and his colleagues did, and reconstruct the kinesics categories from a mother changing a diaper and a woman lighting a cigarette. Then debate whether a speaker's delivery, as Quintilian and Burke saw it, is symbolic action or mere style, and code touch and time cues with the heritage's linguistic labels.
key_concepts: Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria, written circa 90 CE, treated the delivery of a speech as a rhetorical moment when nonverbal cues were seen as essential to persuading the audience.
Hawhee (2009) revealed that Kenneth Burke portrayed rhetoric as symbolic action rather than only the study of language form and features.
Burke looked to the body and its movements as what he called a somatic, physical line of inquiry with representational and transformational value.
Cole's 1999 book About Face gave examples of people who lost the ability to move their faces or who have facial deformities that affect how human others think they are.
Bixler (2010) found that moving the body, rather than just giving money, became an important symbolic activity for breast cancer walkers.
Birdwhistell opened Kinesics and Context with the conviction that body motion is a learned form of communication patterned within a culture and breakable into an ordered system of isolable elements.
Birdwhistell and colleagues reviewed a data corpus ranging from a mother changing her baby's diapers to a scene of a couple where the woman lit and smoked her cigarette.
Birdwhistell proposed an elaborate set of categories that characterized the movements he witnessed, which he called kinesics.
For Birdwhistell, meaning is not created a priori but is understood within its context and is a social endeavor conducted between people.
The linguistic heritage produced labels that mirror linguistics, such as calling touch cues haptics or tacesics and referencing time features as chronemics.
E. T. Hall proposed that proxemics, the use of space as communication, is rule-governed and meaningful yet takes forms that vary across groups and cultures.
Gottman and his colleagues built the Specific Affect Coding System upon the Facial Action Coding System and used it to help predict divorce.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Audit the Sociological and Cultural Heritages: Interaction, Meaning, and Community
assets.visual_frame_description: An observation-room console with a two-way mirror shows a conversation being coded into colored function tags as it happens; beside it a culture card rack holds a Finnish silence code, a clock-gift dilemma, and a contact-versus-noncontact proxemic chart, with a verdict stamp that drops onto each audited cue.
assets.player_mission: Run a live audit of an interaction: observe a doctor-patient gaze sequence the way conversation analysts do, tag each nonverbal act for its function (interaction management, relational message, impression management), and check every cue against the cultural rulebook of a high-context community. Verdict each behavior as serving social order, reflecting relationship appraisal, or encoding cultural meaning, and note where cross-group misunderstanding can arise.
key_concepts: Albert Scheflen provided foundational work on nonverbal communication that initially focused on kinesics and rejected the idea that behaviors are a direct reflection of a person or his or her state of mind.
Scheflen's grounding premise focused on social order and meaning, which he referenced as a communicational point of view.
Conversation analysts study nonverbal cues as they occur in everyday interaction with an emphasis on how the behaviors act in interaction and what they do for the interactants.
Robinson (2006) showed the inseparability of nonverbal and verbal behavior by examining the gaze patterns of physicians and their patients.
Goffman's 1963 book Stigma examined how problematic bodies alter the social system and the forms of engagement within them.
Goffman argued that people are meaning-making creatures who develop and alter their sense of themselves and the world through their engagements with others.
Burgoon and Hale (1984) called relational messages the nonverbal cues that reflect how interactants appraise the relationship between them.
Relational messages comment on interactants' intimacy or their power vis-a-vis one another and can sometimes change relationships through nonverbal means.
Gerry Philipsen is credited with bringing the ethnographic form to the study of communication, work referred to as the Ethnography of Communication.
E. T. Hall noted that high-context cultures are particularly nonverbal in that less of their social meaning is encoded in what they say to one another.
Hall (1966) divided cultures into contact and noncontact groups, with contact cultures more likely to engage in touch and to have smaller proxemic zones.
Matsumoto and Kupperbusch (2001) found that U.S. women who were more collectivistic tended to mask their negative emotions when communicating with others.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Ethological Universals versus Psychological Mind
assets.visual_frame_description: A glowing decision matrix grid fills a laboratory wall; cards float in and settle into cells labeled universal-biological versus cognitive-individual, while three animated figure silhouettes illustrate spontaneous eye-widening, a pseudospontaneous acted surprise, and a symbolic thumbs-up, each snapping to its stream column.
assets.player_mission: Build a two-axis matrix that pits universal, biologically based claims (Darwin's legacy, universal emotions, adaptive value) against individual and cognitive claims (automatic processing, personality links, rapport, thin slices). Drop each evidence card - deaf-blind children's expressions, FACS-based smile distinctions, Milgram's status experiments, Henley's subordination hypothesis - into the correct cell, and sort Buck's spontaneous, pseudospontaneous, and symbolic streams into their columns.
key_concepts: Darwin's The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals relies on the study of animals, at least to some degree and usually within context, to understand human behavior.
Floyd (2006) suggested an evolutionary approach to nonverbal research, one brand within the ethological heritage, for which Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection is most salient.
Ethological and evolutionary studies assume that certain nonverbal cues will occur universally, as they are based in who we are as humans.
Ekman, Matsumoto, and their colleagues showed that people from an array of cultural backgrounds all can decode particular facial expressions accurately.
Basic or primary emotions expressed the same way across cultures include happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, and disgust.
Children who are hearing or sight impaired, or limbless, still express universally recognized emotions they could not learn through sensory experience.
Ekman's 1977 introduction of display rules highlighted the role that culture plays even within work on the universality of expression.
Fridlund and Russell (2006) argued that facial movements should be viewed as a social tool that communicates attitude, acknowledgment, and agreement.
Buck and VanLear (2002) described three co-occurring streams: spontaneous cues, pseudospontaneous cues, and symbolic cues such as an okay thumbs up.
Buck (1984) provided evidence that the different streams of behavior are neurologically processed differently.
Gifford (2006) noted that physiognomists have been certain since Aristotle's time that they can discern personality solely from a person's facial features, an approach firmly discredited over time.
Rosenthal (1974) showed that expectancies show up in nonverbal communication and may work as a self-fulfilling prophecy in classrooms and research laboratories.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Boss Level: The Cross-Cultural versus Universal Showdown
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena where a towering split figure represents the nature-nurture clash: one half pulses with a FACS muscle map and an animal-mother scene, the other half with a Finnish silence rite and a classroom expectancy experiment; answer prompts raise or lower a verdict scale until the two halves merge into a single heritage map.
assets.player_mission: Confront the field's central controversy head-on: decide whether emotional expressions are universal and biologically based or socially and culturally derived. Weigh competing evidence - display rules, the social-tool argument, developmental and sensory-deprivation studies, and the relational-skills research - then issue a verdict that reconciles the heritages and maps how method evolved from naturalistic observation to coding systems and thin-slice experiments.
key_concepts: The biggest legacy of the ethological heritage is controversy regarding the degree to which emotional expressions are as universal and biologically based as they may appear.
Research grounded in the cultural and sociological traditions features the social and cultural influences that complement or supersede biology.
Motley (1993) provided evidence that facial cues are most typically in the form of communicative interjections suggesting agreements, queries, and concerns.
Andersen (2008) argued that only spontaneous cues should be called nonverbal communication, with the rest better seen as part of language.
Researchers query whether nonverbal cues are processed automatically or with greater awareness and control, creating a heated battle over the nature of nonverbal behaving.
Ambady and Rosenthal (1993) showed how little it can take, observing thin slices of interaction, to judge certain states or traits accurately.
Tickle-Degnen (2006) defined rapport as a meaningful human experience of close and harmonious connection that involves common understanding.
Rapport is established through nonverbal expressivity, positive affect, and the coordination of behavior, and brings a wide range of social benefits.

Judith A. Hall and her colleagues asserted that the vertical dimension of power has little support in explaining sex differences in behavior, which are better explained by how males and females are skilled differently.
Duke and Nowicki (2005) focused on particular, often congenital, conditions such as dyssemia that make communicating nonverbally difficult.
Segrin (2000) focused on more transitory states such as depression and the influence they have on people's use of nonverbal skills.
The psychological heritage allows researchers to see where real differences lie and to show where stereotypes may exist, because people often perceive more connection than research suggests exists.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Life and Times of Nonverbal Communication Theory and Research: Past, Present, Future

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: Two Traditions from Darwin to the Computer-Vision Era
assets.visual_frame_description: A video-scrubber console spans the chapter's history: the playhead ticks from 1872 through the 1960s tipping point into today, and each stop lights up a card with the theory's name, its scholars, and a figure icon - a FACS face grid, two overlapping tradition circles, a cowbird display, or a lens diagram - while a caption bar states the milestone.
assets.player_mission: Drag the scrubber across Keating's timeline of the field and tag each landmark - Darwin's 1872 expression book, Tomkins, Ekman and Izard's basic emotions, Bateson and Birdwhistell's system theory, Fridlund's behavioral ecology, the status cues perspective, Brunswik and Scherer's lens models, Zebrowitz's affordances, and Patterson's parallel process model - as belonging to the emotion tradition or the communication tradition, then flag the quote or event that marks each era's turning point.
key_concepts: The chapter traces two distinguishable scholarly traditions: one emphasizing affective states underlying expression, and the second emphasizing communication as an interactive process contextualized by social relationships and social motives.
Knapp (2006) considered the 1960s a tipping point in the modern incarnation of nonverbal communication research, and Knapp, Hall, and Horgan (2014) described it as a nuclear explosion of the topic.

Silvan S. Tomkins persisted in studying human emotion from a Darwinian perspective despite World War II and Skinnerian psychology, and his ideas gathered steam in the late 1960s and 1970s as Paul Ekman, Cal Izard, and their colleagues synergized the field.
Ekman, Sorenson, and Friesen's (1969) seminal research on cross-cultural facial expressions of emotion was published in Science, and Izard (1971) published his findings in The Face of Emotion.
Irenaeus Eibl-Eibesfeldt (1972), a student of ethologist Konrad Lorenz, published his extensive work on culture and nonverbal communication in Hinde's (1972) edited volume Nonverbal Communication.
van Hooff (1972) argued compellingly that the primate grin face and the human smile are homologous.
Hewes (1973) argued in Current Anthropology that gesture was at the root of human language, an idea that survives in new forms today.
E. O. Wilson's (1975) Sociobiology carried the central message that human and nonhuman social behavior fit patterns shaped by natural selection.
Dennett's (1978) Brainstorms maintained that the behavioral displays of animals reflect social intentions akin to those inferred for humans.
Today, nonverbal communication skill is believed essential to emotional intelligence and, for better or worse, to charismatic leadership.
Although the central foci of the two traditions are discernibly different, they share substantial overlap: some theorists have operated within each tradition, whereas others have blended them.
Signaling intentions and status was a way to avoid costly, physical confrontations and to enhance biological fitness because signaling was less risky and energetically cheap.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Dialogue with Darwin, Ekman, and Izard: The Emotion-and-Expression Tradition
assets.visual_frame_description: A study-room scene faces three portrait busts - Darwin, Ekman, and Izard - that lean in as you ask questions; behind them a wall fills with posed facial photos, a FACS muscle diagram, and a cross-cultural map with pins in Papua New Guinea, while counter-argument cards from Russell and Widen slide in from the side.
assets.player_mission: Hold a dialogue across a century of emotion research: question Darwin about his 1872 expressive categories and his evidence for universality, press Ekman and Izard about their basic emotions and the display rules that bend expression to culture, then confront the critiques - Russell's methods worries, Widen and Russell's disgust-as-anger children, and the orgasm-versus-pain face puzzle - and decide how tightly emotion and expression are really tied.
key_concepts: Darwin published The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals in 1872 and envisioned core human expressive categories including joy, grief, fear, surprise, anger, contempt, disgust, pride, and shame.
Darwin linked blushing to shame and considered it to be the most human of all expressions.

Darwin took his core set of expressions to be universal, offering as evidence that they each appear early in life, are evident among blind-born people, and can be found in every culture, and he attributed their ubiquity to genetic inheritance.

Darwin described an evolution of expression separate from emotion itself, arguing that expressive elements evolved sometimes as functions of the nervous system, sometimes as serviceable habits, and sometimes because display elements made counter responses unlikely.
Darwin observed that the two expressive hallmarks of disgust, the wrinkling of noses and tongue protrusions, were linked to common sources for feelings of disgust.
Ekman and Izard took strong, universalist positions, arguing that basic categories of emotion were common to humankind and therefore had shared expressive features.
Izard (1971), who studied infants, included an emotion he designated as interest, and eventually Ekman, following Darwin's lead, added contempt to his basic six.

Precise study of the facial movements accompanying different emotions led to the eventual development of the Facial Action Coding System (Ekman & Friesen, 1978), which proved to be a valuable coding tool for researchers.
Researchers identified cultural habits of expression, or display rules, that modified the communication value of expressions, with these modifications often induced by social contexts.

The idea that both face and body are potential sources of leaked emotion and deception clues has pop culture appeal, as evidenced by the popular Fox TV series Lie to Me, which is based on the Ekman group's research on deception.

Research pioneers in lie detection began by analyzing frame-by-frame videotapes of clinical patients, and more recent success has been achieved by identifying split-second, microexpressions that presumably flag true, underlying emotion.

The uniformity of cross-cultural emotion results depends to some degree on methodology, and generally the more constrained the procedures, the greater the agreement, so some question whether the most basic universalist assumptions are fully supported by the available data.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Audit the Communication-Process Traditions: Interaction, Ecology, and Status
assets.visual_frame_description: An observation console shows a therapist-client session being coded into kinesic and proxemic tags as it runs, a waveform ticks under a speech clip to catch gesture timing, and a three-panel evidence wall displays Rothstein's cowbird sequence, a women-in-a-bar flirting clip, and CEO facial-width photos, each waiting for an audit stamp.
assets.player_mission: Run a live audit of each communication-based approach: code a therapist-client session the way Scheflen and the systems theorists did, time gestures against words the way Bavelas and Chovil did, score the behavioral ecology view against the status cues perspective, and check whether naive judges' cues match Gifford's valid head-nod signal. Issue a verdict on which approach best explains a flirting scene, a cowbird display, and a leadership photo.
key_concepts: At Stanford, anthropologists Gregory Bateson and Ray L. Birdwhistell and, later, psychiatrist Albert E. Scheflen embraced a new, holistic, systems-theory perspective on human interaction.
Scheflen (1974) expressed that we could not find meaning in words any more than we could find consciousness in a nerve cell or love in a gonad.

Scheflen's analyses breathed life into the study of kinesics, proxemics, and paralanguage, and, contrary to predecessors such as Birdwhistell and Hall, they incorporated what was known at the time about nonhuman primate communication.
Researchers deciphered patterns of nonverbal behaviors that regulated interaction, including greeting and leave-taking, and conversation.
An analysis of more than 1,700 gestures embedded in speech revealed that 70% of them were associated with words simply by timing and not by intrinsic meaning.

Human courtship behavior is a lot about timing: characteristics of motion such as the speed of offset and onset of behaviors, rather than the specific behaviors themselves, predict female interest in males.

From the behavioral ecology view, social motives are better predictors of facial displays in real-life interactions than are emotions, and automatic readouts of emotion would be expected to be rare and deception much more common.

Rothstein (1980) determined that the appeasement elements in cowbirds' displays allowed the signalers to appraise the aggressiveness of invaders, so the cowbirds were assumed to feel neither angry nor fearful, though they acted like it.
Observations of women in bars reveal that flirting combines nonverbal signals of dominance and submissiveness that signal coyness and are likely meant to invite qualified approach.

The status cues perspective holds that static, age-related signals in the structure and features of the face are carriers of status information that convey dominance, which signals threat, and submissiveness, which invites approach.
Keating and Bai (1986) showed that U.S. preschoolers selected male and female adult faces with broad jaws and receded hairlines as people who tell others what to do.

Facial width-to-height ratios predict perceptions of competence and leadership among corporate leaders, and Fortune 500 corporate profits can be predicted from the facial widths of their chief executive officers.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Lens Models, Affordances, and the Social-Cognitive Engine
assets.visual_frame_description: A luminous matrix grid fills the wall, with cards for lens, affordance, and parallel-process models drifting into their cells; a demonstration row shows Gifford's head-nod slippage, baby-faced adults judged weak and kind, Rosenfeld's chameleon-like participants, and a two-track animation of Patterson's controlled and automatic channels running side by side.
assets.player_mission: Build a two-axis matrix sorting the remaining communication-side theories: place Brunswik's probabilistic functionalism and Scherer's modified lens model, Gibson's affordances and Zebrowitz's baby-faced overgeneralization, Rosenfeld's social-goal experiments, and Patterson's parallel process model into cells defined by perception-versus-signal and conscious-versus-automatic processing, then predict how each framework explains error in person perception.
key_concepts: Brunswik (1955) argued that perceptual systems were adapted to their environments by expectancies established through experience in a particular ecology, and his probabilistic functionalism meant that perception operated probabilistically.
Perceivers need only beat the odds some percentage of the time to come away with a winning, perceptual hand, so a certain degree of error was to be expected in social perception.

Gifford (1994) found that communicators who scored high on personality measurements of warmth and agreeableness frequently nodded their heads during interactions, but naive observers actually deployed several postural cues that were unassociated with the communicators' dispositions.

Theorists have applied lens models to vocal quality signals, rapport, mimicry, and deception, and because the approach can distinguish between what is expressed and what is detected, it has also been applied to emotional expression.

Scherer and his colleagues applied a modified version of Brunswik's lens model to their appraisal theory of emotion, allowing the signaler's expressive behavior to be considered separately from the beholder's perception and inference.

Scherer and colleagues demonstrated that expressors do not display, and perceivers do not utilize, facial action units at the level of precision or reliability that theorists such as Ekman predict, although recognition accuracy for emotions remained high.
The ecological theory of social perception, developed in the 1980s, holds that facial structure conveys affordances, defined as opportunities for certain types of interactions.
Baby-faced adults are perceived as having characteristics associated with babies - dependent, weak, and kind - whereas mature facial appearances make individuals look dominant, strong, and cunning.
Affordance-based perceptual habits can become self-fulfilling prophecies, as targets conform to social expectations created by their physical appearances.
Zebrowitz and her colleagues incorporated connectionist modeling techniques and used dynamic as well as static stimuli in support of the affordances perspective.

Rosenfeld's (1965, 1966) experiments showed that participants were chameleon-like: their gestures, postures, expressions, and use of interpersonal space were transformed by the explicit, social goal operating at the time.
Patterson's (1999, 2006) parallel process model attempts to expose the ways controlled and automatic processes operate in tandem in the production of nonverbal communication.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Why Nonverbal Systems Err - Overgeneralization, Sloppiness, or Design?
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena is dominated by three towering positions - a baby-faced overgeneralization column, a sloppy lens column, and a hard-read deception shield - with thin-slice judgment clips of faces flashing in seconds-long loops; answering correctly charges a portal marked with high-speed cameras, virtual reality headsets, and motion-detection gear that leads to the chapter's future.
assets.player_mission: Face the chapter's closing question: why do we make mistakes when judging the feelings, personalities, intentions, lies, and truths of conspecifics? Weigh the Gibsonian affordances answer (error is overgeneralization), the lens model answer (probabilistic sloppiness), and the behavioral ecology answer (imprecision is strategic, since being a hard read has evolutionary advantage), then issue a verdict on the future of error research armed with the tools of the computer-vision era.
key_concepts: Only brief samples of nonverbal behavior, thin slices lasting just seconds, are needed to create impressions of one another.
Thin slices lead to consensus about the likely trustworthiness and altruism of others, but the trouble is that the impressions themselves are not always to be trusted.

From the Gibsonian affordances platform, error is the result of overgeneralization: perceivers perseverate in making inferences based on attunements appropriate in other contexts, such as age and anger.
Lens model theorists argue that the sloppy, probabilistic shaping of encoding and decoding systems is to blame for mistakes in nonverbal judgment.
Both the basic emotions and Gibsonian affordances theoretical positions have harnessed the power of cross-cultural, cross-species, developmental, and multidisciplinary approaches to make their case.

Basic, prototypical emotion facial expressions generate impressive agreement and consistency in how they are perceived across cultures, but expressers around the world rarely display them in actual, social situations.
From a behavioral ecology perspective, being a hard read, especially to outsiders, might lend an evolutionary advantage, both proximately and ultimately.

The behavioral ecology view predicts ingroup advantages to encoding and decoding nonverbal signals, as is evident in humans and in the special, nonverbal dialects that develop among family groups in other species.
Future research should investigate error patterns and imprecision in nonverbal communication to better understand its complex role in human sociability.

Increasingly sophisticated technologies such as high-speed, high-definition digital recording, motion-detecting cameras, virtual reality headsets, and even Google glasses make studying nonverbal communication in its natural habitat feasible.

Nonverbal communication is no longer the disdained, nameless, orphan child of psychology that Burgoon described it to be in 1980, and today it belongs to the family of important, human psychological processes.

Keating's early plan as a graduate student was to photograph a range of emotions on the faces of everyday people, but her lens captured only one instance of true emotion, the stricken face of a man standing outside his burning house with his dog still inside, teaching her that studying public expression reveals much about communication but little about emotion.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: Signs, Signals, Symbols, and Darwin's Principles
assets.visual_frame_description: A savanna diorama at dusk shows labeled behaviors floating over a crowd of hunter-gatherers - raised eyebrows, a wink, a perfume bottle, a snarling face - each tagged VOLUNTARY or INVOLUNTARY. A three-column ledger (Sign | Signal | Symbol) glows as you drag each behavior into place, while a dual meter tracks its survival value against its reproductive value, and Darwin's three principles scroll across a chalk-stone panel.
assets.player_mission: Drag the scrubber across the chapter's foundation layer and classify each nonverbal behavior - raised fear eyebrows, a deliberate wink, perfume, a snarl, an emblem gesture - as a sign, a signal, or a symbol, and mark whether it is voluntary or involuntary. Then tag each behavior with the Darwinian principle (serviceable habits, antithesis, or nerve force) that best explains its design, and rate its value for survival versus reproductive fitness.
key_concepts: The vast majority of human existence on the planet has been in the hunter-gatherer world of more than 100,000 years ago, so the nonverbal behaviors we see today did not evolve to meet the challenges of today such as electronic communication.

Analyses of the skeletons of humans found in ancient cities suggest that close to 30% of males died from homicide, and up to 25% of males in some preliterate, indigenous rain forest peoples died from homicide even into the 1970s.

Two characteristics of human beings are most amenable to survival: a hard-wired response system that motivates behavior without much contemplation, and living in groups, which permits aid when ill, allies in war, shared resources such as food, and remote warnings for danger.
Signs are defined as part of an experience, or the physical reaction to a stimulus, absent of meaning or information, and typically they are not intentionally produced by a sender.

Signals communicate information about one's experience or reaction to a stimulus, and they can be intentionally produced, as when someone deliberately fabricates signs of anger to signal a different but not felt emotional state.
Symbols are signs external to the individual used to connote symbolic information, and the determination of whether a sign is a signal or a symbol is often in the eyes of the beholder.

Darwin identified three principles underlying the production of facial expressions that underscore their evolutionary roots: the principle of serviceable habits, the principle of antithesis, and the principle of nerve force.

The principle of serviceable habits argued that the precise configuration of an expression served the purpose of the particular emotion, as when anger moves blood to the upper body to prepare to fight and fear moves blood to the legs to facilitate escape.

The principle of antithesis argued that for some emotions their adaptation was to appear opposite, or at least distinctly different, to another emotion so as not to confuse the two, as with the dog that makes itself small when submitting to its pack leader.

The principle of nerve force meant that the impulse for the emotion expression is involuntary, and Darwin further argued that because of this nerve force one cannot fully mimic a genuine emotional expression, as some facial muscles are harder to move deliberately.
Research suggests there are anywhere from five to nine basic human emotions, with most researchers settling on seven: anger, contempt, disgust, fear, enjoyment, sadness/distress, and surprise.

Ekman and Cordaro stipulated up to 12 criteria for determining the evolutionary underpinnings of an emotion, including distinctive universal signals, distinctive physiology, distinctive appearance developmentally, presence in other primates, quick onset, brief duration, and unbidden occurrence.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Dialogue with the Expresser: Reading the Face, Voice, and Body
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen observation room shows the expresser's face with live muscle-action readouts, a voice waveform that spikes in pitch, and a full-body skeleton display tracing forward lean, arm swing, and step length. On the other side, a grid of seven emotion cards waits to be matched, and a rewind reel slows a 0.2-second microexpression that flickers across the face mid-sentence.
assets.player_mission: Confront a live expresser and match each of the seven basic emotions to its facial configuration, vocal pattern, and bodily action tendency, then decide which of the expresser's behaviors are involuntary signs of felt emotion and which are deliberate signals. Watch the slow-motion replay of a concealed anger episode and catch the microexpression that leaks out before the voluntary motor systems regain control of the face.
key_concepts: Emotions affect the autonomic nervous system, which by altering heart rate, blood pressure, blood flow, and sweat glands produces the sensations we know as emotions.

Anger moves blood to the upper body and increases muscle tension to prepare to fight and/or attack, whereas fear moves blood to the large muscles of the legs to facilitate escape and increases sweat to improve the grip in hands and feet.
Disgust slows the heart rate and prepares the body to eject some ingested item, or stops the person from ingesting altogether.

In anger, the eyebrows lower and the upper eyelids raise in a glare, narrowing focus onto the object or individual that needs to be removed or potentially attacked, while the lips narrow to move out of the way so a bite can be executed.
In fear, the eyebrows and the upper eyelids raise, permitting more information to enter the perceptual realm of the individual to enable maximum information processing to assess any potential danger.
Disgust involves the wrinkling of the nose and raising of the upper lip, a response purported to reduce the sensory information of a potentially sickening ingestible item.

When individuals pose a fear expression, the amount of sinus cavity surface area expands compared to a neutral face, while a posed disgust face reduces the sinus cavity surface area, just as Darwin had predicted.

The pyramidal motor system drives voluntary facial actions and originates in the cortical motor strip, whereas the extrapyramidal motor system drives the more involuntary, emotional facial actions and originates in the subcortical areas of the brain.

When an emotion is triggered, the subcortical area sends an involuntary ballistic-like signal to the facial nerves, and when the subcortical impulse is strong enough the expression will leak onto the face very briefly before voluntary motor systems regain control, a process that is the biology of a microexpression.

Spontaneous emotional expressions tend to have dynamic qualities different from deliberate, false emotional signals, such as smoother onsets, more symmetry, and a circumscribed duration lasting between 0.5 and 5 seconds.

Anger is associated with more forward body lean and greater arm swing (attack), whereas fear has shorter steps and less forward lean (to retreat), and the body expression of pride features upward posture with arms and hands upward, whereas defeat or shame features the body bent downward.

Most studies show an increase in pitch for anger and fear in the voice, but a universal vocal signature for each emotion remains elusive, although vocal signs of anger, fear, happiness, and sadness are judged accurately both within and across cultures.

assets.topic: Audit the Evidence: Universality, the Blind, and Posed versus Spontaneous
assets.visual_frame_description: A forensic lab table holds three evidence folders labeled Born Blind, Cross-Cultural, and Posed versus Spontaneous, plus a claim-board pinned with Darwin's three principles. Each claim card flips open to reveal its studies - Minangkabau autonomic data, Ekman's cross-cultural judgment studies, Susskind's sinus cavity findings, the Moebius syndrome patients - and a verdict stamp slams down onto the card.
assets.player_mission: Run a forensic audit of the chapter's central claims: review the evidence from people born blind, from cross-cultural judgment studies of face and voice, and from the posed-versus-spontaneous distinction, then stamp each claim SUPPORTED, CHALLENGED, or UNRESOLVED. Pay special attention to the Moebius syndrome case and the rhesus monkey with a severed facial nerve, and decide how strong the case is that expressions are part of our wiring.
key_concepts: Emotional expressions are expected to develop regardless of social learning opportunities, and research evidence supports this in those born blind, including studies of congenital blind children by Galati and colleagues and Matsumoto and Willingham.
The Minangkabau people, a matrilineal, Muslim society in Indonesia, show the same autonomic nervous system patterns for the same emotions as university students in the United States.
Research shows that emotions are not necessarily exclusive to humans, as chimpanzees, rats, and other mammals also have emotions and corresponding brain circuits.
A plethora of research has repeatedly found high agreement rates across all cultures between particular facial expressions and their emotion sign in judgment studies.

A comprehensive review of the literature showed that the vocal signs of anger, fear, happiness, and sadness were judged accurately both within and across cultures, with the highest agreement for anger and sadness and the lowest for happiness, which is opposite to what judgment studies of the face show.

Almost all of the judgment studies of facial expressions of emotion, starting with Darwin and restarting with Tomkins, used posed expressions, in which individuals posed with facial expressions resembling anger, contempt, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise even though they were not actually experiencing those emotions.
Research shows that acting emotions in the voice is quite effective, and people can recognize the emotion attempted at rates greater than 70% agreement.

Adults with Moebius syndrome, who cannot express through their faces, still feel and experience emotions, but their social lives are often disrupted by their inability to produce signs that signal their emotional states to others.

A controlled study of a Rhesus monkey that had its facial nerve surgically severed and was then returned to a social group showed that the monkey lost its place in the social hierarchy and had more aggression turned toward it.

The research documenting differences between posed and spontaneous facial expressions was reliable enough that prior to modern soft tissue imaging technology, observations of the two types of expressions served as the primary diagnostic criteria for certain brain lesions.
Later work has shown that individuals do show emotions even when they deliberately attempt to conceal them, in studies of deception such as Ekman and colleagues and Porter and ten Brinke.

The evidence, particularly in light of perceptual centers in the brain for these expressions and the developmental progression among children and among the blind, strongly suggests that expressions are part of our wiring and thus instrumental to our survival as a species.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Health, Fertility, Receptivity, and Dominance Cues
assets.visual_frame_description: A holographic matrix rotates two human silhouettes - one male, one female - each node of the body pulsing with a color-coded tag: health in green, fertility in pink, receptivity in red, and dominance in blue. Dragging a node into the classification grid tests it against the evidence, and flawed cues such as fluctuating asymmetry measurement flicker and partially disintegrate, while valid cues such as the 0.7 waist-to-hip ratio lock into place.
assets.player_mission: Build the reproductive fitness matrix by classifying cues of health, fertility, sexual receptivity, and dominance as signs, signals, or symbols, and rate each cue's validity as evidence for mate choice. Sort facial symmetry, waist-to-hip ratio, digit ratio, pupil dilation, red attire, testosterone markers, and body size into their correct cells, and flag the cues that research has challenged or left unresolved.
key_concepts: Nonverbal signs are what comprise attractiveness, a catch-all category for signs or traits that are desirable, or those highest in reproductive fitness, with fertility applying almost exclusively to females and dominance exclusively to males.

Individuals with more homogenous skin texture and distribution of color in their faces are seen as healthier and more attractive, and redness signals cardiovascular health while yellow signals consumption of healthy carotenoid-bearing vegetables and fruits.

The immunocompetence handicap hypothesis posits that hormones responsible for sexual differentiation may also compromise one's immune system, so only the most physically capable men can afford to display highly masculinized features.

Facial features such as heavy brow ridges and strong jaw lines are signs of compromised immune systems that females may interpret as signaling strength, and women will sometimes prefer males with such appearance because it suggests the male is of high quality if he can overcome that high testosterone handicap.

Facial symmetry is the extent to which the right hemisphere of one's face or body matches the left hemisphere along the sagittal plane, and departures from facial symmetry indicate lower genetic health and greater susceptibility to perturbations during development.
The more symmetry one displays, the more attractive he or she is perceived by others, and this effect tends to be stronger for faces (effect size = .30) than for the body (effect size = .14).

A face appears more feminine, with larger eyes, fuller lips, a proportionally smaller chin and nose, and higher cheekbones, under higher levels of the primary female hormone estrogen, and women with more feminine faces did in fact produce more offspring.

A woman's waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) is one of the most researched body signs of fertility, with men in America and European countries viewing a WHR of 0.7, regardless of overall weight, as more attractive, presumably because it is a valid signal of fertility.

Among women, a WHR greater than .85 is related to increased health risk factors such as increased heart disease and Type II diabetes because such women exhibit greater concentrations of visceral adipose tissue.

During courtship, a woman signals interest in a romantic partner through increased blood flow to the face resulting in blush on the cheeks, swelling of the lips, and pupil dilation, all involuntary actions and therefore signs and valid signals of sexual receptivity.

The ratio between one's second digit (2D) and fourth digit (4D) is a proxy for sex hormone levels during critical periods of neural development, and 2D:4D is correlated with verbal aggression and overall aggression in males.

The key driver of dominance nonverbal cues is the hormone testosterone, and more dominant men will touch others more and invade personal space more than less dominant men, while more aggressive sports teams wear black uniforms.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Survival Value, Identity, and the Nonverbal Verdict
assets.visual_frame_description: A council chamber of ancestors sits around a fire, each holding a torch labeled with an emotion, while a cave wall ledger lists the survival functions - identifying threats, establishing hierarchies, calling for aid, smoothing social interaction. A final chart plots six million years of nonverbal history against the 150,000-200,000 or so years of articulate language, and a verdict gavel stamps your answer onto the chamber wall.
assets.player_mission: Face the chapter's closing synthesis: for each of the seven basic emotions, articulate its survival value for the group and the individual, then explain how person recognition, kin recognition, and group behavior made nonverbal communication central to human evolution. Deliver the final verdict on why involuntary nonverbal cues are more genuine markers of internal state and genetic fitness than entirely voluntary verbal communication.
key_concepts: Showing anger has the advantage of often preventing a fight and obtaining compliance without the risk of injury or infection, since the vast majority of interactions are with ingroup members, and threats are inexpensive ways to obtain compliance unless one has to follow through.

An anger expression causes others to react by stopping a transgressor from violating social norms, engaging in avoidance behaviors, showing fear, and triggering submissive actions such as an apology, which research shows quickly dissipates the emotion of anger.

Contempt is important to signal because indicating the relative status of individuals maintains the social hierarchy, and societies with strong social hierarchies are more stable and typically feature less internal violence.

Communicating to group members that a particular item is not ingestible is a life or death matter, since rancid meat and poisonous berries were among the major threats to survival in the ancient world, with typhoid fever dropping from 100 per 100,000 in the 1920s to less than 2 per 100,000 in 1999.

Fear signals to an angry conspecific that one does not intend to fight, and vocalizing fear allows the message to transmit over a longer distance, helping bring allies to battle the threat or giving those farther away additional time to flee.

An individual who shows a genuine sign of a positive emotion is seen as more pleasant, more genuine, and generally more positive than when the same individual signals an emotion with a posed smile, and knowing someone was approachable and friendly was a life or death judgment in the homicidal ancient world.

Sadness or distress expressions demonstrate that an individual needs attention and are essential in infancy, as an infant can only show distress nonverbally, and adults who display expressions of distress are able to generate help and sympathy from others.

Surprise can show novelty and alert others to the novel event to obtain assistance to help comprehend it, but the inherent neutrality of valence for surprise often affects its interpretation, as when the same surprised face accompanies finding a gift versus a decapitated cat head.

Darwin argued that a tribe including many members who possessed a high degree of patriotism, fidelity, obedience, courage, and sympathy would be victorious over most other tribes, and that this would be natural selection.

There are sections in the human brain that respond directly to faces, and people are also quite good at recognizing individuals from their voices and their odors, as well as recognizing kin from nonkin.

Verbal communication can accomplish many of the goals of nonverbal communication, but the fact that verbal communication is entirely voluntary renders it suspect as a clear definitive sign of health, fertility, or approachability, whereas nonverbal cues are more likely to be involuntary and thus more genuine markers of internal states and genetic fitness.

The 5.8-million-year head start that the signs and signals of nonverbal communication got on verbal communication, which has existed for only 150,000-200,000 or so years, has helped it maintain its presence within us, and it continues to influence us today.

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: Culture, Norms, and the Expressive-Reserved Spectrum
assets.visual_frame_description: A globe splits open into two hemispheres, one labeled OBJECTIVE with floating artifacts such as architecture, clothes, food, and art, and one labeled SUBJECTIVE with attitudes, values, beliefs, and norms, while items drift between them to be dragged into place. A second panel shows a spectrum bar with EXPRESSIVE on one end and RESERVED on the other, and each channel behavior glows as it snaps into position, while a tightness-looseness meter swings between severe sanctions and high tolerance for deviant behavior.
assets.player_mission: Drag the scrubber across the chapter's culture layer and classify each item - an etiquette rule, a tight-society sanction, a display rule, a value or belief - as an objective or subjective element of culture, and tag each norm as a proscription of appropriate behavior or a definition of what is inappropriate. Then sort each channel behavior (animated face, soft voice, direct gaze, rigid posture, close spacing) into the Expressive or Reserved column, and rate whether its culture is more tight or loose in its sanctioning of deviance.
key_concepts: Culture is defined as a unique meaning and information system, shared by a group and transmitted across generations, that allows the group to meet basic needs of survival, pursue happiness and well-being, and derive meaning from life.

The elements of culture divide into objective elements, which are physical artifacts such as architecture, clothes, foods, and art, and subjective elements such as attitudes, values, beliefs, and norms, with the subjective elements being most relevant to understanding nonverbal communication.
Norms are generally accepted standards of behavior for any cultural group, comprising behaviors that members of a culture have defined as the most appropriate in any given situation.

Not only do norms proscribe socially appropriate, desirable behaviors, but they also define what is inappropriate and undesirable, so cultures generate social sanctions and punishments, ranging from explicit penalties like jail time to implicit ones like social isolation, for norm transgressions.

Etiquette is a code of behavior that describes expectations for social behavior according to contemporary cultural and conventional norms within a cultural group, and etiquette-related behaviors are considered signs of maturity and sanity within each culture.

Tightness versus looseness has two key components: the strength of social norms, or how clear and pervasive norms are within societies, and the strength of sanctioning, or how much tolerance there is for deviance from norms.

Pelto (1968) identified the Pueblo Indians, the Hutterites, and the Japanese as examples of tight societies with clearly expressed norms and severe sanctions, and the Skolt Lapps of northern Finland and the Thais as loose societies with high tolerance for deviant behavior.

Settings are associated with three components: beliefs about being watched, uncertainty, and anxiety, and settings associated with the belief that one's behavior is not judged, such as an anonymous Internet chat room or a dark theater, produce much less regulatory effects on behavior.

Social roles define the expectations for behavior for individuals who occupy a position in a social system, and they are like scripts in a play that delineate the types of behaviors expected in specific situational contexts.

Expressive cultures have developed norms that encourage the broad, outward expression of nonverbal behaviors, such as more animated facial expressions and gestures, voices with higher intensity and range, direct gaze, relaxed and open postures, and closer interpersonal spacing.

Reserved cultures have developed norms that encourage restricting one's expressive behaviors, facial expressions, and gestures, using softer voices, avoiding direct gaze, and adopting more rigid, closed postures at relatively greater distances.

Nonverbal behaviors serve the same general function across cultures, to facilitate the sharing of social intentions, but the norms governing those behaviors differ depending on the ecological-cultural context within which those behaviors occur.

assets.topic: Dialogue with the Expresser: Display Rules Among Family, Friends, Colleagues, and Strangers
assets.visual_frame_description: A split observation room shows the expresser in four settings - a family dinner, a gathering of friends, an office meeting, and a room full of strangers - each tinted differently to signal its display rule context. A response deck glows as you choose one of six behavioral reactions, and an individualism meter rises and falls with each choice while ingroup and outgroup counters tick on the wall beside the expresser's face.
assets.player_mission: Confront a live expresser who is experiencing an emotion in a specific context and choose the display rule response that the expresser's culture endorses, then decide how much expression is allowed toward ingroups versus outgroups. Track how culture-level individualism versus collectivism shifts the expresser's overall expressivity, and catch the moments when the expresser suppresses, exaggerates, or expresses feelings as is, just as the Display Rule Assessment Inventory requires.
key_concepts: Cultural display rules, a concept first described by Ekman and Friesen (1969), are rules learned early in childhood that help individuals manage and modify their emotional expressions depending on social circumstances.

Display rules were first invoked to explain the cultural differences in expressive behavior that occurred in Friesen's (1972) study comparing the facial expressions of emotion of American and Japanese students as they watched emotionally evocative films.

In the Display Rule Assessment Inventory, participants choose one of six behavioral responses when they experience different emotions with family, friends, colleagues, and strangers (Matsumoto, Takeuchi, Andayani, Kouznetsova, & Krupp, 1998).

Individuals of all cultures reported that they suppress their expressions in some contexts, exaggerate their expressions in others, and express their feelings as is in others (Matsumoto et al., 2008).
Individuals of all cultures had a display rule norm for greater expressivity toward ingroups than toward outgroups (Matsumoto et al., 2008).

Collectivistic cultures were associated with less expressivity overall than individualistic cultures, suggesting that overall expression management for all emotions is central to the preservation of social order in these cultures.
Individualism was positively associated with higher expressivity norms in general and for positive emotions in particular.

People in individualistic cultures learn to express their emotions to their ingroup members, whereas people in collectivistic cultures learn to suppress or regulate their expressions, even to their ingroups.

Toward outgroups, people in individualistic cultures learn to express less negative and more positive emotions, whereas people in collectivistic cultures learn to express more negative and less positive ones.

Cultures achieve emotional expression regulation by moderating the types of emotions people have in specific contexts in the first place, by regulating people's expressive behaviors when emotions are elicited, and by regulating the way in which people perceive the emotional expressions of others.

In a study of congruent face-context pairings, agreement rates in judgments were near perfect with no cultural differences, suggesting that previously documented cultural differences in emotion recognition rates may have been the result of methodological artifacts (Matsumoto, Hwang, & Yamada, 2012).

When faces and contexts were incongruent, American judgments were more influenced by faces, whereas Japanese and South Korean judgments were more influenced by context (Matsumoto, Hwang, & Yamada, 2012).

assets.topic: Audit the Evidence: Universal Recognition, Intensity Ratings, and Face versus Context
assets.visual_frame_description: A forensic lab table holds three evidence folders labeled Universal Recognition, Intensity Ratings, and Face versus Context, plus a claim-board pinned with the seven universal expressions. Each claim card flips open to reveal its studies - Biehl et al., Elfenbein and Ambady, Masuda et al., and the congruent and incongruent face-context pairings - and a verdict stamp slams down onto each card as the audit proceeds.
assets.player_mission: Run a forensic audit of the chapter's central claims about emotion perception: review the pancultural recognition studies, the absolute-level differences in agreement rates across cultures, the intensity-rating differences, and the face-versus-context judgment literature, and stamp each claim SUPPORTED, CHALLENGED, or UNRESOLVED. Pay special attention to the Matsumoto, Hwang, and Yamada (2012) studies and decide whether prior cultural differences in recognition were methodological artifacts caused by judging faces alone.
key_concepts: The seven universal facial expressions are panculturally recognized, and there is pancultural similarity in judgments of relative intensity among faces, meaning that people of different countries agree on which expressions are more strongly expressed (Ekman et al., 1987; Matsumoto & Ekman, 1989).
There is cross-cultural agreement in the association between perceived expression intensity and inferences about subjective experiences, and in the secondary emotions portrayed in an expression.
Americans typically have higher agreement rates when judging emotions than observers from other countries (Biehl et al., 1997; Elfenbein & Ambady, 2002; Matsumoto, 1989, 1992).
Japanese tend to rate emotional expressions lower in intensity than Americans (Biehl et al., 1997; Ekman et al., 1987; Matsumoto, 1990, 1993).

Studies involving incongruent response linkages have generally demonstrated a face primacy effect, indicating that the signals in the face tend to override the signals provided by the context (Ekman & O'Sullivan, 1988; Ekman, O'Sullivan, & Matsumoto, 1991).

In Masuda et al. (2008), Americans were more likely to label the central figure consistent with its own emotion despite the emotions portrayed by others, whereas Japanese were more influenced by the others' expressions when labeling the central figure.

Gait refers to the pattern of movement of the body when walking, and Montepare and Zebrowitz (1993) found cross-cultural agreement in perceptions of age, sex, strength, and happiness but cross-cultural differences on perceptions of dominance in judgments of walking.

Studies of the speed with which individuals across cultures move through their cities have demonstrated that pace is associated with punctuality, coronary heart disease, and a variety of attitudinal and personality traits (Levine & Norenzayan, 1999).
Nonverbal vocal cues are called paralinguistic cues and include the tone of voice, intonation, pitch, speech rate, use of silence, and volume.

Anger produces a harsh edge to the voice with louder volume and increased speech rates, fear produces higher pitch and sudden inhalations, disgust produces yuck or gagging sounds, and sadness produces softer voices and decreased speech rates.

In a mock crime interview study, Hispanic and Middle Eastern immigrants consistently spoke with higher vocal intensity and higher speech rates than the Chinese and European Americans (Matsumoto & Hwang, 2013b).

Around the world, a commonly held belief is that people who do not look one straight in the eye are likely to be lying, but there is little or no empirical support for the belief that gaze is reliably associated with lying (DePaulo et al., 2003).

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Channels of Nonverbal Norms Across Cultures
assets.visual_frame_description: A six-cell matrix rotates with channels - Face, Gesture, Voice, Gaze, Space and Touch, and Posture - on one axis and Expressive versus Reserved norms on the other, and behaviors drift in to snap into their correct cells. A second world map shows emblem hotspots, with the A-OK sign pulsing different meanings in different countries, and a hand flipbook animates the moutza's origins in the streets of ancient Greece.
assets.player_mission: Build the cultural norms matrix by sorting each behavior - speech illustrators, emblems, gaze, paralinguistic cues, interpersonal distance, touch, posture, and gait - into its correct channel and matching it to the Expressive or Reserved norm that its culture endorses. Then map emblem meanings across cultures, such as the A-OK sign, the reversed peace sign, and the Greek moutza, and flag the gestures most likely to be misinterpreted when they cross cultural boundaries.
key_concepts: Gestures are body movements, primarily of the hands, that are used as part of the human communication system, and they are a form of embodied cognition in that they are movements that express some kind of thought or the process of thinking (Kinsbourne, 2006).

Speech illustrators are movements that are directly tied to speech and illustrate or highlight what is being said, whereas emblems are gestures that convey verbal meaning independent of words and are also known as symbolic or emblematic gestures.

Efron (1941) found distinct gestures among immigrant Jews and Italians in New York City who adhered to their traditional culture, but these gestures disappeared as people were more assimilated into the larger American culture and their children adopted the illustrators typical of Americans.

Expressive cultures such as Latin American and Middle Eastern cultures encourage the use of large, illustrative gestures when speaking, and in Italy one is expected to speak with your hands, whereas large gestures are considered impolite in British culture and East Asian cultures discourage such gestures, especially in public.

Emblems are culture specific, and the North American A-OK sign means OK in some cultures, an orifice having sexual implications in some cultures, money in some cultures, and zero in still others (Morris et al., 1980).

The reversed peace sign, with the forefinger and middle finger up in a V shape and the palm facing inward, is an insult in England and Australia meaning screw you, so when emblems are interpreted across cultures there is a large probability of misinterpreting the sender's meaning.

Morris et al. (1980) called some emblems relic emblems because they were trace representations of specific behaviors, such as the Greek moutza, an insult emblem that represents the tossing of garbage or urine and whose origins were thought to be in ancient Greece.

Some emblems such as come, go, hello, goodbye, yes, and no are becoming recognized across cultural boundaries despite differences in origin, a process likely driven by the strong influence of mass media around the world, particularly television, movies, and the Internet (Matsumoto & Hwang, 2013a).

Gaze is associated with dominance, power, or aggression in both humans and nonhuman animals (Fehr & Exline, 1987) as well as affiliation and nurturance (Argyle & Cook, 1976), and Arabs gaze much longer and more directly at their partners than do Americans (Hall, 1963; Watson & Graves, 1966).

Hall's (1966, 1973) classic work specified four levels of interpersonal space use depending on social relationship type: intimate, personal, social, and public, with intimate distances in the United States being less than 18 in. (45.72 cm) and personal distances ranging from 18 in. (45.72 cm) to 4 ft (1.2 m).

Postures communicate attitudinal states and general affect as opposed to the specific emotions communicated by face and voice, and people of different cultures interpret postures according to the same dimensions (positivity, status) but place different weights of importance on specific aspects (Kudoh & Matsumoto, 1985).

In a study of whole body, triumphant displays of dominance produced by Olympic athletes after winning matches, athletes from status-oriented cultures tended to produce more of these behaviors than athletes from more egalitarian cultures (Hwang & Matsumoto, 2014).

assets.topic: Boss Level: Intercultural Encounters and the Silent Language
assets.visual_frame_description: A glass-walled meeting room shows a conversation between an expressive-culture speaker gesturing broadly with a loud voice and a reserved-culture listener with a rigid posture, with attribution bubbles floating above their heads: untrustworthy, inscrutable, and sly on one side, and arrogant, loud, and rude on the other. A subtitle scrolling at the bottom reads the silent language, and a final control panel offers the four expectations that turn the encounter into a platform for staging the sharing of goals.
assets.player_mission: Face the chapter's closing synthesis: explain why cultures facilitate context-specific norms for nonverbal behavior, then walk through a live intercultural interaction in which a person from an expressive culture meets a person from a reserved culture. Diagnose the automatic negative attributions each side makes, trace them back to enculturation and cultural filters, and deliver the final strategy for reducing uncertainty so that the interaction becomes a platform for the development and exchange of ideas.
key_concepts: Cultures facilitate different context-specific norms related to nonverbal communication and nonverbal behaviors because they facilitate social coordination and reduce the potential for social chaos, all of which enhance the possibility of the increased social sharing of intentions.

Cultural differences in nonverbal communication are often difficult to experience and to interpret in intercultural interactions, especially because nonverbal behaviors are the silent language (Henley, 1977) and many people focus on the words being spoken and not the nonverbal behavior.

Intercultural communication is more likely to be marred by uncertainty and ambiguity than intracultural communication, not only because of questions concerning the verbal messages but also because of cultural differences in the nonverbal messages that co-occur (Gudykunst & Nishida, 1984).

Differences in nonverbal messages often lead to aversive reactions that increase the potential for misunderstanding, miscommunication, and misattributions about intent or character, which disrupts social coordination and increases the potential for conflict.

It is easier for people from expressive cultures to judge those from reserved cultures as untrustworthy, inscrutable, sly, deceptive, or shifty, whereas it is easier for people from reserved cultures to judge those from expressive cultures as arrogant, loud, rude, immature, or vulgar.

These negative reactions occur unconsciously and automatically because they are rooted in cultural filters for interpreting the appropriateness of behavior that are developed early on through the process of enculturation within one's culture.

Many of these interpretations and attributions may be misguided because the cultural filters with which one interprets the nonverbal communications of others may not be the cultural framework within which the person's behavior is rooted.

One of the goals of intercultural interactions is to reduce the uncertainty inherent in the situation (Gudykunst, Nishida, & Chua, 1986), and one way to do this is to realize that cultural differences in nonverbal communications exist and that they exist for a reason that makes sense either now or in the past for the culture in which those behaviors are imbedded.

By creating the expectations that cultural differences exist, that engaging with them may produce negative emotional reactions, and that these differences and reactions are a normal and inevitable part of the communication process, intercultural interactions become a platform for the development and exchange of ideas rather than an obstacle.

Humans have a very complex and differentiated signal system in the body, including face, voice, gesture, and whole body movements, and the function of communication is for the purpose of facilitating the sharing of social intentions.
The sharing of social intentions allows humans to achieve social coordination and reduces the possibility of social chaos, in turn facilitating group efficiency and ultimately impacting survival.

Humans have the cognitive ability to share their intentions with others, and shared intentionality may be at the heart of social coordination, which allows for the creation of human culture (Fiske, 2000).

assets.topic: The Developmental Niche and the Three Ontogenetic Forces
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall of video monitors plays children of different ages being asked to make happy, sad, and angry faces, each face rendered progressively sharper and more differentiated from age 2 to adulthood, with the lower face glowing first. Beside the monitors, a world map sprouts icons of the niche: a smoke-filled hut, a mother's breast, a sumo-style crying contest, and a mother's smiling face looming over a baby's crib.
assets.player_mission: Chart the three ontogenetic forces that shape nonverbal communication development - preparedness, increasing voluntary control, and differentiation - and explain how the developmental niche bends each of them. Use the Lewis, Sullivan, and Vasen (1987) face-posing study and the cross-cultural examples of Baganda, German, Nso, Hausa, and Zinacanteco infants to show how culture and custom channel expressive development, then account for why researchers still lack a comprehensive view of the nonverbal communication whole.
key_concepts: Nonverbal communication development is driven by three ontogenetic forces: biological preparedness, increasing voluntary control, and differentiation.
With development, responses become less diffuse, undifferentiated, and nonspecific and more distinctive, refined, organized, and directed.
Though facial musculature is considerably differentiated at birth, the ability to use it to express a range of discrete emotions seems less so.
Super and Harkness (1986, 2002) conceptualized the developmental niche as a set of dynamic properties and forces that create unique environments for a child that the child, in turn, impacts.

The developmental niche includes the physical and social settings, customs and practices of child rearing, the psychology of caretakers, characteristics of the child (e.g., sex, temperament), and local meaning systems.

In the Lewis, Sullivan, and Vasen (1987) study, 2-year-olds' posed expressions were barely distinguishable with unexpressive upper face regions, whereas adults conveyed nearly the full array of distinct emotions using both upper and lower regions of the face.
Traditional Baganda newborns begin formal training soon after birth to encourage social smiling, and these charming babies smile earlier than most.

German mothers frequently interact face-to-face with their babies, whereas Cameroonian Nso mothers rarely do, and at 12 weeks of age German infants smile more frequently and imitate their mother's actions more than their Nso counterparts.
Cranky Hausa babies are immediately quieted at a mother's breast, and they consequently survive drought conditions better than their less expressive cohorts.

Researchers tend to specialize in studying one signal channel or another and rarely examine the interplay among modalities in shaping meaning, leaving a piecemeal account of what should be a developmental whole.

Children's nonverbal behavior is often used only as a convenient indicator of social status or emotionality rather than studied as a developing social communication competence or skill set in and of itself.
