assets.topic: What Is Gesture? Anatomy of Cospeech Gestures
assets.visual_frame_description: A gesture lab shows looping clips of speakers, with toggles to flag affect displays, regulators, adaptors, emblems, and illustrators, and a per-frame overlay tagging iconicity, deixis, metaphor, and rhythm. A side panel contrasts ASL's phonological, morphological, and syntactic structure with gesture's unstructured freedom, with example hands demonstrating an OK sign, a thumbs up, and a Bulgarian head toss.
assets.player_mission: Sort a stream of video clips into Ekman and Friesen's five categories of nonverbal behavior, then classify each cospeech gesture as iconic, metaphoric, deictic, or beat by the way it conveys meaning. Compare gesture with sign language on structure, combinatoriality, and syntactic rules, and justify why each clip belongs where it does.
key_concepts: Sign languages are produced in the manual modality like gesture, but they display the same underlying structural features as spoken languages, including phonological, morphological, and syntactic rules.

Gesture lacks the regular structures and rules that are central to language, does not exhibit combinatorial properties, and lacks syntactic rules, but this lack of structure provides greater freedom for individual variation.

According to Ekman and Friesen's (1969) classification, the kinds of nonverbal behavior produced during spontaneous communication fall into five categories: affect displays, regulators, adaptors, emblems, and illustrators.

Emblems are gestures that have shared conventional meanings, are culturally specific, and come with expectations about how they should look and when they should be used, so variation from these learned forms makes a gesture difficult to understand.

Emblems, more than other types of gestures, are like words or sentences in that they have specific, shared meanings, are used consciously by speakers to communicate particular concepts, and can be produced either with or without accompanying speech.
Emblems are not assembled into sequences: each emblem has a specific, learned meaning (e.g., OK, great, bye-bye), but emblems are not combined with one another according to structural rules.

Illustrators, also called cospeech gestures, are movements produced alongside speech that often illustrate the concepts conveyed in speech, and their meanings rely heavily on the spoken contexts in which they are produced.

Iconic gestures convey meaning by recreating an aspect of their referent's shape or movement, for example by representing physical objects or events through a hand performing an action, the hand as an object, or a finger tracing a path.

Metaphoric gestures represent abstract ideas or concepts by illustrating them with visuo-spatial schemas such as height, weight, containment, or forward movement, as when a lifting gesture accompanies the word improve.
Deictic or indexical gestures direct attention toward objects, people, events, or locations in the surrounding environment, and pointing with the index finger is the paradigmatic deictic gesture.

Beat gestures are rhythmic movements of the hands or head that correspond to, and serve to highlight, the prosody of speech, and although they have no imagistic or indexical meaning, they can segment and emphasize elements in speech like a gestural highlighter.
The categories of cospeech gesture are not mutually exclusive, as a gesture may easily fall into more than one category, such as a direction-giving gesture that is both iconic and deictic.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Gesture-Speech Integration: One Integrated System
assets.visual_frame_description: A dual timeline renders the speech waveform and prosodic contour on top and the gesture movement phase below, with peaks snapping into alignment, and cards for each gesture-speech pair to tag the semantic relationship. A brain diagram lights up Broca's area for semantic gesture processing and shows an ERP waveform with a large N400 negativity when speech and gesture contradict.
assets.player_mission: Analyze gesture-speech pairs and label each as complementary, supplementary, or disambiguating, then time the stroke of each gesture against the peak prosodic emphasis of its clause. Judge whether each pair is a true error or a gesture-speech mismatch, and interpret the N400 consequences of contradiction, mismatch, and match at the neural level.
key_concepts: More than 90% of all gestures occur in the presence of speech, and the gesture-speech relationship in adults is characterized by both temporal and semantic integration.

The movement phase of a speaker's gesture co-occurs with the point of peak prosodic emphasis in the accompanying clause, and gestures show greater synchrony with accompanying speech than manual actions do (Church, Kelly, & Holcombe, 2014).
Gesture can complement information in speech by reinforcing size, shape, movement, path, or location information that is conveyed in speech.
Gesture can supplement information in speech by adding information about size, shape, movement, path, or location that is not expressed anywhere in that speech.

Gesture can disambiguate information in speech by specifying the referent of an underspecified speech act, as when a point accompanies utterances like that one or put it there, which would otherwise be ambiguous.

Gesture-speech mismatches, in which gesture conveys different information from speech, indicate that the learner is in a transitional period with respect to a concept and, if given instruction, is likely to make significant progress (Goldin-Meadow & Alibali, 2013).
When phonological production breaks down, as in stuttering or aphasia, gesture production stops as well, providing further evidence for the tight temporal synchrony between gesture and speech.

At the lexical level, gesture can both reflect and compensate for gaps in a speaker's verbal lexicon, as when complex shapes that are difficult to describe in speech are conveyed in gesture (Emmorey & Casey, 2001).

At the syntactic level, gestures are influenced by the structural properties of the accompanying speech, so English speakers produce a single gesture combining manner and path while Turkish speakers produce two separate gestures.

Listeners glean information from both gesture and speech and integrate the two pieces of information, reporting in their own speech information that was conveyed only in gesture, and they cannot ignore gesture even when explicitly instructed to do so.

Event-related potential work found that video stimuli in which gestures and speech conveyed contradictory information produced a large negativity at 400 ms (the N400 effect), whereas gestures conveying different but integratable information were processed no differently from matches at that stage.

Gestures accompanying speech are processed in Broca's area with a pattern consistent with semantic processing, whereas noncommunicative actions show a pattern more consistent with mirror system activation (Skipper, Goldin-Meadow, Nusbaum, & Small, 2007).

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Gesture in Development: Predicting Language Before Speech
assets.visual_frame_description: A timeline from 8 to 24 months plots gesture types, gesture-word combinations, and vocabulary growth, with predictive arrows running from gesture milestones to later speech milestones. A clinic panel shows a 12-month-old's gesture counts against typical ranges, flagging autism-risk and early-brain-injury comparisons, and highlighting children who catch up versus those who remain delayed.
assets.player_mission: Track a simulated child's communicative development from first points and hold-ups through complementary and supplementary gesture-speech combinations, and predict the timing of two-word speech and first complex sentences. Screen for language delay using gesture rate and pointing as early markers, and decide which children are late bloomers and which need intervention.
key_concepts: Children typically begin to gesture between 8 and 12 months of age, with these early gestures mainly deictic points and hold-ups, and children begin gesturing before they can speak.

Once children acquire their first spoken words, they do not immediately combine those words with gesture, and in the earliest stages of speech children produce either gesture or speech alone, rarely combining the two (Butcher & Goldin-Meadow, 2000).
There comes a critical point in the one-word period where children begin to combine words with gestures in earnest and to synchronize their production of gesture and speech in those combinations.

Children's early gesture-speech combinations are complementary in that they reference the same object or event in both modalities, and additive or supplementary combinations emerge only after gesture and speech have become temporally synchronized.

The age when a child first produces supplementary gesture-speech combinations predicts the age when that child will produce his or her first two-word utterance, and children produce first complex sentences in gesture and speech several months before producing them entirely in speech.

The number of different meanings children communicate in their gestures during early vocabulary building predicts the total number of spoken words they will acquire in the next few years (Rowe & Goldin-Meadow, 2009a).
A child's early deictic gestures reliably predict which nouns are likely to enter that child's spoken vocabulary in the next 3 months (Iverson & Goldin-Meadow, 2005).

Low gesture rates early in development may be a signal that a child is likely to experience delays in language learning, providing an opportunity for early interventions (Sauer, Levine, & Goldin-Meadow, 2010).

In a study of low verbal children whose vocabularies were in the lowest 10% of their age group, the children who were the most competent in gesture caught up with their peers within the following year, whereas children who fared poorly on gesture remained delayed a year later (Thal, Tobias, & Morrison, 1991).

A study of children with early brain injury found that children whose gesture rates were within the typical range were the most likely to catch up with their typically developing peers, whereas children with below-range gesture rates were likely to display persistent language delay.

Infants who were later diagnosed with autism had gestured less overall and produced very little pointing at 12 months compared with typically developing infants, and younger siblings of children with autism who displayed smaller communicative repertoires in gesture had an increased likelihood of receiving an autism diagnosis.
Robust gesturing in children who have low language skills relative to their peers signals that they are ready to learn and are late bloomers who will catch up without the need for intervention.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: When Gesture Becomes Language: Homesign, Emerging Sign Languages, and Gesture's Uniqueness
assets.visual_frame_description: A workshop shows a homesigner's gesture strings becoming segmented and linearized into sentences, with a cohort diagram of NSL signers adding increasingly complex linguistic structure across generations. A comparison grid lines up gesture versus action (representational, free of object affordances), gesture versus voice (analog versus digital), and human versus ape gesture (iconicity, synchrony, and declarative meaning).
assets.player_mission: Build a homesign system from scratch: assemble a lexicon, morphological parts, and structured sentences, then pass it through successive cohorts of learners to see linguistic structure grow from child homesign to adult homesign to Nicaraguan Sign Language. Then compare gesture with action, voice, and ape gesture to identify what is unique about human gesture as a communicative medium.
key_concepts: Deaf children born to deaf parents learn their parents' sign language as naturally as hearing children learn spoken language, but most deaf children are born to hearing parents and communicate with the hearing people in their worlds using gestures called homesign.

Homesign is characterized by many, although not all, of the properties found in natural languages, including a lexicon, morphological structure, structured sentences, grammatical categories such as nouns and verbs, and gestural lexical markers for negation and questions.

Homesigners use their gestures not only to make requests but also to comment on the present and nonpresent, make generic statements about classes of objects, tell stories, talk to themselves, and talk about language, serving the typical functions that all languages serve.

Analyses of adult homesigners in Nicaragua have uncovered linguistic structures that may go beyond the structures found in child homesigners, including the grammatical category subject and morphological devices that mark number.

Nicaraguan Sign Language (NSL) emerged when deaf individuals in Nicaragua, who were likely to have been homesigners, came together in the late 1970s and began to fashion a shared communication system.

The second cohort of NSL signers takes the sign system developed by the first cohort as input and changes that input so that the product contains increasingly complex linguistic structure, showing the impact that passing a language through a new generation of learners has on language structure.

The structures found in children's homesigns cannot be traced back to the spontaneous cospeech gestures that the children's hearing parents produce while talking to them (Goldin-Meadow & Mylander, 1983).

When hearing speakers of English, Spanish, Chinese, and Turkish are asked to describe animated events using only their hands, they abandon the order typical of their spoken languages and produce gestures that conform to the same order, agent, object, action, although they do not display other linguistic properties found in homesign, such as consistent form-meaning pairings akin to morphemes.

Gesture is a relatively analog form of communication because gestures are holistic and can blend into other gestures in flexible ways, whereas speech is discrete and combinatorial, giving it expressive power that gesture lacks.

Gesture is representational and not tied to the affordances of the physical environment, unlike action, and gesturing about performing an action encodes features of the action in greater detail than performing the action itself.

In a study of mathematical equivalence learning, all three types of hand movements helped children solve the problems on which they were trained, but only gesture led to success on problems that required generalizing the knowledge, suggesting that gesture promotes transfer of knowledge better than action.

Great apes use gestures in seemingly intentional and meaningful ways and take the gaze of their partners into account, but their gestures are not richly iconic, are not temporally synchronized with vocalization, and seem to have only imperative meanings, whereas human gesture can convey both imperative and declarative meanings.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Gesture for Thought: Cognition, Memory, Learning, and Real-World Applications
assets.visual_frame_description: An experiment console toggles gesture allowed, forbidden, or scripted (correct, partially correct, or none) and graphs word recall, math learning, and transfer to new problems. An applications board shows a classroom where teacher and student gestures are highlighted, a clinical screening panel for language delay, and a forensic interview transcript with gesture annotations.
assets.player_mission: Run experiments that manipulate gesturing to test its causal role in lexical access, conceptualization, working memory, and the creation of new knowledge, then use those findings to design classroom lessons, early-intervention programs, and forensic interview protocols. Decide when and how gesture changes thought, and justify each application with the evidence.
key_concepts: Gesturing can support the planning and production of speech by facilitating lexical retrieval, by helping speakers find words, and speakers are particularly likely to gesture during unrehearsed speech or when they use words that are unpredictable given the surrounding context.

When lexical access is impaired during experimental manipulation or in patients with aphasia, rates of gesturing increase, and adults and children are more successful at finding correct words when they are allowed to gesture than when they are not allowed to gesture.

Speakers gesture more on problems that are conceptually difficult even when there are no lexical demands, as when adults describing dot patterns gesture more for patterns without lines connecting the dots, suggesting gesture can do more than facilitate lexical access.

Adults and children who were asked to remember an unrelated list of items while explaining how they solved a math problem recalled more items when they gestured during their explanations than when they did not gesture, showing that gesturing reduces demands on verbal working memory.

The working memory benefit of gesture was found even when gestures were directed at objects that were not present in the context, and it was not being told not to gesture that increased demands on working memory.

Goldin-Meadow, Cook, and Mitchell (2009) found that children required to produce gestures that instantiated a correct procedure during a math lesson learned more than children required to produce partially correct gestures, who learned more than children required to produce no gestures.

After the math lesson, children who had gestured produced in speech the procedure that had been instantiated only in their gestures, showing that gesturing had brought new knowledge into their repertoires.
Researchers may be able to lay the foundations for new knowledge simply by telling learners how to move their hands.

Speakers gesture more when they can be seen, as gesture rates decline when a screen is placed between speaker and listener, but speakers experience no decrease in gesturing when they repeat the same message to different listeners (Jacobs & Garnham, 2007).

Congenitally blind speakers, who have never seen another person gesture, produce gestures when they speak even when speaking to blind listeners, suggesting that gesture may be playing a role for speakers as well as listeners.

Lessons that contain gestures promote deeper learning, including new forms of reasoning, generalization to new problem types, and retention of knowledge, better than lessons that do not contain gestures, and encouraging students to gesture can activate implicit knowledge and make them receptive to instruction.

In forensic interviews with child witnesses, the interviewer's gestures served as a source of information and at times misinformation that led children to report incorrect details, while the gestures the child witnesses spontaneously produced conveyed substantive information that was not always conveyed in their speech and so would not appear in written transcripts.

assets.topic: The Eye Region: Why People Are Drawn to the Eyes
assets.visual_frame_description: An eye-tracking heatmap blooms over portraits and faces, showing nearly 70% of fixations on the eyes, with side panels contrasting a whole face with eyes concealed versus a schematic pair of dots that makes an infant smile. A test console flashes eye-region crops and mental state options, with score bars split by trait, gender, age, and culture.
assets.player_mission: Study portraits and face stimuli with an eye-tracking overlay, recording where fixations land, then decode mental and emotional states from eye-region images alone using the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test. Classify how trait, gender, age, and culture shape eye-region decoding, and spot the deficits that mark autism, schizophrenia, and other disorders.
key_concepts: An analysis of famous portraits dating back 5 centuries found that one eye was almost always painted on or very near the horizontal center of the portrait, presumably reflecting the inner character of the subject (Tyler, 1998).

The ability to process gaze information is believed to play a pivotal role in the development of theory of mind, the ability to understand that others have mental and emotional experiences different than your own (Baron-Cohen, 2002).

Early research on young adults in England demonstrated that nearly 70% of fixations are allocated to the eye region of a given face stimulus, revealing a preference for looking at the eyes over other facial features (Walker-Smith, Gale, & Findlay, 1977).
Infants naturally attend to the presence of two large, horizontally arranged eyespots, ignoring similar single- and triple-spot schematic arrays (Hess, 1975).

Within the first 2 months of life, the presentation of two horizontally configured dots is enough to evoke a smile response in an infant, yet a whole face presented with eyes concealed failed to produce such smiling (Ahrens, 1954).

Upper face muscles, including those around the eye region, are more tightly connected to the extrapyramidal motor system, which is relatively more difficult and grossly coordinated, so researchers suggest the eye region is more revealing because it is less prone to volitional, deceptive displays.

The orbicularis oculi surrounds the eyeballs and is responsible for the actual opening and closing of the eyes as well as the wrinkles found alongside the eyes during Duchenne smiles, which are smiles automatically elicited in response to spontaneous positive emotion (Duchenne de Boulogne, 1862/1990).
Basic emotions are accurately decoded from just the eye region when it is presented separately from other regions of the face (Baron-Cohen, Wheelwright, & Jolliffe, 1997; Nummenmaa, 1964).

The Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RME) was developed to assess abilities to decode complex mental states from the eye region alone, such as playful, insisting, and regretful (Baron-Cohen, Wheelwright, Hill, Raste, & Plumb, 2001).

Adults and children on the autism spectrum perform worse on the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test than typically developed children, and even parents of children diagnosed with autism perform worse than parents of nonautistic children (Baron-Cohen et al., 1997, 2001).

Individuals with schizophrenia show deficits on the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test, and these deficits are accompanied by hypoactivation of the left inferior frontal gyrus (Irani et al., 2006; Russell et al., 2000).

Consistent, yet small, gender differences have been found on the RME, with females tending to score higher than males, and fetal testosterone levels, which differ strongly between males and females in utero, predict children's performance on the RME (Kirkland et al., 2013; Chapman et al., 2006).

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Tears and Pupils: The Lesser Studied Eye Behaviors
assets.visual_frame_description: A lab bench shows a lacrimal gland diagram with three tear streams, basal, reflexive, and emotional, feeding into a crying data panel split by trait, gender, age, and culture. A pupil close-up meter tracks dilation against slides of babies, nudes, landscapes, and sad faces, with a historical card on 15th-century belladonna use.
assets.player_mission: Trace the production, social signaling, and perception of tears across contexts, then measure pupil dilation responses to images, attraction judgments, and emotion displays. Predict who cries, when pupils dilate or constrict, and how perceivers read pupil size as a social cue.
key_concepts: Tears are produced by the lacrimal glands of many vertebrates as a method of lubricating the eyes, and there are three types of tears: basal, reflexive, and emotional (Murube, Murube, & Murube, 1999).
Emotional tears, which are produced in response to an emotion-eliciting event, are believed to belong solely to humans (Frey & Langseth, 1985).

Sjogren's syndrome prevents the lacrimal gland from producing a sufficient amount of tears, and many individuals with the disorder are also diagnosed with alexithymia, an inability to properly express and experience emotions, and are more at risk for depression.
Sad faces with tears removed were rated as significantly less sad than faces with the tears, and the tearless faces were rated as more ambiguous in valence (Provine, Krosnowski, & Brocato, 2009).

Hasson (2009) argued that tears evolved partly as a social signal of appeasement and a call for help, because tears obscure vision and can signal to others that aggressive acts toward them are unlikely, making an approach from another to offer assistance more likely.
Individuals who are higher in neuroticism report more crying episodes, whereas extraverted individuals are more likely to report feeling cathartic relief from crying (De Fruyt, 1997).

Numerous studies have shown that women tear up more than men, and one suggested reason is that women hold less power and status in society and are therefore expected to display more submissive expressions such as sadness (Fischer et al., 2004).

When information about the catalyst of a crying episode was not given, participants rated women as less stoic and more sad than males, suggesting that gender stereotypes are used to fill in the gaps in context, and in a work context crying men are judged as more emotional and less competent than crying women (Fischer, Eagly, & Oosterwijk, 2013).
Men that sniffed the odorless tears of women produced during a negative emotive state showed decreases in sexual arousal and decreases in testosterone (Gelstein et al., 2011).

Pupillary dilation is a physiological marker of heightened arousal, and in Hess and Polt's (1960) study men showed the greatest dilation to nude female photos while women showed the greatest dilation to the nude male, so pupil size could be used to index level of interest in a visual stimulus.

Pupillary constriction is often found in response to viewing negative emotional stimuli such as mutilated bodies or crippled children, and Janisse (1974) argued that pupil size varies curvilinearly as a function of valence, with dilation largest at the negative and positive ends of the continuum and smallest in the center.

The amygdala is sensitive to perceiving pupil size, even in the absence of subjective awareness, and as far back as the 15th century Italian women put belladonna drops in their eyes to dilate their pupils and appear more attractive, with heterosexual males judging female faces with larger pupils as more attractive (Demos et al., 2008; Heiser, 1987; Bull & Shead, 1979).

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Gaze as Information Gathering: Joint Attention and Gaze Cueing
assets.visual_frame_description: A monitor shows an avatar glancing toward targets, with reaction-time bars confirming reflexive orienting toward the gazed-at location, and a neural panel lighting up the STS, inferior occipital gyrus, and parietal cortex. A scan-path viewer compares healthy, autistic, schizophrenic, and socially phobic faces, painting eye, mouth, and nose fixations in different colors.
assets.player_mission: Follow gaze cues on screen, time your shifts against averted and direct gaze, and trace the flow from eye direction detection to shared attention to theory of mind. Then diagnose visual scanning patterns in autism, schizophrenia, and social phobia, and weigh gender, age, and culture effects on gaze following.
key_concepts: Eye gaze tells where in the environment someone is looking, and such shared, or joint, attention has been demonstrated in monkeys and apes as well as in human infants and adults, appearing to be an obligatory behavior necessarily occurring in response to perceiving another's averted gaze (Frischen, Bayliss, & Tipper, 2007; Driver et al., 1999).
Some have argued that humans have evolved a contrasting white sclera to facilitate detecting the gaze of others (Kobayashi & Kohshima, 1997).

Seeing a face with its gaze averted to the side leads to facilitated identification of a target in the gazed-at location, and this effect is so powerful that instructing participants that the target is four times more likely to appear opposite the gazed-at location does not reduce early attentional biases (C. K. Friesen & Kingstone, 1998; Driver et al., 1999).

The primacy of gaze following appears across numerous species of primates and in human infants, and even goats can utilize gaze following of other goats to find food (Kaminski, Riedel, Call, & Tomasello, 2005).

Gaze cueing is primarily mediated by bilateral activity in the inferior occipital gyrus and right medial occipital gyrus, whereas arrow cueing shows more extensive activations, suggesting that gaze cueing elicits more automatic shifts of attention while arrow cueing is driven by more voluntary attentional shifts (Hietanen et al., 2006).

According to Baron-Cohen (1995), the innate capacity to process gaze information plays a critical role in the development of theory of mind, and he proposed four mechanisms constituting the mindreading system, of which the three gaze-related mechanisms are the Intentionality Detector, the Eye Direction Detector, and the Shared Attention Mechanism.
The Intentionality Detector is considered a mechanism that allows motion to be interpreted in terms of volitional mental states driving goals or behavioral intent (Baron-Cohen, 1995).

The Eye Direction Detector presumes that there are brain cells specialized for the processing of different eye gaze directions, and Perrett and colleagues found cells in areas of the STS that are sensitive to particular eye gaze directions, many of them simultaneously sensitive to head and body orientation though preferentially sensitive to eye gaze (Perrett & Emery, 1994; Perrett et al., 1985).
Infants as young as 2 days old are able to discern gaze direction, suggesting that this ability is innately prepared (Farroni, Csibra, Simion, & Johnson, 2002).

The Shared Attention Mechanism is defined as the compulsion to follow another's line of sight, requiring eye direction perception to form a triadic representation of an agent and its object or goal in relation to the self (Baron-Cohen, 1995).

Individuals with autism spend more time looking at nonfeatures and look more at the mouth region, whereas controls look more at the eye region, when engaging in general face processing and emotion recognition tasks, and amygdala-lesioned patients make less eye contact (Klin et al., 2002; Spezio et al., 2007).

During facial emotion recognition, men look more at nose and mouth than females, whereas women look at the eyes more, which is associated with better accuracy and faster reaction times when asked to recognize faces, and infants follow the gaze of an experimenter only when it is preceded by communication such as mutual eye contact or speech directed at the infant (Vassallo et al., 2009; Hall, Hutton, & Morgan, 2010; Senju & Csibra, 2008).

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Gaze as Social Signaling: Self-Relevance, Affiliation, Dominance, and Emotion
assets.visual_frame_description: A control room flashes faces whose gaze flips between direct and averted, with meters for face memory, likability, skin conductance, and amygdala activation, and a cafeteria poster experiment counts littering when eyes watch the viewer. An emotion-by-gaze grid pairs anger, joy, fear, and sadness with direct and averted gaze, lighting up congruent and incongruent threat pairings.
assets.player_mission: Toggle gaze between direct and averted on faces, scenes, and posters, and record effects on face memory, liking, cooperation, dominance ratings, and arousal. Test the shared signal hypothesis by pairing gaze direction with emotions and deciding when congruent versus incongruent gaze-emotion pairs are processed faster or more ambiguously.
key_concepts: Ellsworth (1975) suggested that eye gaze does not carry a specific sign-referent meaning and that its interpretation is dependent on context.

Faces with direct gaze are remembered better by infants, children, and adults, and the cross-race effect, in which memory for same-race faces is better than memory for cross-race faces, is only found when the eyes are looking toward the viewer and not when they are averted (Farroni et al., 2007; Hood et al., 2003; Adams, Pauker, & Weisbuch, 2010).

Categorizing faces by gender is faster, and stereotype-congruent information is easier to access, when the faces display direct gaze versus averted gaze, and individuals are rated as more likable and more attractive when they gaze toward us rather than away from us (Macrae et al., 2002; Mason, Tatkow, & Macrae, 2005).

Simply displaying posters with pictures of eyes with direct gaze in a cafeteria reduced the amount of littering behavior that ensued, while the verbal message included, whether antilittering or unrelated, had no impact on littering behavior (Ernest-Jones, Nettle, & Bateson, 2011).

Argyle and Dean (1965) put forth an equilibrium model of affiliativeness suggesting that there is an optimal level of psychological closeness communicated by immediacy cues, and participants would more closely approach an experimenter, by 23%, when the experimenter's eyes were closed versus open.

Increasing the physical space between participants has been found to increase direct gaze, and individuals make less eye contact with a listener as the level of intimacy of the topic they are discussing increases (Exline, Gray, & Schuette, 1965; Schulz & Barefoot, 1974).
Perceiving direct eye gaze increases skin conductance responses, which are associated with increases in arousal, relative to averted gaze (Helminen, Kaasinen, & Hietanen, 2011).

A meta-analysis by DePaulo et al. (2003) shows inconsistent evidence for the common belief that liars can be identified by gaze aversion, since analysis of subjective ratings of eye contact showed liars make slightly less eye contact than nonliars while an objective measure yielded no effect.

Low-status patas monkeys engage in more looking behavior toward higher status conspecifics but not vice versa, and individuals who engage in more direct gaze looking behavior are rated as more dominant or powerful, whereas subordinate individuals avert eye contact when looked at by dominant members (McNelis & Boatright-Horowitz, 1998; Hillabrant, 1974; Dovidio & Ellyson, 1982; Ellsworth, Carlsmith, & Henson, 1972).

Direct gaze can be used as a cue of dominance and can serve to increase the potency of a message, and students in a classroom behave more when verbal reprimands are paired with direct gaze (Ellsworth, 1975; Exline et al., 1975; Van Houten et al., 1982).

When a person makes eye contact with others, it conveys an increased probability of approach and social engagement, whereas averted gaze signals active avoidance and is at times considered itself an act of hiding (Ellsworth & Ross, 1975; Grumet, 1999; Redican, 1982).

According to the shared signal hypothesis (Adams & Kleck, 2003, 2005), direct gaze facilitated processing efficiency, accuracy, and the perceived intensity of approach-oriented emotions such as anger and joy, whereas averted gaze facilitated processing of avoidance-oriented emotions such as fear and sadness, and direct eye gaze is recognized faster when paired with angry faces while averted eye gaze is recognized faster when paired with fearful faces (Adams & Franklin, 2009).

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Eye Behavior and Gaze: Development, Integration, and Real-World Consequences
assets.visual_frame_description: A timeline scrolls from 2-day-old gaze discrimination through infant gaze following and 4-month gaze-emotion integration to older adults' positivity bias in looking. A brain model lights up the STS, amygdala, and FFA as congruent and incongruent gaze-threat pairs flash at 33 ms versus 2 seconds, while a world map panel contrasts eye-contact norms in Western and East Asian cultures.
assets.player_mission: Build a developmental timeline of gaze processing from newborns to older adults, then integrate gaze with emotional expression in a neural model of the STS, amygdala, and fusiform face area. Apply the findings to deception detection, prosocial interventions, and cross-cultural interaction, and argue why the eyes are the most remarkable source of nonverbal information.
key_concepts: A central assumption of all this work is that the eyes capture a disproportionate amount of attention compared to other aspects of nonverbal behavior, particularly considering their relatively small size.

Infants as young as 4 months of age seem to integrate eye gaze and emotion, being more responsive to direct gaze relative to averted gaze displayed by a happy face, but they do not demonstrate integration for fearful faces, suggesting experience is important for integrating compound social cues (Rigato, Menon, Johnson, & Farroni, 2011).
Before learning to crawl, gaze behavior is the primary mechanism by which an infant can approach or avoid others, in an effort to regulate an ideal level of arousal (Stern, 1977).

Older adults tend to demonstrate a positivity bias in visual attention, showing preferential looking toward positive images and an avoidance of negative images, and divided attention reverses this positivity bias, suggesting that sufficient cognitive resources are necessary to control the natural tendency to focus on negative stimuli (Isaacowitz & Murphy, 2010; Knight et al., 2007).

In Western cultures, eye gaze is generally seen as a sign of respect and a failure to make eye contact may be interpreted as suspicious, whereas in East Asian cultures making eye contact can be impolite and averted eye gaze, especially downward shifts, can be seen as respectful (Argyle & Cook, 1976; Knapp, Hall, & Horgan, 2013).
U.S. Caucasian participants tend to look a same-culture experimenter in the eye when answering a question, whereas Japanese participants tend to look away (McCarthy, Lee, Itakura, & Muir, 2006).

Gaze direction can moderate neural activity in response to other-race faces, since White participants showed greater right amygdala activation to Black faces with direct than averted gaze, an effect not found for White faces (Richeson, Todd, Trawalter, & Baird, 2008).

In most primates, direct eye contact accompanies anger and attack whereas averted eye gaze generally accompanies fear and flight, yet in many Old World monkeys and apes direct eye gaze also serves an affiliative function such as greeting and grooming (Hinde & Rowell, 1962; van Hooff, 1976, 1972).

Eye gaze and emotional expression are thought to be predominantly processed along similar neural pathways, yet they have also been demonstrated to have distinct neural systems, so the two cues can be perceptually integrated but need not always be (Haxby, Hoffman, & Gobbini, 2000; Engell & Haxby, 2007).

Adams et al. (2003) found greater amygdala activation to fear than anger when coupled with direct gaze faces but opposite patterns for averted gaze faces, fitting Whalen's (1998) proposal that the amygdala is instrumental in processing stimulus ambiguity.

Adams et al. (2011) crossed eye gaze with threat expressions and found greater neural activation, particularly in the right hemisphere including the right amygdala, for congruent threat cues under conditions of restricted awareness (33 ms), whereas under sustained processing (2 s) greater overall activation was found for incongruent, ambiguous threat cues.

It is remarkable that behaviors representing mere millimeter shifts and dilations of the eyes can have such a powerful impact, giving people troves of information about the intentions of others that can be processed in isolation or within the context of other social cues such as emotional expression.

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Signs, Signals, and Symbols in Olfactics

assets.topic: Mood Signs: Fear, Disgust, and Happy Chemosignals
assets.visual_frame_description: A middle school science room shows students stuffing gauze pads into coded buckets and a -80 C freezer storing them, while a face-morphing console slides from neutral to angry, fear to happy, and neutral to happy with judgment-bias meters. Side panels show an amygdala activation map and a grid contrasting the scrubbed, deodorized modern environment with odor-rich natural air.
assets.player_mission: Collect body odors under mood inductions, run double-blind identification trials with coded gauze pads, and trace how fear, disgust, and happy chemosignals shift facial judgments, reaction times, and behavior in perceivers. Then classify each compound as a sign and evaluate why perceivers remain skeptical of their own detection abilities.
key_concepts: Human olfactics, the nonverbal communication using airborne compounds such as odors, scents, and semiochemicals, has long been neglected in human research despite an extensive research history for nonhuman olfactory communication (Claussen, Howes, & Synnott, 1994).

More of the human genome is dedicated to olfaction than to any other sensory system, and humans can discriminate more than a trillion olfactory stimuli, so olfaction may be the most integrated and complex of the sensory systems rather than primitive (Buck & Axel, 1991; Bushdid, Magnasco, Vosshall, & Keller, 2014).

In an early classroom study, middle school students who smelled coded gauze pads worn in the axillary area matched fear and happy body odors to the mood-induction videos significantly above chance, and Chen and Haviland-Jones (2000) found the same results in a larger, more controlled version that launched the new field (Haviland-Jones & McGuire, 1999).

With multiple trials and a more conservative comparison task, about half of a sample was nearly 100% correct at identifying mood odors after five exposures with no feedback, suggesting that some people are highly accurate and that others possibly can be trained (Haviland-Jones, Wilson, & McGuire, 2014).

Exposure to anxiety chemosignals leads people to attribute more negative and less positive emotion to neutral or ambiguous faces, and the anxiety chemosignal reduced the effectiveness of a happy prime in judging the emotion of a neutral face (Pause, Ohrt, Prehn, & Ferstl, 2004).

Using morphing software, three studies showed that anxiety or fear chemosignals affected judgments at points of facial ambiguity but not at the extremes of the morphs, always leading to a more negative emotional bias (Mujica-Parodi et al., 2009; Zhou & Chen, 2009; Zernecke et al., 2011).

Exposure to a fear mood odor slowed reaction times instead of speeding them up, which researchers suggested could be adaptive because if a threat can be smelled but not seen, freezing or moving cautiously may be the smarter reaction (Chen, Katdare, & Lucas, 2006).

Both disgust and fear mood odors collected from donors produced matching facial expressions on the part of perceivers as well as associated fear- or disgust-related behaviors, showing that these compounds have nonverbal communicative sign values (de Groot, Smeets, Kaldewaij, Duijndam, & Semin, 2012).

Mood signs are produced as part of physiological emotional behavior, since fear or anxiety chemosignals can be demonstrated to impact brain mechanisms responsible for mood, such as activation of the amygdala (Mujica-Parodi et al., 2009).

Mood odors for the research are gathered much as in the original school study, with donors wearing pads tucked in their armpits while watching mood-induction videos, though some researchers use naturalistic situations such as anxiety-producing exams, sky diving, or a high rope course (Pause et al., 2010; Mujica-Parodi & Strey, 2006; Zernecke et al., 2011).

Hall (1969) wrote that the extensive use of deodorants and the suppression of odors in public places results in olfactory blandness difficult to duplicate anywhere in the world, a loss of richness and variety that obscures the deeper memories that come only from odors.

A question for future research is whether supportive olfactory cues are being eliminated by scrubbing all information from the air in controlled environments, a question relevant to managing well-being in homes, hospitals, or workplaces (Haviland-Jones, Hudson, Wilson, Freyberg, & McGuire, 2013).

assets.topic: Identity Signs: Olfactory Fingerprints, Kin Recognition, and Development
assets.visual_frame_description: A wardrobe wall of numbered t-shirts and gauze pads feeds match-rate meters showing about 92% accuracy for self and 85% for near kin, with a womb-to-adolescence timeline of odor learning from fetal diet exposure to adolescent fragrance use. An HLA gene-card rack pairs immune system similarity bars with mate-preference and perfume-choice panels.
assets.player_mission: Run blind identification trials matching shirts, pads, and fragrances to owners, then chart accuracy for self, kin, friends, gender, and age, and link genetic factors such as HLA to odor preference and mate choice. Trace the developmental timeline from fetal odor learning through newborn orienting, infant soothing, and childhood friend recognition.
key_concepts: People can identify the unique odor signature of themselves about 92% of the time and the odors of near relatives with about 85% accuracy, yet judges in these identification studies are very highly reliable while tending to think they are not reliable (Lundstrom et al., 2008, 2009; Porter, Balogh, Cernoch, & Franchi, 1986; Weisfeld et al., 2003).

People can identify the shirts of newborn relatives even before they have met them, and from odor alone strangers as well as family can usually know a person's gender, often age, and whether the person belongs to their group (Porter et al., 1986).

Neuroimaging studies confirm the basic nature of this olfactory identification system by showing that people have dedicated neurological pathways for the process of identifying self and kin odors (Lundstrom et al., 2008).
Strangers may even gather some information about neurotic personalities and dominance from body chemosensory signs (Sorokowska, 2013).

Human fetuses learn about the olfactory environment through foods digested by their mothers and subsequently respond through facial expressions to exposure to those odors several days following birth, conveying family and cultural information that facilitates adaptation (Schaal, Marlier, & Soussignan, 2000; Mennella, Jagnow, & Beauchamp, 2001).

Newborns are more likely to orient toward a breast pad worn by their own mother than to one worn by an unfamiliar female, and familiar odors such as maternal breast milk odor reduce crying and grimacing as well as cortisol levels indicative of stress (Macfarlane, 1975; Goubet, Strasbaugh, & Chesney, 2007; Varendi et al., 1998; Nishitani et al., 2009).

Neonates exposed to a chamomile-scented balm on their mothers' breasts showed fewer facial expressions of disgust to chamomile scent at 7 and 21 months of age, while children never exposed showed no or negative effects compared with a no-odor control (Delaunay-El Allam, Soussignan, Patris, Marlier, & Schaal, 2010).

Older children can identify the t-shirts of their friends, being significantly more accurate in identifying owners of the same sex than the other sex, with girls somewhat more accurate than boys (Mallet & Schaal, 1998).

Immune system genes, especially those known as human leukocyte antigens (HLAs), play a role in odor-based mate preferences, since people tend to prefer the odors of potential mates whose HLAs are dissimilar to their own, and mate selection in closed communities tends to reflect HLA differences (Wedekind, Seebeck, Bettens, & Paepke, 1995; Ober et al., 1997).

Parents who have very similar HLA types are more likely to suffer from spontaneous abortions and are more likely to have low birth weight infants, suggesting some utility to this type of identity sign (Reznikoff-Etievant et al., 1991).

Genetic markers can be used to predict which perfume ingredients people prefer, and when adolescent girls were asked to use a new fragrance they showed lower levels of social enjoyment, used fewer words indicative of intimacy in written narratives, and had elevated heart rates compared with when they used their preferred fragrance (Hammerli, Schweisgut, & Kaegi, 2012; Freyberg & Ahren, 2011; Freyberg & Bart, 2012).

In 1959 Karlson and Luscher coined the term pheromones for airborne chemicals emitted by one member of a species, detected by a conspecific, that result in specific behavioral, neural, or endocrine changes, and androstadienone (AND) has been shown in women, but not men, to have emotional and attentional effects, to modify autonomic nervous system functioning, and to impact neuroendocrine function (Jacob et al., 2001; Bensafi et al., 2003; Savic, Berglund, Gulyas, & Roland, 2001).

assets.topic: Signals: Scented Products, Lavender, Peppermint, and the Proust Effect
assets.visual_frame_description: A product-testing shelf shows identical sweaters that differ only by scent, with quality ratings and long-term brand-memory bars rising with the longer delay from exposure, while a vigilance monitor tracks brain-injured patients under peppermint versus control conditions. A lavender cold-pressor lab shows flat relaxation meters, and a candle-and-Madeleine timeline maps the Proust effect.
assets.player_mission: Audit how product and ambient scent signals operate by measuring attention, memory, performance, and relaxation under peppermint, lavender, and product scents, and then trace the long-term memory effects reminiscent of the Proust effect. Compare congruent and incongruent scent-product pairings and weigh contradictory aromatherapy findings against methodological issues.
key_concepts: A signal scent does not emanate from the product but is added to it, and it brings attention to the product, enhances its value, and, if congruent, increases the likelihood that details including brand name will be remembered long term (Krishna, Lwin, & Morrin, 2010).

Putting a scent on one of several identical sweaters often leads a consumer to describe the scented sweater as having better quality, and the longer the time delay from exposure to memory testing, the more significant the effects of the scent signal in affecting recall (Claussen et al., 1994; Morrin & Ratneshwar, 2000, 2003).

The long-term memory effects for odors, exemplified by Proust's experience of being swept back to childhood by the scent of tea and Madeleine biscuits, are a remarkable signal effect for olfaction and may well distinguish it from other sensory cues (Proust, 1922/2013; Wysocki & Gilbert, 1989).
Simple exposure to peppermint improved attention and decreased error rates on several tasks for patients with significant brain damage (Sullivan et al., 1998).

Inhaling peppermint improved scores on a number of tasks including verbal memory and discrimination, cinnamon fragrance was slightly less effective but still improved performance, whereas jasmine and cherry did not, and peppermint showed significant advantages on several types of athletic performance compared with other scents (Zoladz, Raudenbush, & Lilley, 2004; Raudenbush, 2004).

Peppermint is one of many scents that affect the trigeminal system, dedicated to the perception of irritations such as burning, itching, or cooling, as well as the olfactory system, and it is a type of irritant that is arousing but also perceived as pleasant (Brand, 2006).

Lavender is commonly used to signal relaxation, and studies show that exposing older adults to certain fragrances including lavender improved posture and gait performance and decreased both falls and agitation in the older adult population (Freeman et al., 2009; Ebihara et al., 2012; Y. Sakamoto et al., 2012).

Lavender benefits vary with context, since exposure to lavender during work breaks maintained performance in one study while another found a decrease in working memory and slower reactions for lavender, and there is little standardization across studies and little attention given to individual differences of age, gender, or ethnicity (R. Sakamoto et al., 2005; Moss, Cook, Wesnes, & Duckett, 2003).

In a cold pressor pain test, physiological and self-report indices showed no benefit for lavender in comparison to lemon oil or a no-aroma condition, making it clear the lavender did not have a calming pharmacological effect against physical pain (Kiecolt-Glaser et al., 2008).

A gift of flowers increased reports of happiness over several days, elicited a 100% display of the true smile when presented, changed social behavior among strangers, and improved episodic memory scores among older adults, and the emotion effects could be produced with a gardenia fragrance alone even when the fragrance was not consciously detected (Haviland-Jones, Rosario, Wilson, & McGuire, 2005; Haviland-Jones et al., 2013).

Several studies have shown anxiolytic effects of rose and citrus flower oils on mice that are comparable to exposure to diazepam, or valium (de Almeida, Motta, de Brito Faturi, Catallani, & Leite, 2004).

Morrin and Ratneshwar (2003) confirmed that fragrance may provide long-term detailed memory of products, so the memory effects of floral scents may be robust and warrant further investigation, and numerous products are infused with scent with some evidence this influences attention to the products and consumers' memories for them (Jellinek, 1996).

assets.topic: Symbols: Fishy, Clean, and Ritual Odors
assets.visual_frame_description: A trust-game terminal shows investment bars falling under fish-oil exposure and rising under citrus cleaner scent, with a crumb-removal counter and donation meter beside it. An incense timeline from 3000 BCE to the present runs alongside a status ladder mapping foul-smelling lower ranks to fragrant higher ranks, with cards for frankincense, myrrh, and the biblical Esther.
assets.player_mission: Run trust games under fishy and clean scent conditions, map the cognitive and behavioral effects of citrus cleaner odors, and analyze how ritual, status, and culture give odors symbolic meanings. Then debate whether each odor is a constructed symbol or a representational sign by tracing its adaptive or learned origins.
key_concepts: In trust games, participants exposed to fish oil invested less money than when they were exposed to another unpleasant odor or the control, inferring heightened suspicion and less trust in their partners (Lee & Schwarz, 2012).

It is not fish per se that is untrustworthy but the smell of decaying fish, since fresh fish should smell like the ocean and only fish that is not fresh smells fishy, so the fishy odor is representational rather than a completely constructed symbol like a word (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, n.d.).

Cultural differences in odor symbolism can result in cultural clashes, as when an Arab colleague perceives trust when he can detect the breath of his North American colleague while the colleague perceives intrusion or aggression, making it difficult to broach other problems (Hall, 1969).

Individuals with lower status due to age, gender, class, ethnicity, religion, or occupation have often been described as foul-smelling, whereas higher ranked individuals are described as especially fragrant and heavenly beings the most fragrant of all, so odors have traditionally been associated with goodness, even godliness (Claussen, Howes, & Synnott, 1994; Rozin, Haidt, & McCauley, 2008).

Participants exposed to the odor of a citrus-scented cleaner, even though they did not identify it, were more likely to identify cleaning-related words in a cognitive task, to use more cleaning-related words in an unrelated dialogue, and to engage in more cleaning behaviors defined as removing snack crumbs from their work environment (Holland, Hendriks, & Aarts, 2005).

Participants gave back more money in an anonymous trust game and indicated greater willingness to volunteer and donate money when they were exposed to the odor from a citrus-scented cleaner (Liljenquist, Zhong, & Galinsky, 2010).

Orange oils and citronella were effective in inhibiting more than 20 tested bacteria strains as well as about a dozen strains of fungi, so citrus odors are signs for good health in addition to being learned symbols of cleanliness, and the separation of odors into categories of sign, signal, and symbol is more difficult than usually suspected (Pattnaik, Subramanyam, & Kole, 1996).

As early as 3000 BCE, Hindi, Jewish, Muslim, and Christian ceremonies have used incense or aromatic spices, and Howes wrote that the fragrances or incense used in ritual, much like the use of drumming in the same type of group context, lead to a shared mood in a group of people (Howes, 1987).

Stoddart (1990) pointed to phytosterols in plants whose fundamental structure is the same as hormones that orchestrate the reproductive system of animals, reported that pine resins contain the male hormones testosterone and androstenedione, and argued that the choice of incense as well as perfumes is based on erotogenic compounds.

Howes (1987) proposed that the transitional symbolism of scents is central to their use as signals, since putrid odors signal the transition to decay, flowering odors signal the transition to spring, and cooking odors signal the transition from raw to edible.

People can learn to like odors such as parmesan cheese that can be confused with the odor of vomit, yet even sophisticated cheese lovers do not wear it and no one puts it on bed sheets, whereas select floral, herbal, and tree scents including lavender, peppermint, gardenia, and frankincense have been used in all these products (Herz & von Clef, 2001).

In some cultures, a young woman may eat flowers or use sweet floral and resinous unguents for a length of time before a romantic encounter or perhaps a wedding to change her body scent to one that is sweeter and more floral, a practice with ancient roots as when Esther prepared for marriage with six months of oil of myrrh and six months with sweet odors (Stoddart, 1990; Esther 2:12).

assets.topic: The Search Engine Hypothesis and Future Directions
assets.visual_frame_description: A greeting-scene simulation shows a lingering disgust cue from a departed person lighting up search paths across faces, memory networks, and contextual panels, with a multisensory booster meter for attention. A neural map shows synaptic output changing at the olfactory sensory neuron when an odor is paired with shock, and a question board scrolls the chapter's open quandaries.
assets.player_mission: Model the search engine hypothesis by simulating how a subconscious olfactory cue triggers rapid searches by other senses, and weigh the evidence that olfactics is mostly implicit, from multisensory attention boosting to synaptic learning in the olfactory system. Then defend the field's future directions and answer the chapter's unresolved quandaries about vocabulary, memory, context, and genetics.
key_concepts: Rather than being a system designed for identification, an information approach more suited to vision, the olfactory system is designed more as a subconscious parallel rapid processor that prompts searches to be carried out often by the other senses, an idea called the search engine hypothesis (Haviland-Jones & Wilson, 2008).

If two people are greeting each other and a disgust olfactory cue is left in the air from a departed person, the semiochemical prompts a rapid subconscious search for related contextual cues or internally from a memory network, but the outcome of the search is not determined and depends on other available information gathered in the search.

Olfactory compounds may affect arousal states even when focused attention is on the visual or auditory aspect of an event, making the perceiver more alert and more likely to scan the environment or memory for significant changes and cues, so olfaction is part of a multisensory attention booster.

Because the olfactory compound is often or usually subconsciously detected, people are very likely to believe the origin of a search was the seen, heard, or touched target or event identified later in the search, skipping the subconscious olfactory cue because they were never aware of it.

Even when not identified, one person's mood sign affects another's facial movements and attributions and alters the semantic web so that words related to the mood odor become more frequent in use and more quickly identified (see Chapter 21, this handbook).

Sela and Sobel (2010) tested the hypothesis that there is a sensory amnesia for odors that naturally interferes with object identification, arguing that the olfactory system operates largely at the unconscious level as a rapid information source for certain types of information but not for objects.

McGann and colleagues found that the synaptic output of the olfactory sensory neurons, the first cells that physically contact odor molecules in the nose, changes when an odor is paired with shock, contradicting previous concepts that associations occurred in the cortical limbic brain regions rather than at the peripheral edge of the system (Kass, Rosenthal, Pottackal, & McGann, 2013).

People exposed traumatically to chemical compounds may report serious reactions to very low levels of the traumatic odor, levels thought to be below threshold, and the change in their ability to detect the offending compound is often unconscious and unlikely to respond to ordinary therapeutic intervention.

Research on automaticity by Bargh and colleagues shows an embodiment of sensory processes in which there are metaphoric associations, such as warm air being associated with warm feelings and heavy weights with seriousness, and in olfaction floral scent is associated with happiness while fishy odors are associated with untrustworthiness (Bargh, Gollwitzer, Lee-Chai, Barndollar, & Trotschel, 2001; Bargh, Schwader, Hailey, Dyer, & Boothby, 2012).

Most people can smell fear odors from other people even though they are mostly skeptical of this, and most people can identify the olfactory thumbprint unique to themselves at nearly 100% accuracy without having confidence in being correct while also being very good at identifying the olfactory thumbprints of their near relatives and often their close friends (Chen & Haviland-Jones, 2000; Lundstrom et al., 2008).

Paradigms and tools to explore the subconscious processes inherent in olfactics need to be expanded and developed, with multisensory processes likely to be paramount, including the effects of olfactory cues on facial and postural movement and on directed attention in vision, audition, and touch (see Chapter 21, this handbook).

Open questions for future research include what the vocabulary of olfactory messages is, whether people differ in reactions to traumatic chemical exposure mainly due to prior experience or genetic sensitivity, whether olfaction affects long-term memory, and how context affects olfactics, such as whether undetected floral odors influence positive social behavior in threatening contexts as they do in safe ones.

chapters.title: Chapter 15: The Body: Postures, Gait, Proxemics, and Haptics

assets.topic: The Reading Room of Postures
assets.visual_frame_description: A softly lit lounge with leather chairs where mannequin-like figures sit in distinctive poses. Overhead captions flash posture labels like 'arms akimbo,' 'legs crossed,' and 'forward lean,' while a progress bar tracks how many postures you have decoded.
assets.player_mission: You enter a study lounge where you must decode the silent vocabulary of the body. Read each scenario card, identify what the posture says about the sitter's attitude, openness, and status, and label the display correctly (open/closed, dominant/submissive, congruent/incongruent) before moving to the next card. Finish by sorting the posture list into its three dimensions: liking, orientation, and attention.
key_concepts: Postures are defined as a position of the body or of body parts, and early research showed they communicate attitudinal states and general affect rather than the specific emotions communicated by the face and voice.

The attitudinal and general affective states communicated by posture include liking versus disliking, orientation (closed or open), and attention (direct or indirect), which together summarize general positivity and status relationships.

Body orientation, the degree to which a person's shoulders and legs are turned toward or away from another interactant, is associated with attitude toward that interactant, with the least direct orientation occurring for disliked interactants.

Open arms and legs in a seated position generally communicate a more positive attitude and openness, whereas arms akimbo (arms on hips) or arms crossed in front of one's body are generally associated with more negative attitudes.
Open body postures also communicate more power, as demonstrated in research on status display (Cashdan, 1998; Hall, Coats, & LeBeau, 2005).

In a study using 176 computer-generated mannequin figures, observers could not distinguish disgust, fear, and surprise beyond chance levels, but anger, sadness, and happiness were reliably attributed to a large number of postures, some with greater than 90% agreement rates.
Anger postures were conveyed by a backward head tilt, absence of a backward chest bend, no abdominal twist, an arm raised forward and upward, and weight transfers either forward or backward.

Happiness was conveyed by a backward head tilt, no forward movement of the chest, and arms raised above shoulder level and straight at the elbow, while sadness was conveyed by a forward head tilt, forward chest bend, no twisting, and arms at the sides.

Mirroring, known as the chameleon effect, refers to the tendency to adopt the postures, gestures, and mannerisms of interaction partners, and it produces positive regard when done naturally, but deliberate mirroring makes partners feel manipulated.
Nonverbal behaviors associated with rapport include smiling, direct body orientation, uncrossed legs, symmetrical arms, moderate eye contact, congruent limbs, and forward leaning postures.

Tickle-Degnen and Rosenthal (1990) suggested that the development of rapport is a dynamic process involving mutual attentiveness, positivity, and posture coordination, with positivity and attentiveness more important early and coordination more important later.

Posture-gesture mergers, movements in which a gesture flows directly into a postural shift, were associated with truthfulness versus deception, frustration, relaxation, and judgments of sincerity and effectiveness.

assets.topic: Triumph or Tremble: The Body Speaks
assets.visual_frame_description: A dim rehearsal studio with a large mirror and a camera tripod. Actors in point-light suits walk and strike poses, and their movements render as moving dots on a screen while you select labels from a dial like pride, triumph, shame, anger, and happiness.
assets.player_mission: You are a movement analyst interviewing actors who must pose a series of whole-body emotions. For each posed emotion, choose the movement profile that matches the evidence (expanded versus contracted, fast versus slow, jerkiness, arm and head positions) and decide whether the display fits pride, triumph, anger, happiness, or shame. Replay each video clip until you classify all five emotions and note which two emotions researchers have not yet cleanly separated.
key_concepts: In a study of 3-second video clips, observers judged angry, happy, sad, and neutral portrayals beyond chance levels, and angry body movements were rated as jerkier, stiffer, harder, more expanded, faster, and with more action than the other emotions.

Participants expressing happiness through free dance movement moved faster, with more acceleration, and made more expanded and more apparently impulsive movements than participants in the sad condition.

Dael, Mortillaro, and Scherer (2012) asked 10 actors to pose 12 emotions and found evidence for patterns of postural movements associated with only three of the 12 emotions: anger, amusement/pleasure, and despair.
The pride expression includes an expanded posture with head tilted back, arms akimbo, and a low-intensity smile on the face, and it is distinguished from other positive emotions.

The pride expression has been reliably recognized in adults across cultures and in children as young as 4 years of age, and it is produced by individuals across cultures as well as by individuals who are congenitally blind.

The triumph expression includes an expanded posture with chest out and head back, arms away from the body and raised above the shoulders, and torso pushed out, along with an aggressive component involving facial grimaces, fists, punching motions, and shouts or utterances.
The triumph expression has been documented in individuals from many cultures and in congenitally blind individuals immediately after a victory in an agonistic context.

Individuals from status-oriented cultures tend to produce more whole-body victory expressions than individuals from more egalitarian cultures, and people of different cultures reliably label these displays as triumph.
The expression of triumph is related to dominance threat displays seen across the animal kingdom and is likely important in the creation and maintenance of status hierarchies in communities.

Behaviors opposite to triumph, such as head tilted forward or down, tongue out, eyes closed, and one or both arms pulled in toward the body, have been labeled shame, but these same behaviors have also been associated with submission.
There is yet to be definitive research delineating the difference between expressive behaviors related to shame and those related to submission.

Movement synchrony between interactants is strongly related to rapport: Bernieri (1988) demonstrated a strong relationship between rapport and movement synchrony in teacher-student interactions, and synchrony has also been related to the quality of mother-infant interactions and opposite-sex courtship rituals.

assets.topic: The Gait Lineup
assets.visual_frame_description: A monochrome security monitor splits into four feeds showing point-light walkers striding across a checkered floor. Each feed displays animated stride lines and readings for stride length, arm swing, velocity, and footedness, while a red flag icon marks your vulnerability decisions.
assets.player_mission: You are a security analyst reviewing surveillance footage of people walking through an airport corridor. For each walker, use the gait evidence (stride length, foot swing, arm coordination, velocity, confidence) to judge emotion, likely vulnerability, and personality, and flag walkers who match the profile of a would-be victim. Match each gait signature to the correct diagnosis or application before the shift ends.
key_concepts: Gait is the pattern of movement of the body when walking, and classic research suggested that gait is consistent with other expressive behaviors within an individual and thus partially accountable for one's personality (Allport & Vernon, 1933).

Early studies showed that observers can accurately judge the sex of a person by gait alone, even when targets wear bulky sweatshirts with only reflectors on their shoulders, elbows, hips, knees, and other joints.

Using a point-light technique in which there are no other visibly observable cues, individuals can reliably recognize people through their gait, and there is also evidence that age and sex can be reliably identified across cultures.

When actors posed emotions of pride, happiness, anger, and sadness, they walked with longer strides and more exaggerated foot pounding (heavy footedness) when posing anger than when posing the other emotions.

Gait patterns are different when people simulate different emotional states or while listening to different types of music, and judgments of the emotional state of individuals carrying a concealed handgun versus a concealed 1-L bottle correlated with arm swing and gait.

Gait can be used as cues to determine sexual advances or inappropriate touching, as slow walkers with slow-length strides and personality traits implying vulnerability were identified as targets for inappropriate touching.

Depressed patients show decreased stride length, decreased coordination of arms in movement, and slower velocity, while Parkinson's patients show reduced stride but can be trained to expand the stride by employing various visual clues.

Convicted criminals agree on which people to victimize based on gait: those chosen as would-be victims had strides too long or too short, did not swing their feet, and moved in only two dimensions compared to three.

Criminals who scored higher on psychopathy were more accurate in identifying previously victimized students from videotape and were more likely to mention gait, particularly the confidence in the gait, as a clue to identifying a past victim.
The suggestion that the additional emotional load (such as anxiety) involved with deceptive behavior may produce gait abnormalities has practical applications such as security screening.

There have been no direct studies examining cultural similarities or differences in gait, but research on the pace with which individuals move through cities shows that pace is associated with punctuality, coronary heart disease, and a variety of attitudinal and personality traits.

One concern about posed-emotion studies is that actors are asked to pose emotions, so the produced behaviors may be mimes of an emotion rather than what actually happens when emotions are elicited spontaneously and naturally.

assets.topic: Bubble Mapping: The Invisible Zones
assets.visual_frame_description: A top-down map of a plaza shows pairs of figures surrounded by translucent concentric bubbles labeled Intimate, Personal, Social, and Public. A slider adjusts bubble radius, and a flash and a frowning face icon appear whenever a bubble is breached, while side notes list intimacy-equilibrium responses.
assets.player_mission: You are a proxemics consultant mapping a crowded plaza with concentric zone overlays. For each pair of interactants, drag the correct Hall zone (intimate, personal, social, public) onto their bubble, then adjust the bubble size to match the culture, context, and relationship of the pair. Complete the map without letting any bubble cross its intruder threshold, and flag the reactions that follow a violation.
key_concepts: Proxemics is the use of space in interpersonal interactions, and E. T. Hall's (1966, 1973) classic work specified four levels or zones of interpersonal space depending on social relationship type: intimate, personal, social, and public.

E. T. Hall suggested that in the United States intimate distances are less than 18 in. (45.72 cm), personal distances range from 18 in. (45.72 cm) to 4 ft (1.22 m), social distances range from 4 ft (1.22 m) to 12 ft (3.66 m), and public distances are greater than 12 ft (3.66 m).

Hall suggested that interpersonal distance helps to regulate intimacy by controlling sensory exposures, because the possibility of sensory stimulation (smells, sights, touch) is enhanced at closer distances.

People of all cultures appear to use space according to Hall's major distinctions, but they differ in the size of the spaces they attribute to them, with cultures around the Mediterranean, Middle East, or of Latin origin generally interacting at closer distances.

Arab males tend to sit closer to each other than American males, with more direct, confrontational types of body orientations, greater eye contact, and louder voices, and Arabs at least in the past learned to interact at distances close enough to feel the other person's breath.

When interacting with someone from their same culture, Japanese sat the farthest away, Venezuelans the closest, and Americans in the middle, yet foreigners who spoke in English adopted the American conversational distance compared to when speaking their native language.

Interpersonal spacing differs according to context: individuals chose relatively greater distances after experiencing social isolation, when they believed their interaction would be observed, and when they expected a long conversation on a personal topic.

The single major factor determining interpersonal distances appears to be the relationship of the interactants, as more intimate relationships produce closer distances, with the affective tone of the interaction the next most important factor.

Intermediate distances are generally rated as more comfortable, preferable, and appropriate than more extreme close or far distances, and violations of culturally appropriate space boundaries bring about aversive reactions.

The intimacy equilibrium hypothesis (Argyle & Dean, 1965) suggests that people take steps to reinstate their space when boundaries are intruded, for example by staring at floor numbers in an elevator, changing body orientation away, or deploying buffers such as books or briefcases to demarcate territory.

A meta-analysis demonstrated that personal space gradually and steadily increases between 3 and 21 years of age, and while a 5-year-old intruding on an adult's rear space makes the adult turn toward and speak to the child, 10-year-olds make adults move, lean away, or fidget.

When people ask permission to invade space, males and females react differently: males left more quickly when the confederate sat closer and did not ask permission, whereas females left more quickly when the confederate sat closer but asked for permission.
