assets.topic: The Touch Code: Reading Contact
assets.visual_frame_description: A grand ballroom rendered in a heat-map style where glowing hand symbols appear between interactants and trace the toucher's arm. A panel shows touch categories (embrace, handshake, pat, adaptor), a compliance meter, and a world map tinted by contact and noncontact culture classifications.
assets.player_mission: You are a cross-cultural etiquette auditor recording touch events at an international gala. For each interaction, log the toucher, the receiver, the touch type, and the greeting ritual, then classify the touch by its function and predict the reaction, including gender asymmetry, compliance effects, and whether the culture is a contact or noncontact culture. Handle every event without misreading a single touch.
key_concepts: Touch (also known as haptics) is related to the use of interpersonal space because it requires close physical contact, and some writers consider interpersonal touch one of humankind's earliest and most basic forms of communication, owing to its importance in early mother-infant caretaking.

Early research indicated that touch conveys positive emotion, closeness, comfort, compassion, intimacy, immediacy, liking, acceptance, warmth, and love, whereas withholding touch can signal negative feelings such as resentment, hostility, anger, or mistrust.
Touch often has different meanings to men and women: men are more likely to interpret touch as communicating affection and sexual attraction, whereas women are more likely to separate those meanings.
Recent research provided initial evidence that touch can communicate distinct emotions such as anger, fear, disgust, love, gratitude, and sympathy across cultures.
Among professional basketball players, increased touch is associated with increased cooperation and improved performance, and touch by female wait staff improved tips offered at restaurants.

Henley (1973, 1977) proposed that higher status individuals have a touching privilege, being allowed to touch others more often than lower status individuals to maintain and express their status differences.
Being touched by close friends of the opposite sex is rated pleasant by both men and women, while being touched by an opposite-sex stranger is unpleasant for women but pleasant for men.

An observational study of 799 intentional touches in public settings reported that other-gender touch was more likely to be initiated by men, and gender asymmetry has been reported in specific types of relationships such as romantic relationships but not others.

Women tend to engage in more same-sex touch than men and report greater comfort with same-sex touch, an effect explained by homophobic attitudes, as men more than women are likely to be seen as homosexual if they exhibit same-sex touch.

Touch increases compliance: in Kleinke's (1977) phone booth study, 96% of people who were touched returned money compared to 63% of those not touched, and touch has also increased compliance with signing petitions, completing surveys, and physicians' requests to take antibiotics.

Cultures regulate touch in social interactions partly through greeting rituals, and Watson (1970) classified 30 countries as either contact cultures (those that facilitate physical contact) or noncontact cultures, a classification largely confirmed by later research.

Self-touching movements, generally called adaptors or manipulators, allow individuals to adapt to internal or external stimuli and have been linked to negative affect, anxiety, withdrawal, hostility, depression, information processing, language construction, Type A behaviors, and attentional focusing, making self-touch an important signal of psychological functioning.

assets.topic: Primate Communication Channels: Faces, Voices, Hands, and Chemical Cues
assets.visual_frame_description: The scene shows a sunlit forest clearing with a chimpanzee baring its teeth toward a groomer while a macaque mother smacks her lips at her infant. Floating labels map each signal to its sensory channel: facial expression, vocalization, gesture, and chemical cue, with arrows linking the bared-teeth display to the human smile.
assets.player_mission: Act as a first-day field assistant for a primatologist and tour the four channels of primate communication. For each channel, identify real examples from the chapter (bared-teeth display, play face, alarm calls, gestures, scent marks) and classify whether the signal is homologous with a human counterpart.
key_concepts: Nonhuman primates communicate with their faces (facial expressions), with their hands and bodies (gestures), using sounds and vocalizations (vocal cues), and through olfactory signaling (chemical cues).

Nonhuman primates produce meaningful, communicative, and functionally relevant body postures, gestures, vocalizations, and facial expressions, many of which appear to be homologous, meaning that they derive from the same ancestral behavior across related species.

The bared-teeth display is a common expression displayed by many primate species, and researchers have hypothesized that this conspicuous expression is related to, or homologous with, the human smile.
Regardless of the specific social context in which it is expressed, the bared-teeth display has an appeasing and/or affiliative function that serves to reduce or avoid conflict.

Duchenne smiles, which are defined by contraction of the orbicularis oculi around the eyes in addition to the zygomatic major raising the lip corners, are used most often by humans in cooperative, sharing contexts.

The play face is a relaxed open-mouth expression whose origin may lie in the movements surrounding biting, ritualized so that the upper lip covers the upper teeth and the mouth appears open and relaxed.
Restricted to social contexts defined as playful, the play face seems to function as a signal to initiate and/or prolong playful activities, possibly confirming that play is only play.
Human laughter has long been considered to be a homologue of the play face, and some primate species have accompanying vocalizations that seem akin to vocalized laughter.
Acoustic similarities between nonhuman primate and human laughter vocalizations match known phylogenetic relationships, supporting the hypothesis that these vocalizations are homologous.

Because calls can travel over considerable distance and can be detected in the absence of direct visual contact, evolution may have favored maintaining unique properties of call sounds across species so that individuals can discriminate conspecific calls from those of heterospecifics.

Primate gestures may be the only nonhuman communication system that can be used intentionally, minimally qualifying for first-order intentionality, meaning the signals are produced with the goal of changing the behavior of others.

A recent study of wild chimpanzees found that many gestures used by the majority of individuals within the community produced reliable outcomes in other group members, indicating that the gestures themselves had meaning.

assets.topic: Measuring Primate Faces: FACS, ChimpFACS, and the Muscle-Based Lexicon
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen shows a split-panel anatomy lab: on one side a human face overlaid with FACS action-unit labels, on the other a chimpanzee face wired for intramuscular electrical stimulation, while a table lists ChimpFACS, MaqFACS, GibbonFACS, and OrangFACS in chronological order with their target species.
assets.player_mission: You are a facial coding trainee. Use the chapter to explain why FACS was modified for nonhuman primates, name the species-specific FACS systems and their order of creation, and walk a colleague through how action units (AUs) are identified and how prototypical expression configurations were built from naturalistic photographs.
key_concepts: The Facial Action Coding System (FACS) is an anatomically based system originally developed in the 1970s to compare expressions across diverse human populations.
The FACS deconstructs facial expressions into their most basic elements, the most minimally observable movements of the face, which correspond to the action of the underlying facial musculature.

The first modification of FACS for use with nonhuman animals was ChimpFACS, developed for chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), followed by MaqFACS for rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta), and later GibbonFACS and OrangFACS.
Development of each species-specific FACS system relied on an explicit understanding of the facial musculature of each species and how it is similar to and/or different from humans.

In some cases intramuscular electrical stimulations were performed to provide direct knowledge of how activation of specific muscles, or combinations of muscles, changes the appearance of the face, leading to the described movement, called an action unit (AU).

The FACS versions have been used to make explicit comparisons between proposed facial expression homologues in humans and chimpanzees, confirming previous observations that many expressions are morphologically similar.

Using FACS coding, researchers have identified movement configurations that represent prototypical forms of facial expressions, such as the smile, which must contain a retraction of the lips, in FACS terms Action Unit 12 (AU12).
Smiles of enjoyment are said to contain AU6, the cheek raiser, which functions to wrinkle the corner of the eyes, referred to as crows feet in the Duchenne smile.
Parr and colleagues coded the movements (AUs) present in more than 250 photographs of chimpanzee facial expressions taken during naturalistic behavioral interactions.

These photographs had previously been categorized as belonging to one of nine expression types using published chimpanzee behavioral ethograms, including bared-teeth display, relaxed open-mouth expression (play face), pant-hoot, scream, alert face, pout, whimper, neutral, and an ambiguous category.

Discriminant functions analyses revealed more than 70% agreement between the ChimpFACS coded movements and the a priori expression categories given to the photographs, with poor agreement for ambiguous expressions, neutral faces, and pouts frequently confused with pant-hoots.

Expression prototypes containing the component movements common to photographs with more than 90% agreement were created using the software Poser, and the bared-teeth display prototype is composed of AUs 10 + 12 + 16.

assets.topic: Observational Science: Allometry, Ecology, and Social Complexity in Primate Signals
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen renders a scatterplot gallery where each panel plots a species variable (body size, arboreality, group size, grooming time) against a communication trait (facial mobility, call fundamental frequency, facial color complexity), with primate icons whose sizes and habitats shift as the regression lines update.
assets.player_mission: As a comparative behavioral ecologist, you must audit an observational dataset linking species traits to communication. Test whether body size, habitat type, group size, and power asymmetry predict facial mobility, vocal structure, and expression repertoires, citing the correlational findings in the chapter.
key_concepts: The evolution of at least some communication signals is subject to allometric constraints, the idea that anatomy, physiology, and behavior scale in relation to one's body size.
In primates, large individuals utter calls that are longer in duration, lower in fundamental frequency, and have smaller formant dispersion than smaller animals.

Body size correlates strongly with facial mobility, such that large-bodied primate species have a higher facial mobility than small-bodied species, even when taking phylogenetic proximity into account.

A direct comparison of the number and organization of the facial musculature across a variety of primates has revealed a very similar muscular plan, suggesting that it is not the number of facial muscles per se but perhaps how they are used that matters for communication.

Gorillas and chimpanzees have the same degree of facial mobility, with 13 anatomically distinct basic movements or AUs each, yet gorillas rely more on gestural communication while chimpanzees display a broad and diverse range of facial expressions.

Although it is often assumed that terrestrial species exhibit greater reliance on facial expressions and higher facial mobility than arboreal species, the comparative relationship was not statistically significant, possibly because arboreality was only measured using a dichotomous scale.

Species living in tropical, dense forests had darker parts of their face and darker faces overall, whereas species living in more open habitats and temperate climates had lighter faces, a pattern that could have evolved to make individuals more cryptic and less vulnerable to predation.

According to the social complexity hypothesis for communication complexity, individuals living in complex societies face greater challenges than individuals living in simpler societies, leading to larger brains and more advanced social cognition.

Facial mobility increased in parallel with group size in several primates, and more socially tolerant species of macaques were found to have a larger facial expression repertoire than species that showed less social tolerance.

In a comparative study of 139 primates, species with larger group sizes had more complex facial color patterns than species with smaller group sizes, and facial color complexity also increased with the degree of sympatry.

The silent bared-teeth (SBT) display is considered homologous to the human smile, and its function ranges from formal subordination, submission, and appeasement to peaceful intentions and even playfulness.

According to the power asymmetry hypothesis, in species with asymmetrical power balance such as rhesus macaques the SBT display is emitted unidirectionally by lower to higher ranking individuals, whereas in species with symmetrical power balance such as Tonkean macaques its meaning can vary broadly with social context.

assets.topic: Experimental Design: Teaching Primates to Match, Sort, and Recognize Expressions
assets.visual_frame_description: The scene is a touchscreen testing chamber where a chimpanzee faces a sample photograph and two choice images, while a live multidimensional scaling plot grows on a side monitor showing bared-teeth displays at one pole and threat faces at the other, with a subordinate-dominant axis labeled in red.
assets.player_mission: You are a lab methodologist designing a matching-to-sample battery for monkeys and apes. Plan the stimulus sets, trial types, and analytic tools (MDS, discriminant functions, Poser prototypes) used in the chapter's recognition studies, and predict which expression pairs produce confusion errors and why.
key_concepts: Kanazawa (1996) trained Japanese macaques to discriminate among several expressions, for example, bared-teeth displays and threat faces, each with examples varying in intensity from peak intensity to neutral, and used multidimensional scaling (MDS) analysis to create a matrix showing the basis of the perceived differences between the expression types.

In Kanazawa's MDS analysis the two expression types varied continuously along a horizontal axis labeled subordinate-dominant, running from bared teeth on one end to threats on the other, and along a vertical axis labeled neutral-tense, ranging from neutral faces to tense mouth expressions.

Correlational analyses revealed that eye-width, mouth thrust, and mouth curve were the prominent features for the subordinate-dominant axis, and brow raise was the predominant feature for the neutral-tense axis.

When discriminating among human facial expressions, the Japanese macaques were able to classify only the smile and were unable to discriminate anger and disgust faces from sad faces, perhaps because these features lacked biological relevance for the monkey.
Parr and Heintz (2009) tested the ability of rhesus monkeys to discriminate among conspecific facial expressions using a matching-to-sample task.

The monkeys easily learned to discriminate between expression types when the matching pair showed identical photographs of a facial expression or when different monkeys made the same expression and the nonmatching image was a neutral portrait of another monkey.

Subjects had a much harder time when the nonmatching image showed a third monkey portraying one of the other expression categories, meaning the monkeys had trouble discriminating between different expression categories when the expressions were also portrayed by different individuals.

In the Parr and Heintz MDS analysis one axis appeared to represent mouth shape, ranging from mouths stretched open to mouths that were funnel shaped, whereas the other axis appeared to represent lip retraction, ranging from lips fully retracted to relaxed and open.

Facial expressions are highly dynamic stimuli ranging from subtle microexpressions to fully charged affective displays, and presenting them as static photographs diminishes their signal value, resulting in poor performance and perhaps forcing subjects to attend to other cues.

Parr and colleagues tested the extent to which chimpanzees could discriminate expression prototypes using only their individual component movements in a matching-to-sample task where each trial paired a prototype with three combinations of its component movements.

Not all component movements were equally salient for expression discrimination, and chimpanzees spontaneously chose the most representative movement over the other possible combinations, showing that discrimination can be accomplished by the presence of a single component movement as long as it is the most salient in the configuration.

When discriminating among the prototypes themselves, the chimpanzees became confused, making mistakes, when the two expressions shared not the greatest number of individual movements but the most prototypical movements.

assets.topic: The Big Picture: Multimodality, Context, and Mood in Primate Communication
assets.visual_frame_description: The final scene is a control-room wall of screens: one shows a macaque looking longer at a video whose vocalization matches its mouth movements, another replays an incongruent audio-visual chimp trial where screams are matched visually and pant-hoots auditorily, and a live social-network graph colors dyads by whether their bared-teeth displays precede grooming or withdrawal.
assets.player_mission: Synthesize the chapter as the lead investigator of a final report on why primate communication must be studied multimodally and in context. Integrate the Partan and Marler framework, modality-preference results, context-dependent bared-teeth functions, and mood effects on attention, then state the chapter's conclusions about future research needs.
key_concepts: According to the Partan and Marler framework, individual components of composite signals can provide either redundant or nonredundant information, and redundant signals elicit similar responses in a receiver when presented alone regardless of modality.

Redundant signals presented together in a multimodal form can cause either the same response (equivalence) or an increase or decrease in the intensity of the response (enhancement and antagonism), and they can be particularly efficient in improving the salience of multimodal signals so that different channels back up each other.

Nonredundant signals elicit different responses from a receiver, but when combined in a multimodal form they can elicit an increased or decreased response (modulation) or the emergence of a totally new response.

In macaques, lipsmacks accompanied by a soft grunting vocalization are more likely to lead to an affiliative physical contact than when given alone, demonstrating an effect of enhancement on receivers' responses to the visual display.

In Parr's (2004) study, chimpanzees matched facial expression videos with still photographs and showed a strong preference to match screams using the visual modality and pant-hoots using the auditory modality, with a slight bias to match the play face using its distinctive laughter vocalization and no preference found for the bared-teeth display.

Ghazanfar and Logothetis (2003) found that young rhesus monkeys looked longer at the video corresponding to the vocalization played in more than 67% of trials, significantly greater than the 50% looking time expected by chance, and showed greater congruency detection for the coo videos than for the aversive threat videos.

The frequency of mouth movements during nonhuman primate communication is the same frequency as that seen during human speech, providing evidence for an evolutionary relationship between primate facial expressions and human speech.

Flack and de Waal (2007) found that pig-tailed macaques sometimes used bared-teeth displays in peaceful contexts, and that aggression was less frequent and grooming was more frequent among dyads of monkeys in which the bared-teeth display was given outside of conflict contexts, acting as a type of insurance against future aggression.

In rhesus macaques the bared-teeth display has been described as a formal signal of submission because it is used unidirectionally, given by lower ranking individuals to higher ranking individuals but not in the other direction.

Beisner and McCowan (2013) identified two nonconflict usages of the bared-teeth display in rhesus macaques, bared-teeth leave and bared-teeth stay, and found higher rates of grooming and lower rates of aggression among individuals who used the bared-teeth stay signal.

Bethell and colleagues (2012) found that rhesus monkeys in a positive mood maintained their vigilance toward a negative facial expression, whereas monkeys tested after an aversive event followed their initial vigilance with a period of sustained aversion, avoiding looking at the negative expression.

Communication is essentially multimodal and contextually determined, and multimodal signals can lead to qualitative as well as quantitative changes in receivers' responses, yet more research is needed to understand their characteristics and their social function.

assets.topic: The Facial Coding Toolkit: From Darwin's Principle to FACS, MAX, and EMG
assets.visual_frame_description: The scene is a coding lab with six workstations: one screen shows the MAX atlas of three facial regions, another shows a photographic FAST atlas with criterion photos for eyebrow/forehead, eyes/lids, and lower face, a third plays a certified FACS coder scoring action units, and a smaller monitor displays a face with two surface EMG electrodes and live muscle traces.
assets.player_mission: Act as a new lab trainee learning the measurement systems for facial expression. For each technique (MAX, AFFEX, FAST, FACS, EMFACS, facial EMG), state what it codes, how coders are trained or certified, and what the chapter says about its sensitivity to subtle expression.
key_concepts: Most techniques for facial expression measurement stem from Darwin's (1872/1998) analysis and presume that certain patterns of facial expression are naturally associated with specific emotions.

The MAX system scores movement in three facial regions separately and independently, and it has the advantage of forcing attention to the disconnected details of expression while avoiding effects of general inferences about the emotion being experienced.
A MAX coder's reliability is assessed by requiring at least 80% agreement (onset and offset points within 0.5 s) with the master code in the MAX training manual.

The AFFEX system trains judges to observe the whole face, identify discrete facial cues, identify their temporal sequence and duration, and label the emotion directly, arguably retaining advantages of holistic judgments based on simultaneously observing movement patterns in all areas of the face.

The FAST, developed by Ekman and colleagues, scores movement in three facial areas (eyebrow/forehead, eyes/lids, and lower face) using a photographic atlas with 8 criterion photographs for the eyebrow/forehead, 17 for the eyes/lids, and 45 for the lower face.

Unlike MAX, AFFEX, or FAST, the FACS focuses on facial musculature points underlying all facial movements, not only those associated with emotion, and it identifies action units (AUs), their intensity, and degree of asymmetry.

The FACS extended the concept of animation units first described by the Swedish researcher Carl-Herman Hjortsjo in 1969, renaming them action units, and persons purchasing, studying, and successfully completing online tests become certified FACS coders.

The EMFACS uses the FACS to score only the AUs and AU combinations considered by Ekman and colleagues to be relevant to detecting emotion, and it is made available only to persons who are certified FACS coders.

The authors caution that EMFACS should not be used to study emotion blends, disguised or highly controlled emotions, or very subtle expressions, and the empirical evidence supporting its choices of AUs is mixed.

Facial EMG records the electrical activation of facial muscles that may not be associated with visible movement, ordinarily with two small surface electrodes (less than 4 mm) located close to one another over a facial muscle of interest.

In a classic experiment, Dimberg (1982) showed that pictures of happy and angry facial expressions evoked different facial EMG response patterns, with increased zygomatic region activity to happy expressions and increased corrugator region activity to angry expressions.

Compared with the analysis of visible facial expression, facial EMG has an advantage in sensitivity because it detects activations of facial muscles so faint that they are not associated with any visible facial movement, and there is evidence that such responses are automatic and unconscious.

assets.topic: The Machine Eye: History and Competitions of Automated Facial Emotion Detection
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen shows a timeline gallery: a 1973 dissertation page and a 1978 conference paper with 20 facial points, then 1990s workstations with Gabor filters and the MPEG Facial Animation Parameters, and finally two competition banners (FERA 2011 and EmotiW 2013) with a live confusion matrix of six emotion categories on the winner's screen.
assets.player_mission: You are a historian explaining the development of automated emotion detection systems (AEDS) to a colleague. Trace the timeline from the first attempts in the 1970s through the FERA and EmotiW competitions, name the three required stages of an AEDS, and describe what the meta-analyses concluded was solved versus still challenging.
key_concepts: All attempts at automated facial emotion recognition have required researchers to consider what the human eye and brain are doing while observing, processing, and interpreting facial emotions (Pantic & Rothkrantz, 2000).

AEDS generally require three stages: face acquisition, feature extraction, and emotion expression recognition, and they fall well short in their capacity to contextualize the scenarios in which facial emotions are being displayed.

Most sources suggest that the first attempt to automatically recognize emotions through facial displays was a dissertation by Kanade (1973), followed by a 1978 conference article proposing automatic expression analysis using 20 facial points (Suwa, Sugie, & Fujimora, 1978).

By 1992, research on computerized facial recognition was limited because images had to have no occlusion, no facial hair, no glasses, and no scars or other distinct facial anomalies, and databases of faces were limited (mostly White males).

Systems designed from 1991 to 1995 lacked the capacity to classify emotion expressions in terms of AUs, and only one system of the 11 reviewed by Pantic and Rothkrantz (2000) was able to perform in real-time.
None of the AEDS reviewed by Pantic and Rothkrantz (2000) were able to extract data from images with occluded faces or to accurately classify all 44 facial AUs.

Essa and Pentland (1997) used a combination of previous methods to generate the FACS+, an extension of the FACS coding system, and in 1999 the Moving Pictures Experts Group's Facial Animation Parameters became the international standard for computer animation.

Valstar et al. (2012) concluded that inferring discrete emotions from video of known subjects may well be considered solved, meaning that automatic detection of the six basic emotions has only marginal room for improvement.

The FERA 2011 challenge data set was a portion of the Geneva Multimodal Emotion Portrayals, a collection of more than 7,000 audiovisual emotion portrayals (of 18 emotions, 26 facial AUs labeled frame-by-frame) enacted by 10 actors, and the data suggested that modeling appearance dynamics over geometric features alone was more efficient.
In the EmotiW 2013 challenge, Kahou et al. (2013) won the emotion recognition competition with a recognition accuracy rate of 41.03% (well above the test fusion baseline of 25%).

Kahou et al. (2013) found that typical SVMs were overfitting models by scanning very small spaces and that multilayer perceptrons were also overfitting, and their solution was to aggregate per model and per class predictions via random search over simple weighted averages.

The FACET software (formerly CERT) allows an integration between physiological responses and overt displays by synchronizing in real-time the collection of facial affect, skin conductance responses, heart rate, and eye movement, and it achieves 90% accuracy on posed and 80% on spontaneous expressions.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Unresolved Issues: Bottom-Up Analysis, Emotion Detection Versus Communication, and the Posed Database Problem
assets.visual_frame_description: The scene is an audit room with four dossier screens: one contrasts predefined emotion categories with raw facial feature data from 22 or 37 tracked points, another shows a dyad conversation annotated with AEDS output, a third displays the MMI Facial Expression Database browser, and a fourth plays posed versus spontaneous smile videos side by side.
assets.player_mission: As a reviewer, you must audit the four unresolved issues in the facial coding field. For each issue, summarize the chapter's arguments, compare the top-down FACS/MAX approach with the bottom-up machine-learning approach of Ahn and colleagues, and evaluate whether existing facial expression databases can support spontaneous expression research.
key_concepts: Research based on FACS and MAX can be considered top-down in the sense that these systems target facial muscle movement patterns and do not consider other possible sources of facial expression and display.

There is evidence that the face can communicate emotion without scorable FACS movements (e.g., Vanger & Ellgring, 1989), and the cues used in such communication may include slight tendencies to raise or lower the head, blanching or blushing, and changes in pupillary response.

Tomkins's original primary affects included interest/excitement displayed by eye behavior and shame/humiliation displayed by head lowering, yet these emotions were excluded from the primary affects of Ekman and Friesen (1978), perhaps because they could not be expressed in static photographs of posed expression.

According to Ahn et al. (2010), the bottom-up automated technique promises cost-effective detection with greater accuracy, reliability, and the ability to detect micro-expressions that may be lost to the human eye, and it avoids the approximately 1 hr needed to score 1 min of facial behavior into FACS AUs.

In the bottom-up approach, the facial feature data extracted from video clips can involve either 22 or 37 points on the face, based on the Neven Vision or OKAO Vision libraries, and these are mapped to participant behavior that is predicted from facial expressions extracted 3-5 s before the behavior occurs.

In a study of real-time classification of evoked emotions, the percentages of correct classifications in classifying amusement or sadness were 90% and 72%, respectively, and the predictions of emotion intensity correlated significantly with rated intensity at .53 for amusement and .23 for sadness.

The bottom-up approach may have advantages over the category-based systems in terms of sensitivity to all sorts of facial behaviors, not only those preselected as involving specific muscle movements or emotions.

Little research has applied facial coding or AEDS software to study human communicative scenarios as opposed to one-way behavior recognition, animation, and human-computer interaction, and studies of gelotophobia and of dyadic conversations over video show how AEDS could enhance communication research.

The MMI Facial Expression Database presented by Pantic et al. (2005) includes more than 1,500 samples of posed expressions, both static images and brief sequences showing the onset, apex, and offset of the expression, with faces presented in both frontal and profile views.

All of the face databases considered by Pantic et al. (2005), including their own, employed intentionally posed facial expressions, and Bettadapura (2012) pointed out the need for a shift from the analysis of posed to spontaneous expression.

Posed expressions are lacking in that they depict persons not actually experiencing the emotion in question, whereas Ekman and Friesen's (1975) analysis of posed displays convincingly demonstrated pancultural features of facial displays.
It is widely recognized that facial expressions reflect a combination of an innately based emotion display and learned management of the display (Buck & Powers, 2013).

assets.topic: The Slide-Viewing Technique: Measuring Sending Accuracy Across Adults, Children, and Clinical Groups
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen shows a live SVT setup: a sender watches slides (Sexual, Scenic, Pleasant People, Unpleasant, Unusual) while an unobtrusive camera records her face and skin conductance electrodes trace SCDs, and on a side panel receivers guess slide type and rate emotions while a bar chart fills with percent correct and emotion correlation scores.
assets.player_mission: You are a researcher running an SVT laboratory. Design the slide-viewing procedure from the chapter, describe the two communication accuracy measures, classify senders into externalizing versus internalizing styles, and predict the findings for women versus men, preschool children, and the clinical groups studied.
key_concepts: The Slide-Viewing Technique (SVT) was developed from the Cooperative Conditioning Technique used by Robert E. Miller (1967) to study the communication of affect in rhesus monkeys.

In the SVT, participants (senders) view a series of emotionally loaded images while being filmed by an unobtrusive camera, and after each slide the sender rates the emotions felt while viewing the slide.

The filmed expressions are rated by receivers, who attempt to judge what sort of slide was presented on each trial and the sender's emotional response, yielding two measures of communication accuracy.

The percent correct measure is the percentage of slides that receivers correctly categorize, a situational reference task, whereas the emotion correlation measure detects specific emotions as rated by the sender and is correlated across the slides with the sender's ratings.

Communication accuracy is defined in terms of sending accuracy, an individual's spontaneous tendency to send accurate nonverbal emotional messages across receivers, as well as receiving ability, an individual's ability to receive accurate nonverbal emotional messages from others across senders.

In initial studies with young adults, women were significantly better senders than men on both the percent correct and emotion correlation measures, and better senders had smaller increases in skin conductance deflections (SCDs) and heart rate accelerations when beginning to speak.

An externalizing style combined high sending accuracy with low autonomic responding, whereas an internalizing style showed low sending accuracy with high autonomic responding, with a tendency for males to show an internalizing style and females an externalizing style.

In studies with 3.5- to 5-year-olds, a new Familiar People slide category showed the child and friends at the nursery school, which had the advantage of reliably eliciting strongly positive emotional responses that are otherwise difficult to elicit.
Among preschool children, sending accuracy was negatively correlated with age among boys, meaning that as boys got older between 3.5 and 5 years their sending accuracy tended to decline.

Sending accuracy in children was positively related to teacher ratings of extraversion, activity, and having many friends, and also positively related to being aggressive, bossy, and often hard to get along with, while being negatively related to ratings of introversion, shyness, and being solitary.

In the SVT studies with patients with brain damage, aphasic patients were quite expressive when viewing the slides even though they could not speak, and they actually had the highest percent correct scores, significantly higher than the right-hemisphere-damaged (RHD) and Parkinson groups.

Buck and Duffy (1980) suggested that pantomime and PICA measures involve the intention to communicate with arbitrary, learned, culturally patterned symbols whose content is a proposition, whereas the SVT measures spontaneous communication that is a sign of a state and is nonpropositional because it cannot be false.

assets.topic: The Golden Mean: Expressiveness, Social Biofeedback, and the Comprehensive Analysis of Emotional Communication
assets.visual_frame_description: The final scene is an auditorium with a model of the social biofeedback cycle: the sender's display (Emotion II) is read by the partner and fed back to educate the labeling of subjective experience (Emotion III), while a golden-mean curve shows sending accuracy peaking at moderate expressiveness and a montage plays CARAT sequences, segmentation breakpoints, and FACS-coded peaks.
assets.player_mission: Synthesize the chapter as its lead author for a final lecture. Integrate the three levels of emotion (physiological, display, subjective experience), social biofeedback and alexithymia, the curvilinear relationship between expressiveness and sending accuracy, the segmentation technique and the CARAT database, and the three-step strategy for comprehensive analysis.
key_concepts: Emotion is unique in that different aspects of its expression are differently accessible to the responder and the interaction partner: physiological responses (Emotion I), displays (Emotion II), and subjective experience (Emotion III).

The responder has sole access to Emotion III subjective experience, the interaction partner has the best access to Emotion II display behavior, and neither has very good access to Emotion I physiological arousal.

The way that a child learns to label and understand Emotion III experience is through social biofeedback from the partner's response to the display, which naturally leads to emotional education, emotional competence, and social bioregulation.

If a sender is insufficiently expressive, or too expressive, the interaction partner will be confused about the sender's actual emotional state, social biofeedback will be compromised, and the resulting lack of social biofeedback will result in deficits in labeling and understanding Emotion III feelings and desires.

Nemiah and Sifneos (1970) coined the term alexithymia (no words for mood) to describe emotional expression in patients with psychosomatic disease, and such persons cannot describe emotions in words and show high levels of autonomic nervous system responses.

Sending accuracy and expressiveness may actually show a curvilinear relationship, such that sending accuracy will tend to be greatest at moderate levels of expressiveness and low at the extremes of low or high expressiveness, the principle of the golden mean.

Hypoexpressive alexithymia would be associated with extreme introversion, internalizing, high ANS responding, and low sending accuracy, whereas hyperexpressive alexithymia would be associated with extreme extraversion and externalizing, low ANS responding, and low sending accuracy.

The segmentation technique devised by Newtson, Engquist, and Bois (1977) has observers press a button when one meaningful action ends and another begins, and their button presses tend to occur together at high-information points of change called consensual breakpoints (CPs).

When single frames were removed at consensual breakpoints, a new group of observers was much more able to detect the breakpoints (78% vs. 35%), suggesting that observers naturally increase their attention at CPs.

The digital CARAT-S and CARAT-SPR databases contain spontaneous expressions (and, for CARAT-SPR, posed and regulated expressions) judged by clinically normal individuals with 90%+ accuracy, and they are intended for use in studies of brain responses to facial expressions as a supplement to the Pictures of Facial Affect.

The SVT answers the unresolved issues in automatic facial expression analysis because it involves spontaneous, dynamic, and ecologically valid facial expressions; it allows a bottom-up analysis; it is sensitive to communicative aspects of expression; and it generates a facial database independent of the emotion categories used to construct the analysis technique.

The comprehensive three-step strategy is to use communication scores to assess the functional significance of expressive behavior, to use the segmentation procedure to determine when important communicative displays occur, and to use facial coding instruments such as MAX, FACS, facial EMG, and AEDS to analyze the nature of the behavior, since the ultimate function of the display is communication.

assets.topic: The Acoustic Workbench: Low-Level Voice Features
assets.visual_frame_description: A waveform editor highlights a voiced region with a blue pitch track and a green intensity curve drawn over it. Side panels list normalized f0 statistics, jitter and shimmer scores, and a syllable-rate meter, while a live scatter plot tags each utterance by its inferred speaker state.
assets.player_mission: You are a voice analyst digitizing a corpus of emotion interviews. For each recorded utterance, extract pitch (f0) statistics from the voiced regions, intensity means and ranges, speaking rate in syllables per second, and voice quality measures of jitter, shimmer, and harmonics-to-noise ratio. Normalize every feature with z-scores on log-transformed values, then tag which pauses and disfluencies appear to cluster with deception and emotion markers.
key_concepts: A low-level acoustic-prosodic feature is defined as one that is objectively quantifiable and automatically and unambiguously extractable using standard acoustic analysis software.
Pitch features, computed from the voiced regions of speech, include maximum, mean, minimum, standard deviation, range, and counts of rising, falling, doubled, and halved frames.
Intensity (energy) features can be extracted in raw, median-filtered, or stylized form and include maximum, mean, minimum, slope, and standard deviation.
Voice quality measures such as jitter, shimmer, and harmonics-to-noise ratio are used to quantify breathiness, harshness, and vocal fry, which can indicate age and emotion.
Pitch and energy contours are typically constructed with a 10-ms frame rate, so a 20 to 200 ms window corresponds to a mean of 2, 5, 10, or 20 data points.
Pitch halving and doubling errors of pitch trackers occur especially in the presence of vocal fry or diplophonia and have been found to correlate positively with deception.
Pitch and energy reset features, calculated as differences of means, maxima, minima, and z-scores across words or phrases, capture dynamics useful for emotion detection and phrasing prediction.
Speaking rate is typically measured in syllables per second, and automatic speech recognition output can serve as a reasonable proxy when manual orthographic transcription is unavailable.
Preboundary lengthening is detected through the lengths of word-final vowels, syllables, and syllable rhymes, normalized both by phone identity and by speaker.
Range normalization scales data points so the maximum value is 1 and the minimum is 0, but it is very sensitive to the presence of outliers such as pitch halving and doubling errors.
Z-score normalization assumes the underlying data follows a Gaussian distribution, so it is more reliable to apply it to log f0 and log energy than to raw values.
Filled and unfilled pauses and other disfluencies are valuable indicators of speaker state, and ratios of filled pauses across conditions can help distinguish emotions or deceptive behavior.

assets.topic: Prosody on Trial: Pitch Accent and Meaning
assets.visual_frame_description: An utterance is shown as a word strip with accent symbols such as H*, L*, and L+H* placed above syllables and a pitch contour drawn beneath. A legend maps each accent type to meanings like contrastive stress, new information, or uncertainty, while a bar chart shows how often energy versus pitch predicted each accent.
assets.player_mission: You are a prosody consultant for a conversational speech corpus. For each utterance, mark which words are accented, tag each accent with its ToBI type, and decide whether it conveys contrast, new information, uncertainty, or incredulity. Then compare the human labels against acoustic predictors such as duration, energy, and pitch excursions.
key_concepts: Accenting, or intonational prominence, has the effect of drawing a listener's attention to a particular portion of a spoken utterance.
In general, content words such as nouns, verbs, and modifiers are more likely to be accented than function words such as prepositions and articles, although not all content words are accented.

Words that have been uttered earlier in a conversation (given information) are usually less likely to be accented when produced again, whereas items introducing new information are more likely to be prominent.
In SAE ToBI, accented words may bear one of five accents: the simple accents H* and L* and the complex accents L+H*, L*+H, and H+!H*.
The starred tone in an accent label indicates alignment of the accent with the primary stress of the word, while H and L indicate high and low tones.
The L+H* accent, in which the high tone aligns with the stressed syllable and the f0 rise is rapid, can be used to produce a sense of contrast, often termed contrastive stress.
In the L*+H accent the low tone is associated with the stressed syllable and the rise to the high tone is gentler, resulting in more of a scooped accent.

The alignment difference between L+H* and L*+H accents is critical to interpretation, conveying an impression either of uncertainty or of incredulity depending on other prosodic and contextual features.
H* accents, which are typically found in standard declarative utterances, convey that the accented item should be treated as new information in the discourse, as part of what is being asserted.
L* accents convey that an accented item should be treated as salient but not part of what is being asserted, and they are typically seen in yes-no question contours.
Human agreement on the pitch accent detection task falls somewhere between 81% and 91% word accuracy, depending on the experience of the labelers and the genre of the material.
Silipo and Greenberg found that in spontaneous speech duration and energy are the most important acoustic parameters underlying accent, with pitch playing only a minor role.

assets.topic: The Boundary Inspector: Intonational Phrasing
assets.visual_frame_description: A spectrogram with a boundary marker tool shows candidate sites between words, and each site displays cue meters for silence length, preboundary lengthening, and energy slope reset. A verdict panel classifies every site as intonational boundary, intermediate boundary, or none, and an accuracy score is updated against the reference labels.
assets.player_mission: You are a phrasing analyst for a speech-processing pipeline. Listen to each sentence and mark intonational and intermediate phrase boundaries, noting the presence of silence, pitch and energy reset, preboundary lengthening, and final tonal changes. Use these cues to disambiguate ambiguous sentences such as 'Bill doesn't drink because he's unhappy' and score your detection against gold-standard BURNC labels.
key_concepts: Intonational phrasing is the mechanism by which speakers break up speech into meaningful chunks of information, and boundaries typically occur at linguistically meaningful points.

Phrasing can disambiguate syntactically ambiguous sentences, so 'Bill doesn't drink because he's unhappy' without a boundary means Bill drinks but not for that reason, whereas with a boundary before 'because' it means he does not drink at all.

The five major acoustic indicators of prosodic phrasing are the presence of silence, pitch and energy reset, preboundary lengthening, changes in speaking rate, and tonal changes at the end of a phrase.
Silence is the most reliable indicator of disjuncture and is the single most powerful indicator of intonational phrase boundaries, although some boundaries occur without it.
In the f0 domain, the gradual decrease of pitch over the course of a phrase is known as declination, while pitch and energy reset occur at the beginning of new phrases.
For SAE ToBI, the phrase hierarchy consists of an intonational phrase composed of one or more intermediate phrases, each of which contains at least one accented word.
Intonational phrase boundaries are differentiated from intermediate phrase boundaries by the presence of a final tonal event, called a boundary tone.
Intermediate phrase boundaries represent a smaller degree of perceptual disjuncture and frequently are not accompanied by silence.
Words that end intonational phrases are significantly longer than those that do not, signifying preboundary lengthening, although accented words also tend to be longer than deaccented ones.
Detection of intermediate phrases is more difficult than detection of intonational phrases, and energy is more reliable for detecting phrase boundaries than pitch is.
In SAE, declarative utterances typically end with falling intonation and yes-no questions end with rising intonation.
Phrasing is indicated by perceived disjuncture commonly signaled by acoustic reset, and a dramatic increase in energy slope at a boundary may contribute to human perception of disjuncture.

assets.topic: The Annotation Atlas: Standards for Prosody
assets.visual_frame_description: A four-tier labeling window shows orthographic text, break indices from 0 to 4, a tone tier with H and L stars, and a miscellaneous tier, all aligned over a waveform and f0 contour. A world map lists ToBI variants per language, and a toggle switches the same contour between categorical labels and continuous tilt or Fujisaki parameterizations.
assets.player_mission: You are building the annotation lab for a cross-linguistic prosody study. Choose a labeling scheme for each language, such as ToBI tiers for Standard American English, ToDI for Dutch, IViE for British English, and Fujisaki or tilt parameters for synthesis work. Annotate the same sample contours in each scheme and compare how categorical and continuous descriptions represent the identical f0 track.
key_concepts: ToBI, the Tones and Break Indices convention, is a widely used prosody annotation standard for Standard American English and is currently the most popular exemplar of the American school.
ToBI includes a set of labeling tiers: an orthographic tier, a break index tier, a tone tier, and a miscellaneous tier, all aligned with the speech file and a representation of the f0 contour.
The ToBI break index tier identifies five degrees of juncture between words, with higher numbers marking a greater degree of juncture.
A standard SAE declarative contour is modeled with one or more simple high pitch accents, a low phrase accent, and a low boundary tone.
A yes-no question contour in ToBI is modeled by sequences of low pitch accents, a high phrase accent, and a high boundary tone.
Categorical annotations describe prosodic events as elements of a fixed inventory of prosodic phenomena, whereas continuous annotations describe prosody by degree rather than by type.
The British school of intonation describes prosody as pitch movements such as rises and falls, whereas the American school uses pitch targets or tones such as high versus low tones.
The Fujisaki superpositional model describes intonation as a superposition of accent contours on a phrasal contour via phrase and accent commands that control f0.
The tilt model compactly captures the shape of the pitch contour using four values describing how much a peak rises and falls and the durations of the rise and fall.

ToBI has been extended and adapted for many languages, including ToDI for Dutch, C-ToBI for Mandarin Chinese, K-ToBI for Korean, J-ToBI for Japanese, G-ToBI for German, GRToBI for Greek, and SC-ToBI for Standard Serbo-Croatian.
The IViE system for British English is modeled on ToBI but has an expanded inventory of tone targets, two additional labeling tiers for rhythm and pitch movement, and no break index tier.
Manual annotation of prosody is very resource intensive, and it can take an expert labeler up to 100-200 times real time to perform a full ToBI annotation.

assets.topic: Voice Intelligence: Applications and Toolkits
assets.visual_frame_description: A processing pipeline diagram flows from an audio file through Praat, openSMILE, and AuToBI boxes into a feature matrix table. Icons for SoX, Wavesurfer, and Transcriber line the sidebar, and a results pane shows classifier accuracy for deception, emotion, and likeability across feature sets.
assets.player_mission: You are a research engineer selecting tools for a speaker-state study on deception and emotion. Pipeline your interview recordings through Praat for annotation, openSMILE for low-level descriptor and functional extraction, and AuToBI for automatic ToBI labeling, then compare the extracted features between deceptive and truthful speakers. Document which tool best serves each stage of the analysis.
key_concepts: Both low-level and higher level voice features can be extracted automatically for use in studies including age, personality, disability, disease, emotion, likeability, deception, and trust as topics of interest.
Acoustic and prosodic features have been used to distinguish deceptive from non-deceptive speech in research such as Hirschberg et al. (2005).

Higher level prosody analysis has been shown to improve automatic speech recognition, speech synthesis, speaker identification, language and dialect identification, story and topic segmentation, punctuation insertion, and speech act classification.
Praat, developed by Paul Boersma and David Weenink at the Institute of Phonetic Sciences of the University of Amsterdam, is a general-purpose speech tool with its own scripting language.
Praat supports the editing, segmentation and labeling, and prosodic manipulation of audio files, and a large community of users has shared numerous scripts for a wide variety of tasks.

openSMILE operates by first extracting a set of low-level descriptors (LLDs) such as intensity, pitch, and Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients at 10-ms frames and then applying functionals such as mean and standard deviation to them.
One recent openSMILE configuration file, provided as part of the Interspeech 2014 Paralinguistics Challenge, extracted 6,373 features from speech.

AuToBI breaks the task of complete ToBI labeling into six component tasks: detecting pitch accents, intonational phrase boundaries, and intermediate phrase boundaries, and classifying pitch accent types, phrase accent and boundary tone pairs, and phrase accents.
AuToBI represents state-of-the-art performance on each ToBI labeling task, and when trained on one corpus and tested on another its performance suffers modestly, by only 2%-5%.

SoX is a command-line library that supports the conversion of digital audio formats and works on Windows, Mac, and Linux, also allowing users to apply effects to audio files and to play and record them.
Wavesurfer is a similar open-source tool for speech manipulation that is derived from ESPS and XWaves software and is primarily used in speech research labs.
The speech field is currently exploring vocal cues in signaling degrees of autistic dysfunction, degree of cognitive and physical load, empathy, and many other social behaviors.

assets.topic: Classifying Gesture: Categories and Kendon's Continuum
assets.visual_frame_description: A classroom screen shows a three-branch tree of nonverbal categories with a horizontal continuum bar running from sign language through emblems and pantomimes to cospeech gesticulations. Flashcard examples such as the OK sign, a charades enactment, and a Hail Mary football gesture slide into their categories as each placement is confirmed, with a score tally in the corner.
assets.player_mission: You are a taxonomy apprentice building a gesture coding manual. Classify observed behaviors as emotional, regulating, or language-associated gestures, then place each language-associated gesture along Kendon's continuum, deciding whether it is a sign, emblem, pantomime, or cospeech gesture. Finally, sort each cospeech gesture into the imagistic categories (iconic, metaphoric) or the nonimagistic categories (beat, deictic) using both form and function.
key_concepts: Using the broadest conceptualization, gestures have been defined as any action with the hands, arms, fingers, facial features, or even the entire body that is used to communicate to another individual.

The authors subdivide nonverbal behaviors into three broad categories: emotional gestures (which express emotion such as smiling, frowning, or looking confused), regulating gestures (which regulate the flow of interactions), and language-associated gestures (which are used as part of the speaking process in discourse).

Language-associated gestures are seen as symbolic and convey information related to the subject matter transmitted in discourse, reflecting aspects of individuals' mental representations during the process of speaking.

Kendon's continuum, informally outlined by Kendon and formalized by McNeill, classifies language-associated gestures according to two dimensions: the degree to which speech is present or absent and the degree to which the gestures are conventionalized.

At one end of the continuum are sign languages, which are conventionally agreed upon, can operate independently of spoken language, and possess conventionalized elements that correspond to phonemic, morphemic, and syntactic elements in spoken languages.

Next on the continuum are emblems, which are defined by a particular culture, may or may not be used independently of spoken language, and can be associated with ideas such as the OK sign conveying that something is okay.

Pantomime gestures do not need to occur with speech to be understood (in fact, for them to be used speech has to be absent, as in charades), but unlike sign languages they do not have conventionalized rules governing their form and meaning.

At the other end of the continuum are cospeech gesticulations, which are almost always produced in the presence of speech and are idiosyncratic, driven by the speaker's own unique conceptualizations, and not conventionalized by formal rules dictated by a given culture.
The first main distinction made in the gesture taxonomy differentiates imagistic from nonimagistic cospeech gestures.
Iconic gestures represent concrete attributes and actions through visuo-spatial representation, as when an individual says 'Let's go play football' while enacting throwing a football.

Metaphoric gestures represent abstract concepts using concrete visuo-spatial imagery, as when an individual says 'To save my business I did a Hail Mary Pass to potential clients' and represents this idea with the same throwing football gesture.

Nonimagistic gestures do not use imagery and are of two types: beat gestures, which are rhythmic movements that occur with speech to highlight or structure speech, and deictic gestures, which are indexical points whose meanings are derived by what is pointed to rather than by the form of the gesture itself.

assets.topic: The Four-Step Coding Protocol: Isolating Gesture Words
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen video player shows a child explaining a math problem while the coder's overlay tints candidate movements green for gestures, red for functional acts, and yellow for ambiguous cases such as combing hair. A timeline below the video displays colored gesture words with their preparation, stroke, and recovery phase blocks aligned against the speech waveform.
assets.player_mission: You are a gesture coder working through a classroom video corpus. For each movement, apply the four criteria to decide whether it is a cospeech gesture, a direct functional act, or another language-associated gesture such as an emblem or pantomime. Then parse the gesture stream into gesture words using changes in form or location and pauses, and mark the preparation, stroke, and recovery phases of each gesture along the speech timeline.
key_concepts: The research dictates the type of communicative context under examination, and once a context is identified the researcher proceeds through four steps: differentiate cospeech gesture from other behaviors, isolate the gesture word or utterance, describe the form and meaning of the gesture, and analyze the gesture to address a particular research question.

Cospeech gestures satisfy all of the following criteria: the hand or body movement occurs in close temporal connection with speech; it occurs when the speaker is actively engaged with another in communication; it is semantically or pragmatically related to the speech content it accompanies; and it is not a direct functional act on the self, another person, or an object.

A child who looks at his mother, holds his hand above a jar, and makes a twisting motion without actually twisting the lid off while saying 'Can I open this mommy?' has produced a gesture meaning twist (the jar).
Someone holding a comb close to her head while saying 'I really need to comb my hair' would not be considered to be gesturing, because the hand performs a direct act on a real object and the self.

A hand movement that depicts the act of combing synchronized with the word 'comb' in the statement 'I really have to comb my hair' fits all four gesture criteria and would be classified as an iconic gesture.

Whereas Criterion b (engagement with another person) and Criterion d (not a functional act) apply to emblems, Criterion a (timing with speech) and Criterion c (iconic imagery aligned with speech) do not, so the hello or goodbye emblem cannot be classified as a cospeech gesture.
Whereas words are two-dimensional and static, gestures are three-dimensional, seemingly fluid, and nonstatic, which makes parsing the flow of gesture into linear units difficult.

Gestural morphemes can be combined in a linear as well as a nonlinear fashion to reflect complex units of information, as in the snow-falling gesture in which the flutter movement of the fingers and the downward movement of the hand are produced simultaneously.

A change in any dimension of the gesture, such as its form or location, can be used to differentiate gesture units, as when a pointing gesture redirected from a table to a countertop indicates the production of two distinct gestures.
A pause between the presentations of two gestures can be used to parse gestural units, although detecting such pauses is often a luxury that has to be reliably observed.

Gestural descriptions in some systems include marking the preparation phase (in which the movement moves from a rest position to an enacting position), the stroke phase (in which the gesture forms its peak image), and the recovery phase (in which the body, hand, or arm returns to a rest position).

Including codes for the phases of gesturing allows for a precise measurement of gesture timing with respect to speech events and anticipates techniques that precisely measure the timing of speech and associated gestures.

assets.topic: Describing Gesture Form: Location, Hand Shape, and Movement
assets.visual_frame_description: A coding grid overlays a video frame of a child solving a math problem, with each active gesture displaying badge chips for location (neutral space), hand shape (B-shaped or C-shaped), palm orientation, and motion type (within-hand versus crossing space). A diagram beside the frame shows a stick figure with an imaginary stage in front of the torso to illustrate the difference between observer viewpoint and character viewpoint.
assets.player_mission: You are a gesture annotator transcribing children's task explanations. For each gesture, record its location (neutral space, body part, or task object), hand shape using ASL alphabet codes, orientation of the palm and fingers, movement trajectory, and number of hands used, then infer its meaning using the accompanying speech and discourse context. Finally, tag each gesture's viewpoint as observer or character.
key_concepts: To determine the meaning of a gesture, the form of the gesture and the context in which it is performed (speech, discourse, or physical referencing) are used, because the form of the gesture resembles what is being described.

There are three primary dimensions of gesture form that are typically coded, borrowed from Stokoe's American Sign Language coding system: location, hand shape, and the movement trajectory of the hand, arm, or body.

Neutral space, called neutral space by McNeill, includes the space in front of the torso from the chin down to the waist, and gestures produced there use the body location as a stage for depicting a particular image rather than as part of the meaning.

When the body itself is part of the meaning, a gesture performed on a body part helps determine its meaning, as in the case of a stroking gesture oriented toward the head that represents the act of combing hair.

In work with children performing spatial tasks, the location of gestures performed near task objects enables coders to infer gesture meaning, as when a balancing gesture placed near numbers on either side of a mathematical equation on a blackboard is used to infer the representation of the idea equal.

Most coding systems use ASL alphabet hand shapes, such as a B-shaped flat hand with fingers and thumb closed, to describe a gesture hand shape in the first pass of coding, which allows a systematic and universal way to code hand shapes across gesture labs.

The shape of the hand is compared to the shape of the referent to determine meaning, so a straight hand and arm might reflect an object with the same straight shape, such as a tree, provided that the speech or discourse context supports this interpretation.

In addition to hand shape, the orientation of the palm and the fingers with respect to the speaker's torso is documented, so a C-shaped hand held with the palm facing down toward the floor could lead to an inference that the gesture represents a round-shaped object such as a turtle.

Whether a right hand, a left hand, or both hands are used is also recorded, and when two hands are used the relationship between them is described, as when one hand represents a hand holding a nail while the other hand represents a hand holding a hammer and hitting the hand that represents the nail.

Motion of the hand or the body is coded either as within-hand motion, which is typically inferred as reflecting a change in the state of an entity, or as crossing-space motion, which is typically understood as an entity moving from one location to another or as an attribute.

Viewpoint can be inferred from the combination of hand shape and location, and McNeill identified two viewpoints: observer viewpoint, in which the gesturing hand represents an animated character like a puppet on a stage in front of the speaker, and character viewpoint, in which the hand or body represents a bodily action.

The discourse context surrounding a gesture is often critical for interpreting it, so a straight hand and arm is interpreted as a tree when the accompanying speech is 'The tree fell over' but would be interpreted as meaning tower if the same gesture accompanied the speech 'The tower fell.'

assets.topic: From Video to Data: Approaches, Tools, and Reliability
assets.visual_frame_description: A project dashboard shows two method cards labeled Linguistic Approach and Cognitive Approach with example outputs, and a video annotation window displays ELAN tiers for speech, right-hand gesture, and left-hand gesture aligned on a millisecond timeline. A reliability gauge displays the coder agreement percentage, and an export panel shows a frequency table of gesture counts per classroom context with a matching table of speech-gesture mismatches.
assets.player_mission: You are the data coordinator for a gesture lab merging narrative and problem-solving corpora. Choose between the linguistic approach, with its catchments and intensive single-narration analyses, and the cognitive approach, which tabulates gestures across many individuals, then set up your video pipeline in ELAN with tiers for speech, right-hand gesture, and left-hand gesture. Establish interrater reliability of at least 80% agreement between two independent coders and export your codes to Excel to count gesture frequencies and evaluate timing among behaviors.
key_concepts: The linguistic (psycholinguistic) approach, characterized by the work of Kendon and McNeill, is less guided by a coding system and more guided by heuristics or principles developed over decades of research, and it attempts to describe how gesture is used in the context of narrative and conversational discourse.

In McNeill's research, gestures are identified and described in terms of their hand shape, location, and motion, and the first pass of transcription involves transcribing everything that is audible in speech, including partial words, speech repairs, breaths, pauses, and laughs.

Catchments are gestures, or features of a gesture, that recur over a piece of discourse for the purpose of narrative cohesion, as when McNeill identified the recurrent use of a door gesture during a participant's description of her house.

The cognitive approach characterizes research in which coded gestures are tabulated not only for a particular person but also across a number of individuals engaged in discourse, treating gesture as a scale or continuous variable or as a categorical variable to determine patterns of frequency.

A categorical analysis could require a researcher to determine how many teachers in a sample produce gesture at any point in a classroom lesson versus those who produce no gestures at all, whereas a frequency analysis would measure how often gesture occurs during a lesson.

Video recording was a major innovation because, unlike live observations, it allowed researchers to examine minute details of cospeech gesture events using slow motion, time lapse, and event capturing software, such as the exact timing differences between the onset of spoken words and accompanying gestures.

Programs such as ELAN, Anvil, and Transana allow the researcher to set up criteria for identifying discrete behavioral units in communication, and researchers can export their codes to programs such as Excel to count units, compare counts across preidentified situations, and evaluate timing among different behaviors of interest.

In ELAN, annotations can occur within layers of information such as speech, right-hand gesture, and left-hand gesture, which are referred to as tiers, and these tiers can be interconnected hierarchically and aligned with time measured at a variety of levels from milliseconds to minutes.

Although software such as ELAN allows for all levels of measurement and the determination of many behavioral features at the same time, it is still not capable of identifying individual gestures, so a researcher must still manually annotate the video before making use of these features.

Interrater reliability is perhaps one of the most critical tools for measuring gesture, because the success of a coding system relies on how well it can direct two or more independent coders to describe the same phenomenon, and high reliability scores of 80% agreement or more in coding gesture are key to making any assumptions about its meaning or function.

In Church and Goldin-Meadow's system, speech strategies were coded independently of gesture strategies because the Piagetian conservation context constrained the interpretation of the gestures, which revealed that in many speech-plus-gesture explanations a strategy expressed in one modality differed distinctly, or mismatched, the strategy expressed in the accompanying modality.

Children who produced speech-gesture mismatches 50% or more of the time were classified as transitional children, and using a pretest-instruction-posttest design Church and Goldin-Meadow found that transitional children were significantly more likely to profit from instruction in the conservation principle than stable children who produced fewer than 50% mismatches.

assets.topic: Gesture in the Brain: fMRI, ERP, and Future Measurement
assets.visual_frame_description: A brain atlas view highlights the left inferior frontal gyrus and posterior middle temporal gyrus in orange while a scalp-topography panel shows the N400 negativity at bilateral temporal sites and the P600 at posterior sites. A stimulus builder window assembles sentences paired with gesture clips marked congruent or incongruent, and a sidebar lists avatar systems such as GALE and point-light motion capture technologies.
assets.player_mission: You are a cognitive neuroscience research assistant designing a gesture processing study. Choose fMRI to localize gesture processing in the left inferior frontal gyrus or EEG with ERPs to time it with components such as the N400 and P600, then build congruent and incongruent speech-gesture stimuli modeled on Willems et al. (2007). Interpret which stages of processing gestures affect and propose a future study using human avatars or consumer motion capture devices.
key_concepts: fMRI is a popular technique for studying gesture because it is noninvasive and provides data with excellent spatial resolution, and with fMRI researchers actually measure the blood-oxygenation-level dependent (BOLD) signal, which is taken as a proxy for neural activity.

The BOLD signal does not increase in a region until approximately 2 seconds after stimulus onset, so the temporal resolution of fMRI is considered inferior to techniques such as event-related potentials, which can consider temporal effects at the level of milliseconds.

In the first study to ask whether the left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) was sensitive to gesture, Willems, Ozyurek, and Hagoort (2007) presented spoken sentences accompanied by congruent or incongruent iconic gestures, and the IFG responded similarly to all three incongruent conditions but differently for the congruent condition, and Dick et al. (2014) later showed that the IFG showed greater activation to ambiguous speech that was disambiguated by a gesture.

Because motion during a scan can cause artifacts in the functional data and increase overall noise, data are generally excluded from studies with adult participants when motion exceeds 1 mm in any direction, so the effect of self-produced gesture on cognition has been understudied, but Macedonia, Muller, and Friederici (2011) trained adults on novel vocabulary words outside the scanner and found that premotor regions showed significantly greater activation to words learned with self-produced iconic gestures than to words learned with unrelated movements.

EEG measures electrical activity that is emitted from postsynaptic discharges of large groups of neurons and is recorded by electrodes on the scalp, and ERPs are portions of the ongoing EEG signal that are time-locked to a stimulus and averaged across many presentations of the same condition.

Kelly, Kravitz, and Hopkins (2004) found that incongruent gesture-speech pairs (saying 'short' and gesturing tall) produced a larger negativity at roughly 400 ms post stimulus at bilateral temporal regions than congruent pairs, an N400 effect that indexes difficulties with semantic integration.

Biau and Soto-Faraco (2013) found that beat gestures produced very early perceptual differences in how the brain processed speech as early as 100 ms after the onset of a spoken word, and Holle et al. (2012) found that beat gestures accompanying syntactically ambiguous words produced a reduced P600 component, reflecting ease of syntactic processing.

Kelly, McDevitt, and Esch (2009) found that people remembered many more foreign words, up to 1 week later, when they learned them with iconic gestures versus without, and ERPs showed that words learned with gesture produced a larger late positive complex, a component that peaks around 600 ms post stimulus and is thought to reflect depth of imagistic memory encoding.
The literature generally supports the view that gesture is processed as a meaningful part of a message, a claim that was once a point of contention in the behavioral literature.

Creating the gesture repertoire of a human avatar could not have been done without the development of gesture coding schemes, and one software-based system, GALE (Gesturing Avatar for Learning and Education), has been incorporated in research activities at The University of Wisconsin by Martha Alibali and colleagues.

Consumer computer technologies have created ways to capture human movement through points of light that can then be projected in three-dimensional space, and this type of technology could be interfaced with software coding programs such as ELAN to capture and code gestures.

Molfese (2000) measured auditory ERPs in newborns and identified early perceptual components (N1, P2, N2) that differentiated with 85% accuracy children who would later develop reading difficulties, and gesture researchers could similarly use ERPs to identify neural profiles of children revealing who may be more or less open to instruction with and without gesture.
