assets.topic: Eye Anatomy and the Reasons We Move Our Eyes
assets.visual_frame_description: A cross-section diagram of the human eye is displayed at center screen, with clickable labels for the cornea, pupil, lens, retina, and fovea. As you hover over each structure, a side panel explains its function, and an animation at the bottom shows light passing through the eye to form an image on the retina.
assets.player_mission: Begin by learning why the eye is built the way it is. Study the anatomy of the cornea, lens, pupil, retina, and fovea, then connect that structure to the gaze-shifting movements that direct the fovea to objects of interest. Identify the three types of gaze-shifting eye movements and the basic alternation between fixations and saccades.
key_concepts: The cornea is the transparent tissue on the front of the eye and is responsible for approximately 80% of the eye's focusing power, but because it is fixed it cannot adjust its focus.
The lens supplies the remaining 20% of the eye's focusing power and changes its shape through the ciliary muscles, which alter the curvature of the lens.
The pupil is the aperture in the iris that controls the amount of light admitted to the eye and is made up of two antagonistic smooth muscles.
The sphincter muscle constricts the iris under parasympathetic nervous system control, whereas the dilator muscle, which opens the iris, is under sympathetic nervous system control.
The retina is made up of visual receptors, rods, and cones, which contain light-sensitive chemicals that transform light into neuronal signals.

Cones function in daylight conditions and provide the perception of color, while rods function under low-level illumination and provide only shades of gray, and cones afford a higher level of visual acuity.
The fovea is an area on the retina approximately 0.25 mm in diameter that contains only cones and lies at the point of focus of the optical system, providing the ability to see fine detail.
Because only a small portion of the retina can provide a high level of visual acuity, it is necessary to direct the fovea to a location of interest, which is why we move our eyes.
Each eye has three pairs of extraocular muscles - superior and inferior rectus, superior and inferior oblique, and lateral and medial rectus - which control gaze stabilization and gaze shifting.
There are three types of gaze-shifting eye movements: vergence movements, smooth pursuit movements, and saccadic movements.
Saccadic eye movements are ballistic movements that abruptly change the point of fixation, such as when viewing an image or reading, and are most relevant to measuring nonverbal communication.
Because fixations are overt indicators of the point of visual attention, their locations and the paths between them can provide insight into the underlying processing of the observer.

assets.topic: Eye-Tracking Technology and System Configurations
assets.visual_frame_description: A laboratory control room scene shows three eye-tracking rigs side by side: a chin rest in front of a monitor, a head-mounted tracker with a scene camera, and a desk-mounted remote camera. Clicking each rig opens a spec card listing accuracy, intrusiveness, and typical use cases, with a small inset showing infrared images of bright and dark pupils.
assets.player_mission: Take the role of a researcher selecting an eye-tracking system for a study of nonverbal communication. Compare the major recording techniques, weigh bright-pupil versus dark-pupil illumination, and choose among chin rest, head-mounted, and desk-mounted configurations. Match each configuration to the application it best serves.
key_concepts: The systematic study of eye movements has been an area of research interest since at least the mid-1800s.
The major eye-tracking approaches have included scleral search coils, electro-oculography, video-oculography, and pupil-corneal reflection methods.
The vast majority of eye-tracking systems in use today employ some form of video-based, pupil-corneal reflection method.

Pupil-corneal reflection eye tracking illuminates the eye with infrared light to avoid natural light reflections and determines the center of the pupil and the reflection from the front of the cornea.
The reflections of infrared light from the front and back of the cornea and lens are known as Purkinje images, with the first Purkinje image being the brightest.
Most eye-tracking manufacturers employ some method of ellipse-fitting to find the center of the pupil, because interference from eyelids and eyelashes can prevent detecting a true circle.
Bright-pupil tracking locates the infrared illuminators coaxially with the camera, producing an effect similar to camera flash red eye, while dark-pupil tracking places the illuminators off-axis.

Bright pupil techniques have been shown to work well with Hispanic and Caucasian individuals, while dark pupil systems perform better for small pupils, bright outdoor illumination, older participants, and Asian populations.

Chin rest systems keep the head stable, provide some of the highest degrees of accuracy, and are useful where stimulus presentation is fixed, but they are intrusive and not suitable for real-world interactions.

Head-mounted and eyeglass-mounted eye trackers often include a scene camera whose images can be correlated with eye-movement behavior, but they cannot differentiate smooth pursuit from saccades, so they cannot provide fixation counts.
Desk-mounted systems allow remote tracking with no attachments to the participant, and most deal with head movement through multiple cameras and algorithms that compensate for it.
One factor common to all remote eye-tracking systems is differentiating movement of the eyes from movement of the head.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Calibration, System Factors, and Threats to Data Quality
assets.visual_frame_description: A dashboard shows graphs of accuracy versus precision, a latency scatterplot, and a sampling-rate selector, while a live camera feed of a participant's eye is annotated with a detected corneal reflection. A checklist on the right flags problems like mascara absorption, bifocal reflections, and bright sunlight through a window.
assets.player_mission: Act as a data-quality auditor inspecting an eye-tracking session that produced questionable data. Review accuracy, precision, latency, and sampling rate, examine the calibration procedure, and identify common threats to tracking such as mascara, eyeglasses, eyelashes, and ambient light. Recommend fixes to recover reliable gaze data.
key_concepts: Accuracy is defined as the average angular offset between the locations of fixations and their targets and is often called validity in social science, while spatial precision is the root-mean-square angular distance between successive samples and corresponds to reliability.

System latency is the average end-to-end delay from an actual eye movement until the recording computer signals that a movement has occurred, and temporal precision is the standard deviation of that latency.
Low temporal precision creates variable delay between eye movement and system recording, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about relationships between events and eye location.
The system sampling rate, measured in hertz, ranges from 30 Hz to 2000 Hz across systems, and faster is not necessarily better because very high speeds increase artifacts from head and body movement.
The majority of current systems sample in the 30 Hz to 250 Hz range, which is more than adequate for most studies related to nonverbal communication.
Calibration requires the participant to fixate on a number of known locations so the system can map the pupil-corneal reflection relationship and extrapolate it to other locations.

Mascara tends to absorb the infrared signal and scatter the light, producing reflections that prevent the algorithms from identifying the corneal reflection, so participants should remove eye makeup before participating.
Long eyelashes and drooping eyelids can occlude the pupil and degrade tracking, and one possible solution is varying the camera position to view the eyes at a steeper angle.
Air bubbles between soft contact lenses and the eyeball appear as multiple corneal reflections under infrared light and can confuse the system, often remedied by slightly unfocusing the camera.

Bifocals and trifocals create numerous infrared reflections at the border between lens sections that prevent locating a single corneal reflection, while progressive lenses do not present this problem.

Direct sunlight carries infrared light far stronger than the eye-tracking illuminators and can disrupt tracking even when it enters through a window, whereas most indoor fluorescent lighting does not adversely affect performance.
Bright incandescent light sources in the participant's field of view can decrease pupil diameter and cause spurious pupil-diameter changes from pupil contraction.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Ocular Measures: Fixations, Saccades, Pupil Diameter, and Blinks
assets.visual_frame_description: A timeline view of raw gaze samples is shown on screen, with a toolbar to run velocity-, dispersion-, or temporal-based fixation detection and color-coded overlay of fixations, saccades, and blinks. A side panel tracks running statistics such as fixation count, mean duration, saccade amplitude, pupil diameter, and blink rate.
assets.player_mission: Take the role of a data analyst who must turn raw eye-tracking data into dependent measures. Compute fixations and saccades with velocity-, dispersion-, or temporal-based algorithms, prepare pupil-diameter measures in millimeters, and validate blink events from zero-value samples. Choose the right measure for each nonverbal communication research question.
key_concepts: Eye-tracking systems essentially measure three parameters directly: x and y eye location in the two-dimensional plane in front of the observer and pupil diameter.
Holmqvist and colleagues described more than 120 measures that can be calculated from eye-movement data and provided a method for conceptualizing and creating new measures.

Fixations refer to times when the eye stops moving and focuses on a given location, and a fixation is a relatively stable eye-in-head position defined by a spatial dispersion of less than 2 degrees, a minimal duration of 100-200 ms, and a threshold velocity below 15-100 degrees per millisecond.

The eye is never completely stationary and is characterized by miniature eye movements of less than 1 degree, including flicks, drifts, and high-frequency tremors, which keep the fovea stimulated so the image does not fade.

Velocity-based fixation methods separate fixations from saccades using point-to-point velocities over some threshold, dispersion-based methods group consecutive points within a maximum separation, and temporal-based methods rely solely on duration, as fixations are primarily in the 200-400 ms range.
Velocity-based and dispersion-based methods perform best in terms of accuracy, while all three fixation-calculation approaches are roughly equivalent in robustness.

Saccades are involuntary, abrupt, very rapid movements of both eyes simultaneously and are characterized by a duration of 30-80 ms, a spatial extent of 4-20 degrees, and a velocity of 30-500 degrees per second.
Most applications focus on the detection of fixations and define saccades as the periods between fixations.
Most systems use head position to correct pupil-diameter measures for distance changes, because the pupil appears larger as the participant gets closer to the eye tracker.

The preferred reporting of pupil diameter is in millimeters of either absolute diameter or change in diameter, and percentage-change reporting can be distorting when groups differ in baseline diameter due to age or ambient illumination.
Pupil-diameter precision should usually be restricted to two decimal places, as most manufacturer specifications indicate that degree best reflects the precision of their sensors.
Blinks are inferred when the x/y position of the eye goes to zero, but care is needed to distinguish true blinks from data-sampling errors or signal loss that also report a location of zero.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Analyzing Eye Behavior and Applications of Eye Tracking
assets.visual_frame_description: A dual-panel analytics workspace shows a scanpath graph of a face with regions around the eyes, nose, and mouth linked by weighted transition arrows, alongside a heatmap of gaze on a store shelf. A results log at the bottom reports entropy values, Levenshtein distances, pupil-dilation curves, and blink-suppression statistics across conditions.
assets.player_mission: Take the role of the lead investigator analyzing a deception study and an advertising study from the same eye-tracking data. Run scanpath analyses using Markov transitions, entropy, and Levenshtein distance, evaluate pupil dilation and blink changes across conditions, and apply the findings to real-world applications in advertising and usability testing.
key_concepts: Eye-movement data can be analyzed into three types of measures: measures of cognitive processing, measures of mental search, and measures of scanpaths.
Measures of cognitive processing include number of fixations, locations of fixations, fixation duration, cumulative fixation time, and cluster analysis of areas of interest.

Measures of search can include number of saccades, saccade amplitude, saccade velocity, and saccade length, and these characteristics can reveal which elements are attended and which features contribute to detection of a search item.

Scanpaths refer to the sequence of the visual pattern employed when viewing a particular stimulus, and methodology provides evidence that viewers attend to informative details and not necessarily the entire stimulus.

One method of quantifying scanpaths models the patterns as Markovian processes, where any transition between states depends only on the current state, and transition probabilities among face regions have been used as a measure of prior knowledge of faces.

Departures from a completely random scanning pattern indicate a level of constraint in how an image is viewed, and the conditional information in transition matrices can be calculated as entropy, where higher entropy means more randomness.

Levenshtein distance is the minimum number of insertions, deletions, or substitutions needed to transform one sequence into another, and it has been used to compare viewing sequences in studies of own-race bias in eyewitness identification.
The pupil is innervated by both the autonomic and central nervous systems, so changes in pupil diameter can relate to both cognitive workload and emotional arousal.

Kahneman and Beatty found a dilation of the pupil with the presentation of each additional digit in a short-term memory task, with the degree of dilation reflecting attentional effort, and Bradley and colleagues showed increased pupil diameter during affective picture viewing.

Blink analysis has proven useful in determining workload, providing information during psychiatric interviews, and as a measure of deceptive intent, with false intent producing a suppression of blinking during relevant questions about a mock crime.
Advances such as the Eyebox2 allow gathering gaze data from many viewers simultaneously without calibration, but do not provide eye position data or pupil diameter.

Eye tracking has moved beyond research roots into advertising, marketing, and usability testing, and open-source tools like ILAB provide advanced analysis but require programming knowledge such as MATLAB.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Choosing an Appropriate Olfactory Stimulus
assets.visual_frame_description: A laboratory bench is shown with three labeled stimulus stations: a vial of androstadienone, a sprig of a plant odor, and a fine-fragrance bottle. A source-map panel traces each odor to its origin, listing fragrance houses such as Firmenich, International Flavors and Fragrances, and Symrise, and a checklist prompts you to consider prior published use of the odor and its ingredient composition.
assets.player_mission: Begin as a researcher deciding which odor to use for a study of nonverbal communication. Review the three broad stimulus categories - human body odors, natural odors, and artificial odorants - then weigh where to obtain the odorant, whether to rely on odors validated in prior research, and how genetic background and active versus inactive ingredients might shape the results.
key_concepts: Researchers can choose among human body odors (such as the putative pheromone androstadienone, or AND), natural odors such as plant odors, and artificial odorants such as fine fragrance, though commercially available fragrances often contain natural elements as well.

Some researchers obtain odor samples directly from fragrance producers such as Firmenich, International Flavors and Fragrances, and Symrise, while natural body odors may be produced in the laboratory context itself and some artificial odors can be bought directly in stores.

The chapter advises that examining what odors have been used previously by other researchers is a good first step, just as methods textbooks urge researchers to use questionnaires that have been used in prior studies before constructing a novel scale.
Researchers interested in attention should consider the literature on peppermint, because previous research has repeatedly demonstrated that peppermint can have a profound impact on alertness.

Emotion researchers may want to consider using human body odors, as research by Haviland-Jones and McGuire (1999) and Chen, Katdare, and Lucas (2006) showed striking mood effects when individuals were exposed to underarm pads worn during mood induction films.

Usually very little information exists regarding the composition of various odorants and why exactly they maintain their particular effects on human behavior, and the effect could come from one identifiable compound or from the combination of multiple components.

Perfumers refer to accords the way musicians describe chords of music, meaning a combination of individual perfume essences that creates a new unified fragrance distinct from its individual components, making it hard to identify the contributing elements.

When using human body odors it can be difficult to pinpoint one specific component that affects emotion and behavior, and there may be a genetic component that can be isolated for its ultimate impact.

Research has demonstrated that mothers and infants can identify each other through smell, and strangers can match samples of genetically related people, such as father and son, but not of socially related people, such as husband and wife.
Research has indicated that genetic background contributes to fragrance selection, and the full extent of the genetic contribution to olfaction is still unclear and should be explored further.

Odorants may be composed of both active ingredients that affect behavior and inactive ingredients that can be detected and co-occur but do not affect behavior, so researchers must be aware that what they measured or detected may not have been the active ingredient.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Determining Intensity and Choosing a Method of Delivery
assets.visual_frame_description: A control-room scene shows two experiment setups side by side: on the left, a participant wearing a nasal cannula in a carefully controlled odor chamber, and on the right, a room with a fragrance diffuser and scented jars. A slider control lets you adjust odor intensity between perithreshold and consciously detectable levels while a validity meter shows the tradeoff between internal and external validity.
assets.player_mission: Take the role of a researcher who has chosen an odorant and must decide how much stimulus to present and how to expose participants to it. Decide between perithreshold and conscious detection levels, consider whether intensity matching across stimuli is needed, and weigh direct bodily delivery against indirect environmental delivery while balancing internal and external validity.
key_concepts: Some researchers choose odors that are above conscious detection, while others suggest that the actual effect of fragrance generally works best at the low or perithreshold level, which is generally below the level of conscious detection.
Phillips and Cupchik (2004) reported that accuracy for recalling story details was lower when fragrance intensity was greater, suggesting that fragrance awareness may undermine specific effects.

If attention is drawn to the fragrance so that it is identified, or an attempt is made by the participant to identify it, associations to the semantic aspect of its name begin to take precedence over other effects.

When participants identify a perfume, correctly or incorrectly, they are more likely to search their memories for associations to the particular odorant, which may matter when the fragrance and its associations are part of the research question.

When researchers study a variety of odors they often determine whether perceived intensities or strengths are similar, either by asking participants to report intensity or by measuring chemical concentrations, but it is unclear what difference intensity matching makes.

Most researchers use average intensity ratings when examining differences in intensity, but those averages often do not reflect the wide range of scores surrounding the average ratings, and large individual differences exist in perceptions of intensity.

Participants can be exposed to odorants directly via the body, for example a scented stick held near the nose, an odor-infused cotton ball taped between the nose and upper lip, an odorous patch on the body, a nasal cannula, or odors applied directly to the participant.

Indirect exposure is typically done within the external environment, and researchers have used fragrance diffusers, fragrance pellets aired by a fan, carefully controlled odor chambers, and olfactory stimuli placed in jars near the participant.
No consensus currently exists regarding the optimum method of delivery, and it is unclear whether differences in delivery method ultimately contribute to the various psychological effects reported.

Some researchers use delivery systems that carefully control the exact amount of exposure and environmental factors such as humidity, while others take a more naturalistic, less controlled approach that mirrors real-world contexts.
Heavily controlled environments that place participants in uncomfortable situations, such as nasal cannulae, may affect the ultimate emotions experienced or the ability to communicate.

Carefully controlled odor delivery systems may remove potential confounding variables in stimulus presentation, but they may contribute to confounds in the study design itself through loss of external validity.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Collecting and Controlling Human Body Odor Samples
assets.visual_frame_description: A sterile collection checklist is displayed over a diagram of the human body highlighting the axillary (underarm) region. Step-by-step cards show a sterile gauze pad being placed in the armpit before a mood induction video, the pad being frozen to control bacterial growth, and multiple donor pads being pooled into a single sample tube labeled as a group representation.
assets.player_mission: Act as a study auditor reviewing a protocol for collecting human mood body odors. Inspect the donor-selection criteria, evaluate the controls imposed on diet, medication, illness, and fragranced body-care products, and verify the collection, freezing, and pooling procedures used to create the stimulus.
key_concepts: The mood odor research is based on the premise that humans emit nonverbal olfactory signs that can be interpreted by others, and previous research has established that such odors can be discriminated by detectors.

Human body odors are obtained by collecting axillary (underarm) secretions, and researchers have generally limited collection to adult male donors to control for possible variations in body odor due to fluctuating hormonal cycles of adult females.
Typically males of approximately the same age are recruited as donors based on the assumption that hormone production is likely to be similar because hormone production changes with age.

Body odor is affected by illness, medications, diet, and chemicals applied to the skin, so individuals who take medications for chronic illness or who are currently unwell would not be considered appropriate donors.
To control for the effects of diet, donors are asked to refrain from eating spicy or odorous foods for several days prior to collection and for the duration of the collection.

Because chemicals applied to the skin, such as fragranced lotions, shampoos, and deodorants, will be part of the collected secretions, donors must refrain from using them for several days prior to and during the collection, and researchers supply unfragranced products instead.

Deodorant is supplied rather than an antiperspirant because antiperspirant builds up on the skin and can remain for several days without reapplication, whereas some researchers concerned with naturalistic mood odor production would not apply such controls.

When researchers want to study human mood odors, some method of mood induction is employed, such as mood-inducing videos whose reliability is widely accepted, while on the naturalistic side Mujica-Parodi et al. (2009) used sky-diving to produce anxiety.
Because more than one type of mood odor is often desired, the same donors are used in each type of collection, thus making the odors within-subject.
The axillary secretions are obtained by placing a sterile gauze pad into the armpit prior to the mood induction procedure, and the collected gauze pads must be frozen to control for bacterial growth.

The frozen gauze pads must be brought back to room or body temperature for odor delivery, and typically the samples of several donors are pooled to create a group of people representation like what one might be exposed to in the natural course of social activity.
It is not yet known which organic compounds in axillary secretions are active for mood communication, so the effect of the other compounds present in axillary secretions is unknown as well.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Measuring Odor Effects with Self-Report and Narrative Methods
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen workspace shows a questionnaire form on one side and a narrative-writing panel with the full personal-experience instructions on the other. As you toggle between methods, a results grid updates with bars comparing self-report ratings with narrative-content scores from software-based text analysis, flagged with notes about social desirability effects.
assets.player_mission: Take the role of a methods analyst choosing how to capture the psychological effects of odor exposure. Compare the strengths and weaknesses of questionnaires with narrative methods, identify when self-reports fail to detect subtle perithreshold effects, and decide how to score narratives for emotion words and intimacy themes.
key_concepts: Questionnaire measures are still considered by many to be the gold standard for studying psychological experience, and within olfaction research self-reports are one of the most common methods for studying how odors impact emotional and social communication.
Self-reports are often used because they are easy, inexpensive, and quick to implement, and within the fragrance industry they are also seen as a valid reflection of an individual's experience.

Social desirability effects can make questionnaires particularly unreliable, and Brody and Hall (1993, 2000) observed that men typically report less emotion than women except in cases of anger, where the pattern is reversed, while behavioral studies often do not show such gender differences.

In work examining emotional and behavioral responses to flowers, men were as likely to smile, socially approach, and initiate a conversation as women, and men's behavior actually showed even more change from baseline than women's behavior.

The use of questionnaires assumes they can properly describe a participant's experience, but some experiences are too complex to be captured through specific questions defined by the researcher, and emotional expressions often travel fast and outside of conscious awareness.

Self-report measures may be too imprecise for studying effects due to odor exposure because such effects are often quite subtle, and individuals exposed to perithreshold odors often did not report emotional changes.

Participants exposed to perithreshold odors incorporated more emotion words in their narratives when asked to write about recent events, and adolescent girls exposed to an unfamiliar fragrance showed no direct self-report effects but indirect effects on social behavior and narrative content.

The authors proposed that fragrance can serve as a biological search engine, so that when a particular odor is in the air people search for events or people that correspond to it, and these processes occur rapidly, indirectly, and usually outside of conscious awareness.

Researchers need to look beyond self-reports to psychophysiology, narrative, or nonverbal behavior to detect search-engine effects because the person having the experience may not be aware of the shift in attention and may not attribute it to a fragrance.

Narrative methods have been used extensively in other areas of psychological research when conscious methods such as self-reports may not be helpful, but their use within olfaction research is only starting to emerge and has already been demonstrated to be useful.

Work from the authors' lab showed that although self-reports indicated no differences in pleasantness or intensity across fresh air, floral odor, and fragrance conditions, differences emerged in narrative content, with participants exposed to floral odors at perithreshold levels incorporating more words indicative of enjoyment.

Research by Freyberg and Ahren (2011) found that reports of social enjoyment and words indicative of intimacy in adolescents' narratives decreased when they wore an unfamiliar fragrance compared to their favorite, but only when they also found the unfamiliar fragrance less pleasant.

assets.topic: Measuring Odor Effects: Psychophysiology, Neuroimaging, Behavioral, and Cross-Cultural Methods
assets.visual_frame_description: A command-center dashboard shows four live panels: a heart-rate and skin-conductance trace overlaid with pleasantness ratings, a PET brain scan with activated regions in attention and social-cognition areas, a behavioral log recording mime-approach and flower-smile events, and a world map flagging industry reports of regional scent preferences. A final report panel compiles findings and flags remaining cross-cultural gaps.
assets.player_mission: Take the role of the lead investigator directing a multisession study of odor effects. Integrate psychophysiological measures such as heart rate and skin conductance, evaluate neuroimaging evidence about brain responses to chemosignals, design behavioral observations of approach and helping, and judge the cross-cultural generalizability of the findings.
key_concepts: Psychophysiological methods such as heart rate and skin conductance have been incorporated into olfactory research as a way of understanding how odors affect participants on a physical level.

Bensafi et al. (2002) observed that heart rate was positively associated with pleasantness ratings, whereas skin conductance was positively correlated with how arousing the particular odor was perceived to be by participants.

Graham, Janssen, and Sanders (2000) found a heightened sexual response by females to a male fragrance during their follicular phase but only when they engaged in a personal sexual fantasy, with no observed changes in self-report.
Several studies involving the semiochemical AND reported a modulating effect whereby reported negative mood and heart rate response or galvanic skin response decreased compared to the control odor.

Kiecolt-Glaser et al. (2008) observed enhanced positive mood via self-report for lemon oil compared to lavender but no changes in heart rate, blood pressure, or salivary cortisol, illustrating that psychophysiology does not always coincide with questionnaires.

Measurement of cerebral blood flow as an indicator of brain activation is obtained via positron emission tomography (PET) or functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and such studies can demonstrate that an olfactory stimulus impacts not only olfactory-processing areas but other brain areas as well.

Jacob et al. (2001) used PET to investigate exposure to AND and found sustained brain changes in areas associated with attention and mood as well as olfactory processing, and these effects were found without conscious exposure to AND.

Lundstrom, Boyle, Zatorre, and Jones-Gotman (2008) found that different neural pathways process body odors compared to nonbody odors, and body odors from friends as opposed to strangers activated different brain areas.

Herz, Eliassen, Beland, and Souza (2004) found with fMRI that a pleasant memory odor cue was significantly more likely to activate the amygdala and hippocampus than an unmarketed control fragrance, showing effects on brain areas associated with emotion and memory.

Participants exposed to floral air were three times more likely to approach and touch an experimenter who dressed and acted as a mime than those exposed to fine fragrance or fresh air, and socially supportive behavior such as smiling and initiating conversations occurred when individuals were presented with flowers.

Baron (1997) demonstrated that participants in a shopping mall were more likely to help a confederate in the presence of pleasant odors, and Holland, Hendriks, and Aarts (2005) found that participants exposed to a citrus-scented cleanser engaged in more cleaning behaviors, such as removing snack crumbs from their work environment.

Ebihara et al. (2012) found that lavender and grapefruit odor exposure improved gait speed in older adults, which the authors suggested may ultimately result in reduced fall rates, and no published academic studies to date have examined cross-cultural or geographic differences in odor exposure.

chapters.title: Chapter 22: Measuring Body Movement: Current and Future Directions in Proxemics and Kinesics

assets.topic: A Long History of Diverging Approaches
assets.visual_frame_description: A museum-like timeline gallery unfolds, showing a plate of hand shapes and supposed meanings from Bulwer's Chirologia of 1644 beside portraits of Darwin and a modern lab with high-resolution motion tracking cameras. Overlay cards flag the two driving forces: pragmatic solutions to theoretical questions and technological advancement.
assets.player_mission: Trace the historical roots of body movement measurement from 17th-century treatises to today's computational sciences. Identify the two major driving forces of methodological development and explain why no golden standard for measuring body movement has yet crystallized.
key_concepts: Methodological development in nonverbal behavior research has two major driving forces: the need for a pragmatic solution to investigate a priori theoretical questions and technological advancement creating new affordances.

The current surge of multimodal accounts of emotion expression and perception demands time-based descriptions of body movement that can be integrated with other time-based accounts from vocal or facial behavior.
Western interest in labeling or describing body movement goes back centuries; Bonifacio (1616) and Bulwer (1644) emphasized the role and importance of body actions as a natural human language.

Darwin (1872) was the first to focus on the functional role of body movement in emotion communication in humans and animals, treating body actions and postures as signs of internal emotional processing.
Clinical psychology focuses on the diagnostic and therapeutic value of nonverbal behavior and, in particular, on behaviors that foster empathy and rapport during clinician-patient interaction.
The multifunctionality, in addition to the anatomical complexity, of the skeletal body system logically leads to a high diversity in descriptive methods.
Even within a research tradition or discipline, there is no consensus on a conceptual framework of body movement from which methods can be derived.
Two scientific virtues seem to stand in opposition to each other in method development: generality and selectivity.

The facial and vocal domains saw a crystallization toward golden standards such as the Facial Action Coding System and standardized vocal extraction techniques, but no such crystallization in measuring body movement has yet occurred.

Researchers tend to focus either on the factors that determine nonverbal behavior at the individual level or microlevel, or on interactions at the macrolevel as influenced by cultural and social dynamic factors.
A research field advances when a common methodology is applied that makes results from different studies comparable.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Kinesics: Coding Systems for Body Movement
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen coder interface shows the Body Action and Posture (BAP) coding system's graphical timeline next to a Labanotation score with effort and shape symbols. Hovering over body part labels reveals whether a description is functional, form-based, or spatio-temporal.
assets.player_mission: Act as a kinesics researcher selecting a coding system for a study of emotional body movement. Compare functional, anatomically based form, and spatio-temporal levels of description, and defend a choice using the chapter's reliability evidence.
key_concepts: Kinesics refers to the study of skeletal body movement, that is, movements of the head, torso, and limbs, excluding gaze and facial expressions.

Birdwhistell, who originally coined the term kinesics, developed one of the first coding systems aimed at exhaustive symbolic transcription of body movement, segmenting it into kinemes, kinemorphs, and kinemorphic constructions.

Laban developed a system of dance notation later referred to as Labanotation, which uses a complex collection of symbols providing highly detailed descriptions of upper and lower body actions and positions.

In kinesics, a posture represents the general alignment of the body to a particular position or configuration, whereas an action is a local excursion of one or more articulators outside a resting configuration.

Gestures are usually distinguished from other body movements by the defining feature that they are voluntary actions arising from the deliberative attempt to convey semantic and pragmatic information.
Based on the work of David Efron, Ekman and Friesen developed a typology distinguishing illustrators, emblems, manipulators or adaptors, and regulators depending on their socioaffective function.

Functional coding systems involve a higher level of inference about the function and purpose of a behavior than pure descriptive coding systems, and form-based descriptions tend to be more reliable than functional ones.

Descriptions of movement form such as direction and orientation are founded in anatomical kinesiology, describing the moving body part with respect to three orthogonal, Cartesian axes (sagittal, vertical, and transversal).
The Body Action and Posture coding system provides 141 codes for the time-aligned microdescription of body movement, which is segmented in posture or action units.
Labanotation puts particular emphasis on the description of the temporal dynamics of body movement, describing movement qualities as aspects of effort and shape.
Intercoder reliability of Laban-derived descriptions has in the past either not been reported or been found difficult to achieve, perhaps due to the high level of subjective interpretation involved.

Gait research in particular has much advanced since the application of refined kinematic analyses derived from motion tracking, and dimension reduction techniques such as principal component analysis are typically applied to model gait.

assets.topic: Sampling Techniques and Human Observation
assets.visual_frame_description: A research lab whiteboard fills with flowcharts of event coding, interval coding, and time sampling strategies, while a video annotation window in ANVIL shows color-coded behavior streams on a timeline. A small table of thin-slice correlations updates beside a reliability panel computing Cohen's kappa.
assets.player_mission: Plan an observational study of expressive body movement in dyadic interaction. Choose sampling and coding strategies, decide between expert coding and human judgment, and specify how reliability will be established.
key_concepts: Altmann's widely cited review presents a summary of the characteristics of seven major types of behavior samples and their recommended uses.

Event coding is probably the most common way of recording observational data, allowing flexible data analysis because the observer detects codable events whenever they occur during the stream of behavior.
In interval coding, time is divided into a number of successive intervals and the observer classifies each interval or codes whether certain events occur during it.
Murphy (2005) tested the use of short behavior-coded segments, or thin slices, to predict behavior across longer interactions, and correlations were high for most categories except self-touch.
The judgment method is perhaps the most commonly used method in studies of nonverbal behavior, in which skilled or naive judges rate behavior on a particular attribute or psychological construct.

Coding schemes provide explicit definitions of the behaviors relevant to the study, and Bakeman and Gottman systematically listed desirable features such as the use of mutually exclusive and exhaustive codes.
A typical coding process consists of trained observers following a standardized protocol, after which they independently code a common part of the material and take an intercoder agreement test.
Expert coding is increasingly facilitated by manual video annotation software such as ANVIL, ELAN, and The Observer, which guide standardized and precise time-locked coding.
In judgment studies, adding more judges increases the mean reliability, but high interrater agreement does not imply that observers correctly perceive the behavior, which is a question of validity.
The most commonly used statistic for establishing reliability of behavior coding is Cohen's kappa coefficient, which corrects for chance agreement.

Wallbott (1985) found that lay judgments of hand movement quality were reliably but incorrectly used in evaluating a patient's psychopathological state, whereas the coded hand movement parameters did not differ between therapy admission and discharge.
Pollick and colleagues found that attributions of emotional activation to instrumental arm movements were positively related to temporal movement parameters such as velocity, acceleration, and jerk.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Automatic Body Movement Processing
assets.visual_frame_description: A high-tech control room displays three capture setups side by side: an optical mocap studio with infrared cameras and reflective markers, a subject in an inertial sensor suit, and a Kinect depth camera with a skeleton overlay. A processing pipeline diagram lights up from body tracking to hidden Markov model classification.
assets.player_mission: Engineer a pipeline for automatic affect recognition from body movement. Select a sensor technology, describe the steps of tracking, segmentation, feature extraction, and classification, and weigh the advantages and drawbacks of each system type.
key_concepts: The most notable systems for automatic tracking of body movements are optical motion capture systems, electromechanical or electromagnetic motion capture systems, and markerless vision-based systems.

Many optical motion capture systems such as Vicon and OptiTrack make use of infrared cameras, generally 8-12, to track retro-reflective markers placed on the body and provide the 3D positions of each marker as output.

Electromechanical or electromagnetic motion capture systems require the person to wear active sensors, such as inertial sensors, accelerometers, or magnetometers, which are generally integrated in a suit for full body capture.
Markerless vision-based systems use video or web cameras to record movement and process the data with image-processing techniques to determine the position and orientation of the body.

Variations in lighting conditions, skin color, clothing, body part occlusion, and touching can cause difficulties in automatically extracting, segmenting, and recognizing body movement from complex scenes with vision-based systems.

The Kinect is a low-cost markerless vision-based sensor that projects infrared patterns for depth recovery of motion, and software libraries allowing the extraction of the 3D body skeleton have made it popular even among non-experts.

Feature extraction approaches can be divided into two main categories: spatial action representation, which focuses on body configuration, and temporal action representation, which models the temporal relations between spatial information.
Image-based model approaches detect the body area, such as its silhouette, rather than identifying the different body parts, and have shown results similar to the body model-based methods.

The most used approach to classify a temporal sequence of movement is the hidden Markov model, which is very good at modeling sequential aspects of an overall movement but not at modeling independent body parts.

Automatic classification schemes are starting to be proposed as a way to substitute and improve existing scales for the measurement of higher order phenomena, such as continuously tracking a patient's body behavior to detect level of depression.
Motion tracking allows the body to be represented as three-dimensional according to Cartesian axes and/or Euler angles, which makes computing feature sets reasonably straightforward.

By just using minimalistic sensors such as a smartphone, activity classification can be carried out by exploiting kinematic features gathered by a gyroscope or accelerometer without having to wear sensors on all body parts.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Future Challenges: Behavioral Patterning and Real-Life Settings
assets.visual_frame_description: A city street scene dissolves into an overlay of the Brunswik lens model, linking a smiling walker's distal kinematic cues to a perceiver's proximal impressions and attribution. Beside it, the Theme software displays hierarchically organized T-patterns over a timeline, while a wearable sensor jacket traces movement data in the corner.
assets.player_mission: Design the next-generation methodology for body movement research: integrate multimodal behavior streams through reliable segmentation and patterning, and move measurement into real-life settings with unobtrusive sensors. Defend the research question as the guide to method choice.
key_concepts: Unlike spoken language, body movement does not form a language that is out there waiting to be deciphered, and its meaning or diagnostic value is best described as probabilistic.
The theoretical perspective of probabilistic functionalism accounts for variability in interpersonal perception and was formalized by Brunswik in his lens model of visual perception.

Effective communication requires both encoding and appropriate decoding and, thus, a shared lens code between expressor and perceiver, and mismatches between encoding and decoding can present valuable insights.
With no objective ground truth available in field studies, self-report or observer ratings often provide the best, though likely erroneous, approximation of the encoded variable.
Nonverbal behaviors rarely occur in isolation, and often compounds of behaviors co-occur and are interdependent within and across modalities such as face, voice, and body.
Principal component analyses and cluster analyses allow the detection of co-occurring events grouped as higher order behavior components or clusters.
The transitional probability is a basic statistic for describing sequences, and lag-sequential methods offer a more flexible approach to investigate sequences comprising more than two events.
Magnusson proposed the computer program Theme, which detects T-patterns, hierarchically organized patterns of recurrent behaviors that do not need to immediately follow each other.

Optical motion capture systems are not practical outside of a controlled environment, so the focus needs to be on unobtrusive and lightweight sensors that can be placed directly on the body without requiring cameras.
Accelerometers have become the preferred choice for continuous, unobtrusive, and reliable human movement detection and monitoring.
Fully wireless EMG systems offer less obtrusive ways to measure muscle activation, and wireless EMG systems have been shown useful in the field of affective body expressions.
Methods in proxemics and kinesics are often used together even though they have different historical origins, and the choice of method should be guided by the research question.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Defining Nonverbal Sensitivity and the Earliest Decoding Tests
assets.visual_frame_description: A seminar whiteboard shows three nested circles labeled interpersonal sensitivity, nonverbal sensitivity, and emotional sensitivity, with arrows marked empathy and emotional intelligence feeding into them. Below, a tachistoscope projects a 1/25th of a second facial photograph beside a video monitor displaying a sender's spontaneous facial reaction to an emotion-inducing slide.
assets.player_mission: Play the role of a research methodologist building the conceptual foundation for a new study of emotion decoding. Distinguish nonverbal sensitivity, emotional sensitivity, and interpersonal sensitivity, explain why performance-based measures are considered superior to self-report ones, and trace the earliest decoding tests from the BART to the CARAT.
key_concepts: Nonverbal sensitivity refers to the ability of individuals to read and decode nonverbal cues in others and, importantly, the ability to correctly interpret the meaning of those cues.

Most often, nonverbal cues involve cues of emotion, cues of dominance or status, or cues about attitudes, intentions, and interpersonal orientation such as likes and dislikes and the desire to terminate an interaction.

Emotional sensitivity is the term that is typically used when focusing solely on nonverbal cues of emotion, and nonverbal sensitivity and emotional sensitivity can be seen as subsets of the broader category of interpersonal sensitivity.
Interpersonal sensitivity deals with the ability to read a person's traits, the ability to detect deception, recognition of adherence to social norms, and sensitivity to subtle cues of appearance.

Nonverbal sensitivity is conceptualized as an individual difference variable, and it is assumed to be an important contributor to the concept of empathy, with the ability to read others' emotions critical for empathic understanding.

Nonverbal sensitivity is seen as one of the building blocks of good interpersonal relationships, and sensitivity to nonverbal cues of emotion is viewed as a core component of the construct of emotional intelligence.

The ability to read nonverbal cues, termed identifying emotions, is one of the core components in the abilities model of emotional intelligence, along with abilities to express emotions accurately and to manage emotions.
From a measurement standpoint, performance measures are superior to other methods because there is an objectively correct answer.

The Brief Affect Recognition Test (BART; Ekman & Friesen, 1974) focuses on accurate decoding of six basic emotions (happiness, sadness, fear, surprise, disgust, and anger) presented as very brief photographs shown via a tachistoscope.
Using the BART, Mufson and Nowicki (1991) found a now well-established difference, with women receiving significantly higher scores on emotion recognition than men.

The Communication of Affect Receiving Ability Test (CARAT; Buck, 1976) uses a slide-viewing technique in which videotaped spontaneous facial expressions are shown to individuals who must determine which type of emotion-inducing slide the sender was viewing.
One advantage of the CARAT over the BART is that video clips are used so that the dynamic movement of the face is visible, as opposed to simply using static facial expressions as stimuli.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: The Profile of Nonverbal Sensitivity (PONS) and the MiniPONS
assets.visual_frame_description: A test interface freezes a 2-second clip of the single actress mid-scene, with 11 channel buttons arrayed around it for face only, face and body, body only, electronically filtered audio, and randomized-spliced audio. Beside the screen, a scatterplot of PONS scores against patient satisfaction ratings updates with each answered item, while a stats panel shows a Kuder-Richardson Formula 20 value of .86.
assets.player_mission: Take the perspective of a researcher who has just adopted the PONS for a large-scale study. Explain how the 220-clip, 11-channel test is structured around four affective quadrants, weigh its documented reliability and predictive validity against its methodological limitations, and decide whether the brief MiniPONS is an acceptable substitute.
key_concepts: The Profile of Nonverbal Sensitivity (PONS; Rosenthal et al., 1979) is one of the most widely researched performance measures of nonverbal sensitivity, and in its full version it contains 220 two-second video or audio-only clips of a single actress expressing various emotional scenarios.

The PONS presents emotions in 11 separate channels: three visual recordings (face only, face and body, or body only) are combined with two manipulated voice/speech recordings in which verbal content is eliminated through electronic filtering or randomized splicing.
A total of 20 different emotionally laden scenes are presented in the PONS, which try to represent four affective quadrants using the dimensions of positivity-negativity and dominance-submissiveness.
The PONS was tested in many different cultures, and accuracy rates were the same across cultures depending on the degree of similarity in terms of modernization.
The PONS has consistently shown that women score on average higher than men, and this difference is consistent across many studies of both the PONS and nonverbal sensitivity in general.
Research on physician-patient communication showed that doctors scoring higher on the PONS had more satisfied patients.

Despite low interitem intercorrelations, the PONS has high internal consistency (Kuder-Richardson Formula 20 of .86), and high scorers had healthier, well-adjusted personalities and were assessed as more interpersonally sensitive by peers and superiors as well as better in their job performance.

Limitations of the PONS are that there is only a single actress represented on the entire test, which limits the ability to assess skill at decoding across senders, and that the actress is posing the emotional scenarios rather than actually involved in emotional interactions with others.

On the positive side, the PONS gives a very detailed assessment of an individual's ability to decode nonverbal cues across channels, and its emotional scenarios are more complicated than the portrayal of basic emotions depicted in the BART and CARAT.
One obvious drawback is the length of the PONS, so brief versions (64 items; 40 items) have been created, but these fail to show good psychometric properties.

The MiniPONS (Banziger et al., 2011) is a short, multichannel version of the PONS that showed a correlation of r = .70 with the full version and correlations ranging from r = .24 to r = .39 with other measures of emotion recognition, but the reduction in test length resulted in lower reliability/internal consistency.
For the MiniPONS, the single-item intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was .02 and the combined-items ICC was .57, while the test-retest correlation was r = .64.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: The DANVA, DANVA2-POS, and JACBART: Decoding Basic Emotions
assets.visual_frame_description: A tablet displays a photo set of child and adult faces with high- and low-intensity portrayals of happiness, anger, sadness, and fear, next to a second screen where a brief emotional expression flashes in the middle of a 1-second presentation of the same sender's neutral face. A radar chart in the corner plots the JACBART's correlations with Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, and Neuroticism.
assets.player_mission: Act as a clinician choosing a brief, well-validated emotion decoding test for work with children and adults. Compare the structure and evidence base of the DANVA, the DANVA2-POS, and the JACBART, and identify the social, personality, and leadership correlates each instrument has documented.
key_concepts: The Diagnostic Analysis of Nonverbal Accuracy (DANVA; Nowicki & Duke, 1994) was designed to assess the nonverbal sensitivity of children, but it was later expanded for use with adults, resulting in the Diagnostic Analysis of Nonverbal Accuracy-2 (DANVA-2).

The DANVA and DANVA-2 consist of three subtests (decoding of facial expressions, postures, and paralanguage) that present a series of photographs of child/adult faces with high- and low-intensity portrayals of the four basic emotions of happiness, anger, sadness, and fear.

Each DANVA subtest uses more than one actor as well as mixed genders, as opposed to the single actress in the PONS, and two additional subtests have audio segments where actors say content-neutral sentences while portraying the four basic emotions.

Nonverbal sensitivity as measured by the DANVA has been used by researchers as a proxy for emotional intelligence, and research on transformational leadership showed that leader emotion recognition ability using the DANVA is positively associated with leader transformational leadership behavior.

Advantages of the DANVA are its relative brevity (48 items; 24 in each of the visual and auditory subtests) and ease of administration, but it suffers from some of the same weaknesses as other measures, such as the use of static facial expressions and the posed nature of the expressions.

The Diagnostic Analysis of Nonverbal Accuracy-2 Posture Test (DANVA2-POS; Pitterman & Nowicki, 2004) measures an individual's ability to identify emotion in human standing and sitting postures, and accuracy scores increased with age and were both internally consistent and reliable over time.

DANVA2-POS accuracy scores were linked to personality traits such as self-esteem, locus of control, social anxiety, and loneliness, were more accurate in participants expected to be more accurate such as dancers, and were shown to be predictive of sports or business performance.

The Japanese and Caucasian Brief Affect Recognition Test (JACBART; Matsumoto et al., 2000) was developed as an improved version of the BART that could be used to explore cross-cultural differences in emotion recognition.

In the JACBART, the emotional expression is presented briefly in the middle of a 1-second presentation of the same sender's neutral facial expression to control for after-images and to allow comparison of the sender's neutral face with the emotional expression.

The JACBART includes the basic emotions of anger, contempt, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise, contains 56 items, and test-takers rate the presence or absence of the seven emotions on 9-point intensity scales or use a forced-choice format.

The JACBART has good internal convergent validity with Cronbach alphas of .40-.85 and a significant test-retest total score of r = .78, and it correlated significantly with Openness and Conscientiousness, positively with Extraversion (r = .47), and negatively with Neuroticism (r = -.45).

Hall and Matsumoto (2004) demonstrated that women are more accurate than men in judging emotional meaning from nonverbal cues using the JACBART, which in terms of limitations focuses only on decoding basic emotions from posed, static expressions.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: CAST, MERT, ERI, and IPT: Context, Multimodality, and Social Intelligence
assets.visual_frame_description: Four browser windows line a wall: the CAST plays a clip from an unscripted news interview, the MERT site shows black-and-white film clips toggling between video-only, audio-only, audio/video, and still-photo channels, the ERI presents Ekman and Friesen photographs on a computer screen with no time limit, and the IPT shows a videotaped interaction followed by a multiple-choice question about the relationship between the interactants.
assets.player_mission: Serve as a consultant assembling a multimodal test battery for a corporate leadership development program. Compare the CAST, MERT, ERI, and IPT on stimulus format, breadth of measured constructs, reliability and validity evidence, and practical feasibility, then recommend which to combine.
key_concepts: The Contextual and Affective Sensitivity Test (CAST; Trimboli & Walker, 1993) was created to overcome many of the perceived shortcomings in existing measures, using clips from unscripted television programs such as news segments and interviews that involve actual interactions and felt emotional states rather than posed expressions.

The CAST contains 32 items: 16 consistent messages where the correct emotion/affect needs to be identified, 8 items with inconsistency in either the verbal or nonverbal cues, and 8 ambiguous messages arranged in two sets of four where additional contextual information is given sequentially.

Trimboli and Walker (1993) stated that the CAST assesses three aspects of nonverbal sensitivity: the ability to identify a feeling or emotion, the ability to attend to the verbal or nonverbal components as appropriate, and the ability to interpret ambiguous information with respect to context.

The Multimodal Emotion Recognition Test (MERT; Banziger et al., 2009) measures the perception of dynamic vocal, facial, and bodily expressions, using 10 actor-portrayed emotions with two variants for each and two different levels of intensity, or arousal.

In the MERT, three film clips illustrate each emotion in four different channels: video only (facial cues), audio only (vocal cues), audio/video (using both facial and vocal cues), and still photographs extracted from the film clips, and the test takes about 45 minutes to administer.

Results of research with the MERT show that emotion recognition is better when emotional cues are present in the voice and face at the same time as opposed to cues from the voice only, though it is suggested that multimodal information does not necessarily lead to better recognition.

The MERT showed test-retest reliability correlations ranging from r = .46 to r = .56 across modes with a correlation of r = .78 for total scores, and construct validity correlations of .22 with the DANVA, .51 with the PONS, and .28 with the Emotion Recognition Index.

The Emotion Recognition Index (ERI; Scherer & Scherer, 2011) is a brief test of emotional decoding skill consisting of two subtests: the Index of Facial Emotion Recognition with 30 items using Ekman and Friesen's Pictures of Facial Affect, and the Index of Vocal Emotion Recognition with 30 items using vocal emotion portrayals from four German professional radio actors.

The ERI facial subscore correlates significantly with the corresponding MERT scores (r = .29) but not with the DANVA (r = .15), and the ERI vocal subscore correlates significantly with the MERT (r = .27) but not with the DANVA or the PONS.

The ERI has been validated with a larger number of managers in international companies, and ERI scores correlate with personality factors such as Extraversion, Need for Social Support, and Emotional Stability.

The Interpersonal Perception Task (IPT; Archer & Costanzo, 1987) takes a much broader approach than other tools, assessing individual differences in the ability to read and decode nonverbal, verbal, and social/situational cues across 30 videotaped scenes of naturally occurring interactions such as telephone calls and interviews after an event.

The IPT assesses ability to decode status and relationship cues, competition, deception, and liking/familiarity; it is psychometrically sound but does not have the high levels of internal consistency found in the emotional decoding measures.

credibility.basis: Peer-reviewed APA handbook synthesizing controlled experiments and established theory across nonverbal communication domains. Claims reflect settled disciplinary knowledge.

assets.topic: Self-Report Measures, Empathic Accuracy, and the Future of Assessment
assets.visual_frame_description: A consultation room wall mounts five documents: the 32-item PDA scale with reverse-coded items, the Social Skills Inventory's Emotional Sensitivity and Social Sensitivity subscales, a flowchart of the empathic accuracy dyadic paradigm with trained coders scoring agreement, a bar graph of lie-truth discrimination hovering just above 50 percent, and a roadmap labeled automated decoding systems.
assets.player_mission: Advise a research team on when self-report instruments can be trusted for nonverbal sensitivity. Review the PDA scale and the SSI, the empathy and emotional contagion measures, the empathic accuracy paradigm, and the deception detection findings, then defend a roadmap for the future of assessment.
key_concepts: The Perceived Decoding Ability (PDA) scale (Zuckerman & Larrance, 1979) was the first attempt to assess nonverbal sensitivity through self-report means, containing 32 items on a 7-point response scale designed to assess decoding skill in both visual and auditory channels.

Initial validation studies of the PDA scale were somewhat discouraging, with only small, often nonsignificant correlations between the PDA scale and performance measures of nonverbal decoding such as the PONS, and the PDA and Perceived Encoding Ability scales have not been used in subsequent research.

The Social Skills Inventory (SSI; Riggio, 1986, 1989) was created to measure basic skills in nonverbal, as well as verbal/social, communication, with the Emotional Sensitivity (ES) subscale assessing skill in decoding emotional and other nonverbal messages in others.

The SSI's Social Sensitivity (SS) subscale assesses verbal listening skill and the ability to decode the subtleties of social situations, including knowledge of social norms and scripts, and it is more closely aligned with some of the decoding skills required in the IPT.

The ES subscale of the SSI correlates significantly with performance measures of nonverbal decoding from the DANVA-2 and from the emotional decoding task of the Multifactor Emotional Intelligence Scale, and there is a positive correlation between the SS subscale and the IPT.

The primary limitation to self-report methodology is whether individuals have insight into their ability to accurately decode nonverbal cues, and an obvious concern is socially desirable responding, as being nonverbally sensitive is typically considered a valued skill, particularly for women.

The Questionnaire Measure of Emotional Empathy (Mehrabian & Epstein, 1972) is a 33-item, self-report scale that measures recognition and responsiveness to emotions in others, and men were consistently found to be less empathic than women.

Emotional contagion occurs when individuals unconsciously attend to others and mimic their emotional and nonverbal behavior, and it is seen as a more primitive form of empathy that is measured by Doherty's (1997) 15-item Emotional Contagion Scale.

Empathic accuracy is everyday mind reading that involves accurately decoding other people's thoughts and feelings, and unlike emotional sensitivity, which involves recognition of nonverbal emotional cues, it involves inferring the specific content of another person's thoughts and feelings.

Meta-analyses of accuracy at detecting deception have found that typical rates of lie-truth discrimination are only slightly more than 50 percent, and professionals such as police officers, judges, customs inspectors, and psychiatrists are no more capable at detecting deception than the average person.

Ekman, O'Sullivan, and colleagues studied a rare group of individuals termed wizards, representing less than 10 percent of the population, who are significantly above chance at detecting deception and do it consistently.
There is a great need for assessment tools that are valid, reliable, and easy to use, and future directions for this line of research include the use of automated decoding systems.
